News.title: 'Doctors said my baby was dead - then he lifted his head'
News.content:
'Doctors said my baby was dead - then he lifted his head'

Clarissa Mansbridge was told she had an hour with little William

View 3 Images Clarissa and William in hospital (Image: Cover Images)

When Clarissa Mansbridge gave birth to her son William three years ago, doctors believed he would not survive the day. Born at just 33 weeks following a placental abruption, William was stillborn and had no heartbeat for 26 minutes before doctors managed to resuscitate him.

‌



Even then, Clarissa's ordeal was only just beginning. Just half an hour after his birth, doctors delivered devastating news.

‌



“The doctor told me: ‘You have an hour with him, you need to call your entire family, every organ has shut down. He needs an MRI, but we are expecting it to show he is globally brain dead’,” said Clarissa, 34.

‌



She waited an agonising 45 minutes for news. But when she eventually held him for the first time, he appeared to lift his head and look straight into her eyes, despite being heavily sedated. "That's what kept me fighting, because I saw that light in his eyes,” Clarissa, from Brisbane, Australia, said.

We've cracked the three simple ways to be happy, WHO tips on avoiding dementia, sleep supplement eases pain, cold and flu tablets don’t work, and can Ozempic prevent cancer? All this and more in our science newsletter

William was diagnosed with severe hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy, a brain injury caused by a lack of oxygen at birth. Although his MRI showed less damage than doctors had expected, the outlook remained bleak.

‌



Clarissa said she was repeatedly warned that if he survived, he may never walk, talk, sit, stand or live independently, and that he would require around-the-clock care for the rest of his life.

View 3 Images Clarissa was worried William would not survive (Image: Cover Images)

At one point he was put into palliative care and at another a doctor warned her to prepare herself for finding him dead in his cot. For weeks, William remained in intensive care before showing signs of improvement and being transferred into high dependency care.

‌



While staying at Ronald McDonald House close to the hospital, Clarissa received repeated calls in the early hours of the morning after William suffered terrifying episodes where his oxygen levels and heart rate plummeted without warning. "I was called at 2.30 in the morning, and they said they had lost him, but they've managed to get him back again,” she said.

The episodes happened over and over again. "His oxygen would go right down from 100 to 30 within seconds... his heart rate would drop down to the 30s. That happened 16 times every two hours, like clockwork."

Eventually William was transferred to a specialist paediatric hospital, where these episodes remarkably stopped. William was discharged in October, two months after he had been born, and the pair went home for the first time. But caring for him alone, single mum Clarissa struggled with fear, anxiety and PTSD.

‌



“I would constantly check his monitor, and zoom in on the baby monitor to see if he's breathing,” she said. “I remember lying in the bath, and I had an iPad up, and it was just watching him 24/7 over the camera. I honestly wanted to just drown at that point.”

But against every prediction, William continued to improve. Today, aged three, he walks, talks, runs and loves construction vehicles and dinosaurs. Apart from some hearing loss, he lives much like any other child.

"Every single day this kid surprises me. Every single day. I am so blessed,” she said. Early on, Clarissa knew she could never return to the demanding entertainment career she had built over 15 years managing celebrities. So, sitting beside William's hospital bed, she had started filling a notebook with ideas for a completely different future.

‌



“In the hours when I couldn’t even touch my own child, I had to think about the future. About money and about what kind of work could sustain us regardless of how complex his needs became,” she said.

View 3 Images Clarissa and William (Image: Cover Images)

“I knew that if I needed to be there for him 24/7 for him, I would need a very flexible working schedule. That’s when I found AI.”

‌



So Clarissa built Mia Andre, an AI-generated influencer built around luxury lifestyle content. She carefully built storylines, locations and experiences that unfolded naturally rather than posting random glamorous images.

The strategy worked. Mia recently finished 2nd in the ‘Oscars of AI’ The Fanvue x OpenArt AI Personality of the Year Awards and today Clarissa earns around 6,000 US dollars a month (£4,500) while working around William's childcare.

While Mia attracts brand attention in her own right, Clarissa said the account had become a portfolio for her wider creative work, with companies commissioning bespoke AI content tailored to their own audiences. But more importantly, she can juggle the work with being a mum.

‌



”My favourite thing is that my phone is no longer glued to my hand,” she said. Now Clarissa is happily juggling her work alongside motherhood and gradually getting rid of the anxiety and fear of those early days.

William’s second birthday, she said, was especially emotional because survival beyond that point had once seemed impossible.

But today, she is reassured by his strength and speed.

Article continues below

"His third birthday just feels like a blessing,” she added. “I can’t wait to see what he does next.”

News.title: NHS 'will collapse' without social care reform, PM tells BBC
News.content:
Andy Burnham has told the BBC "the NHS will collapse" if social care is not reformed but said he could not put a timeline on changes.

In his first major interview since becoming prime minister, Burnham said he would not want to leave office without bringing in "substantial change" to the social care system.

The prime minister also suggested making it harder to claim benefits, saying the country had to get serious about getting the welfare bill down.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has meanwhile written to the prime minister, saying he should rule out tax rises or increased borrowing to fund social care reform.

Burnham told the BBC that if the government did not reform social care, the NHS would "collapse under the weight of trying to care for people who've really not needed to end up in the NHS system".

But pressed on whether he would create a new system before the next election, he said he "couldn't put a timeline on it right here, right now", though he would put "whatever political capital I have into fixing broken social care".

Burnham first proposed a universal system of social care in England in 2009 when he was health secretary under Gordon Brown, and a year later pursued the idea of a compulsory levy to fund it.

One of the options floated by that Labour government was allowing people to defer the payment until after they died, which led to the Tories branding it a "death tax".

Burnham is due to make a speech on adult social care on Wednesday.

The BBC understands the PM will stop short of unveiling plans for a new system in this speech, instead announcing he is speeding up the Casey Commission, an independent review that has been considering possible solutions for social care.

Baroness Louise Casey is not expected to give her final recommendations until 2028, but Burnham wants to bring her schedule forward.

He told the BBC: "Social care was on a longer path and I have brought it straight forward."

Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home with tasks like washing and cleaning.

Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than Â£23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.

Sarah Woolnough, chief executive of healthcare think tank the King's Fund, said the current "punitive system" meant that "quite a lot of people go without care that they need", with one in seven paying in excess of Â£100,000 for social care.

While Burnham has not yet outlined any plans, Woolnough told the BBC Radio 4's Today programme that reforms could range from making social care free at the point of need to placing a cap on the amount people spend.

"The PM has for a long time mooted the idea of a social care system similar to NHS," she said.

"It would be expensive but on the scale of what we spend on other public services - around Â£200bn on the NHS - we are talking for some of these options low billions per year."

Adult social care has proved a complex issue to tackle for successive governments.

Two years ago Sir Keir Starmer was criticised when Labour scrapped plans for an Â£86,000 cap on the amount people in England would spend on social care in their lifetime.

Badenoch wrote in her letter to Burnham that "any solution to the issues around social care must also be fair to those who have made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives".

Layla Moran, the Liberal Democrat MP who chairs the Health and Social Committee, warned against the issue becoming a "political football".

"We do need to discuss where the money is going to come from but also we need to all be putting our political capital into this," she told the Today programme.

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said he was ready to do "whatever I can to find a real and lasting consensus on social care".

He said: "Family carers must be at the heart of any new system, everyone must get the care they need and no one should lose their home as a result."

Reform Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said social care needed fixing but warned the party would fight any proposal for a "universal death tax".

He said: "It's not fair to raid people's life savings and drags hundreds of thousands more families into paying tax when their loved ones pass away."

News.title: Man and woman die after being pulled from sea off Cornish beach
News.content:
A man and a woman have died after getting into trouble in the sea off a popular beach.

The two people were pulled from the water off Fistral Beach in Newquay, Cornwall, at about 21:45 BST on Sunday, about 15 minutes after HM Coastguard said rescue personnel were called.

Devon and Cornwall Police said both were confirmed dead at the scene.

Search and rescue teams from Newquay, Padstow and St Agnes took part in the operation, along with lifeboats from Newquay RNLI and a coastguard helicopter.

News.title: Girlguiding unveils first major redesign of uniform range since 1990
News.content:
Girlguiding has unveiled the first major redesign of its uniform range in more than 30 years, with the aim of allowing its members the "freedom to express themselves".

Under the new, pared-back approach, members will only be required to wear a top from the new range to be considered "in uniform".

The new range has been inspired by feedback from thousands of Guides, Rainbows, Brownies and Rangers that suggested they valued choice and the ability to express their own style.

Girlguiding chief executive Felicity Oswald said "practicality, comfort and sustainability" were at the centre of the redesign, which is the first overhaul of all sections' uniforms since 1990.

The organisation said the uniform combines the charity's heritage with modern colours and prints.

The range is made up of 30 items of clothing, 15 accessories and neckerchiefs - with prices starting at Â£12 for a T-shirt.

Design features include hidden pockets in waist bands, thumb holes and badge sashes which double as cross-body bags.

"It's really comfortable," Isy, 12, who is in the Guides, told BBC Breakfast. "It doesn't feel like the old ones and it's practical to move in."

Poppy, a seven-year-old Brownie, said she wanted "loads of pockets, because I always lose badges, so I wanted somewhere to put them".

She also showed off the new Brownies gilet, which doubles as a pillow. "It has another secret pocket," Poppy added.

News.title: UK's most parched regions miss chance for rain ahead of next heatwave
News.content:
Some of the driest regions of the UK have missed their chances for rain ahead of another heatwave beginning this week.

Parts of the northern and western UK saw some rainfall over the weekend, with further showers and unsettled conditions expected over the next few days.

But southern parts of the country - where the least amount of rain has fallen - are set to see temperatures climb once again, with more dry and sunny weather in the forecast.

It comes as parts of Wales have officially entered drought status, while parts of southern, central and eastern England remain in "prolonged dry weather", the final stage before drought is declared.

The coming days will only exacerbate dry conditions as another heatwave is expected to be declared, with temperatures peaking around 35C (95F) in south-east England.

In advance of the high temperatures, heat health alerts have been issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

The south-west, south-east, London, East of England, West and East Midlands and Yorkshire and The Humber are all under the alerts from 9:00 BST on Tuesday 28 July until 9:00 BST on Friday 31 July.

The UKHSA warns that heat is expected to cause minor impacts for health and social care services, with an increased risk to life for vulnerable people.

News.title: Three dead and several injured in shooting at food festival near Seattle's Space Needle
News.content:
Three people have been killed and several others injured following a shooting at a food festival near the Space Needle in Seattle on Sunday, the city fire department said.

Mayor Katie Wilson said one suspect was taken into custody following the incident at the Seattle Centre, which had been hosting the annual Bite of Seattle food festival across the weekend when the shots were fired at around 18:00 local time.

A second suspect fled the scene and is yet to be apprehended, assistant chief of Seattle Police Tyrone Davis added. He said it is believed the suspects were shooting at each other.

Two deaths were confirmed at the scene, with one person dying later in hospital. Those injured include a two-year-old boy, officials said.

Videos shared online showed people taking shelter inside the city's iconic Space Needle.

People could be seen crouched on the ground, taking cover behind pillars and shelves of merchandise in the Space Needle's lobby during the shooting.

The Seattle Police Department said an investigation remains ongoing and urged the public to avoid the area.

Wilson said in a statement that she wanted to "thank the Seattle police officers who responded to the scene and took a suspect into custody".

She had originally announced two suspects had been taken into custody before updating her statement later on Sunday evening.

Four of the injured were taken to hospital in a stable condition, while a fifth chose not to, the fire department said.

News.title: Trump paused attacks on Iran to make space for talks, US ambassador says
News.content:
President Donald Trump has paused attacks on Iran for the second night in a row to give diplomacy more time, the US ambassador to the UN said.

Speaking to Fox News on Sunday, ambassador Mike Waltz said the president was "giving talks some space, he's giving it a little bit of room".

An Iranian army spokesperson said on Sunday that Tehran had halted "retaliatory" attacks in the region in response. The pause follows nearly two weeks of daily US strikes and tit-for-tat attacks, effectively unravelling the ceasefire struck in June.

Oil prices have dropped sharply in the wake of the pause, opening at $91per barrel on Monday morning after hitting $100 for the first time since May last week.

Asked whether Trump had decided against escalation for now, Waltz told NBC: "I wouldn't go that far at all. The president is keeping all options on the table."

Waltz also rejected reports in the New York Times, external that administration officials had warned expanding hostilities could dangerously drain a diminished stockpile of air defence munitions.

"The US military... has everything that it needs to conduct this campaign as effectively as it needs to be," he said.

As of Sunday evening, Trump had not spoken publicly on the latest developments, but earlier posted computer-generated images on his Truth Social account that depicted US military planes bombing Iranian ships and Kharg island.

Meanwhile, Iran and Oman held several rounds of technical talks in Tehran on Friday and Saturday to discuss management of the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei.

Disputes over control of the strait reignited US-Iran tensions earlier this month and it remains a major block to permanently ending the war.

Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding in June to halt military operations and reopen the strait, as well as to reach an agreement to end the war over the following 60 days.

But after Iranian forces attacked tankers in the Strait of Hormuz on 13 July, the US resumed airstrikes on the country and reinstated its naval blockade on Iranian ports.

Iran retaliated with attacks on US military facilities and bases across the Middle East, killing four American soldiers. The US strikes have since killed dozens of people, according to Iran's health ministry.

In the UK, new Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said he would meet his US counterpart Pete Hegseth in the coming week to discuss the strait, which is one of the world's key transport routes for oil, liquid natural gas and other essential commodities.

"When it comes to securing maritime freedom and free commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, that's where we are absolutely aligned," Streeting told the BBC.

Last week, oil prices hit $100 a barrel for the first time since May, as the renewed fighting stoked fears over global energy supplies.

As the war nears its fifth month, it remains largely unpopular in the US, with a new poll from CBS/YouGov suggesting 57% of Americans are frustrated about the conflict and only 19% optimistic.

Thousands of people have been killed across the Middle East since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February, official figures show, with the vast majority coming from Iran and Lebanon.

President Trump is set to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the White House on Tuesday.

News.title: Luke Littler wins Matchplay and smashes records
News.content:
Luke Littler defended his World Matchplay title in sensational style - and smashed Phil Taylor's tournament and final average records in the process.

The 19-year-old beat seventh seed Gerwyn Price 18-9 in Blackpool to become just the fourth person to win back-to-back Matchplay titles.

World number one Littler finished the week with an average of 111.04, beating Taylor's record of 106.31 in 2010.

He averaged 111.53 in the final, setting a new record as he bettered Taylor's 111.23 against Adrian Lewis in 2013.

Littler claimed Â£225,000 in prize money for winning the event and now has Â£3,143,500 over the PDC's two-year order of merit. That is Â£2.13m more than Luke Humphries in second spot.

"It's been a crazy week, one of the best weeks of my life with the darts I've played," Littler told Sky Sports.

"It's been tough. The stats may look like it's easy, but when you're on this stage with how hot it is, it's not easy."

Price averaged 104.97 in the final and has enjoyed a successful week, climbing to fourth in the order of merit and reclaiming the Welsh number one spot from Jonny Clayton.

News.title: Would you choose £50,000 over the chance of £1m?
News.content:
You have the choice of instantly receiving Â£50,000 or flipping a coin for a 50/50 chance of Â£1m.

Which would you choose?

The vast majority decide on taking the Â£50k, according to a survey of thousands of people by YouGov. Women voted 82% in favour of the guaranteed cash.

The poll has sparked a debate about why Brits appear more risk-averse than people in the US.

So why are the results so clear-cut, and what are the financial and psychological factors at play?

Sadly, there is little chance of ever having such a choice, but there are some interesting lessons for how we manage our money nonetheless.

News.title: Laura Kuenssberg: Our exclusive behind-the-scenes access at No 10 as Andy Burnham became PM
News.content:
Listening carefully during our interview, it seemed Burnham had distinct gears. He was fluent and passionate on his familiar ground: his desire to sort out social care, his track record in Manchester, his desire to run a government that feels relevant and effective where you live, local leaders eager to make many more decisions and able to spend taxpayers' money more freely without permission from Whitehall.

Those are his core beliefs, arguments he's made hundreds, if not thousands of times.

But when it comes to how he'll apply what he thinks in principle to what he does in practice, that was not always so clear. On social care for example, he's long believed there ought to be a National Care Service, like the NHS. But in a speech on Wednesday, that's not likely to be what he unveils.

Instead, he told me he'd "brought it straight forward", understood to mean speeding up the government review by Baroness Louise Casey of what ought to be done, not saying, "here's the plan".

When it came to questions that are on his desk for the first time, there was a contradiction. Burnham told us all many times that he will stick to the manifesto the country voted for in 2024.

But he's also vowed his arrival in office will usher in the biggest change in four decades. You don't have to be a student of political history to find a mismatch there - he's going to stick broadly to Sir Keir's plan, yet shift the government more fundamentally than leaving the EU, or the financial crash? Really?

And beyond the rhetorical tension in several areas, Burnham gave clear indications that he will apply "new eyes". Will he stick to the home secretary's plans to make migrants wait 10 years or more before they can permanently stay in the UK? He's looking at that again he told me, and hinted that care workers could possibly be exempt.

News.title: Funeral boss who lied about burying dad has shown no remorse, daughter says
News.content:
A woman whose dead father was discovered at an undertaker's three months after his funeral says her hellish ordeal has "crucified" her.

The body of Peter Moody, 65, was found by police alongside 34 others and more than 100 sets of ashes at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull in March 2024. One of the bodies had been there for a year.

Former funeral director Robert Bush, 48, of Otley, West Yorkshire, will appear at Hull Crown Court later for sentencing. He previously admitted 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial.

Peter Moody's daughter Joanne Moody, 48, who is expected to join other families wronged by Bush in the court's public gallery, said: "It's broke me, it's crucified me. He has shown no remorse. No sympathy."

News.title: 'Antisemitism felt relentless' - Jewish students on life at UK universities
News.content:
Like many campuses across the UK, Cardiff University has seen pro-Palestine protests in recent years and Oliver said he believed some behaviour he witnessed crossed the line from criticism of Israel into antisemitism.

Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is a form of antisemitism, according to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance.

"That first year was absolutely terrifying," he said.

"You go home and think, 'do I carry on? Do I try to go to the next day?'"

Oliver said he stopped speaking Hebrew outside his home, and hid his Star of David pendant when on campus.

Over the following three years, Oliver said the antisemitic abuse he experienced at university became "relentless".

"I've been in clubs [or] just wandering around the uni and you hear these conversations and you see pamphlets being handed around where it's literally saying that your belief and your history is fake," he said.

"I've been at house parties where, when someone's found out I'm Jewish they started calling me Netanyahu behind my back.

"Like you found out my religion and you've decided I'm a bad person."

Oliver said when he had reported antisemitic incidents that had happened to him and others, he had felt they had been often "swept under the rug" by the university.

Although he said some positive action had been taken, he feels more needs to be done.

Cardiff University said it was sorry that "any student felt unsafe" on campus and that it adopts a "zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination of all kinds".

It said there was no place for antisemitism or hatred at the university and they have "robust procedures" in place for investigating allegations of antisemitism. Where it is found, the university said appropriate action would be taken.

It said it had reached out to the university's Jewish Society and reminded students to report incidents to them.

News.title: Jaxon, 5, praised for calling 999 for injured mum
News.content:
When five-year-old Jaxon's mum fell down the stairs, hitting her head and falling unconscious, he knew exactly what to do.

At home in Dudley with his three-year-old brother, he called 999 and asked for help. His mum, Stacey, had begun vomiting and had slurred speech after waking up.

Able to give out his address, officers who were first on the scene climbed over the back gate and started giving Stacey first aid, with paramedics arriving soon after.

Now, Jaxon has been awarded a chief constable's young person's award for his courage and bravery.

He was presented with the award by Deputy Chief Constable Jen Mattinson, at West Midlands Police's awards evening earlier in July.

Jaxon was also surprised at home by the Stourbridge Neighbourhood Team - who presented him with a bike his parents had bought him as a reward for getting his mum medical help.

News.title: 'I fear for wee families' - home heating oil in NI jumps £100 in three weeks
News.content:
The price of home heating oil has risen again after a period of respite.

Consumer Council for Northern Ireland (CCNI) figures show that in just three weeks the average cost of 500 litres of home heating oil has jumped from Â£346.59 to Â£445.37 â an increase of Â£98.78 (29%).

The organisation's Raymond Gormley said the price rise was in response to the recent escalation in fighting between the US and Iran. On Sunday President Donald Trump paused attacks on Iran for the second night in a row.

About two thirds of Northern Ireland households use home heating oil, by far the highest of any UK region.

Home heating oil prices peaked at Â£612.37 for 500 litres on average in April and had dropped to a low of Â£346.59 for the same amount earlier this month.

The most recent CCNI figures, external, published on 23 July, show 300 litres of home heating oil costing an average Â£276.23 â up from Â£216.44 on 2 July.

A delivery of 900 litres had an average cost of Â£789.07 â an increase of Â£173.84 since 2 July.

News.title: Beach tragedy family backs calls for safety review
News.content:
In a statement released on Monday, he said the family, from Barking, London, had been "devastated by the loss of our beloved relatives".

"We wish to thank the members of the local community who responded to our calls for help for their extraordinary efforts.

"Several local residents and visitors to the beach that day showed exceptional courage, kindness and selflessness as they rushed to assist my family members who were struggling in the water", he added.

"Their actions embodied the very best of humanity, and our family will always be grateful for the bravery they showed in our hour of need.

"Additionally, we would like to express our sincere gratitude to the emergency services, air ambulance crews and coastguard personnel who responded to the incident, as well as the medical staff who continue to assist my son."

Ahmed added: "I strongly agree with the calls from local residents for a review of safety measures at West Mersea beach, including the provision of additional life-saving equipment and clear warning signage.

"While no action now can undo the pain we are suffering, we hope lessons can be learned to help prevent similar tragedies from happening in the future."

News.title: Water returns to Gatwick Airport after major outage
News.content:
Gatwick Airport says its water supply has returned after passengers faced long queues for toilets and closed restaurants and bars after a major supply outage.

Both terminals at the UK's second busiest airport lost running water on Sunday morning after a power failure at a treatment works that serves the area.

People told the BBC of confusion and frustration as all bars and restaurants were shut, some were left with nowhere to sit and waits built up outside toilets.

SES Water, the company that supplies the airport, said earlier the power outage was fixed, with Gatwick reporting on Sunday night that water had returned to "the vast majority of the London Gatwick campus".

The water company, which also supplies parts of Kent, Surrey and south London, said complications caused by a power outage at Bough Beech treatment works meant some customers had experienced low water pressure or a temporary loss of supply.

A spokesperson had earlier confirmed that Gatwick Airport was affected.

On Sunday afternoon, SES Water said its treatment works were back up and running, but later added it would take time for the network to fully return to normal as it had been "a highly unusual and complex issue".

"We want to reiterate that our teams are working as quickly as they possibly can and we are grateful for everyone's patience," the spokesperson added.

Gatwick apologised and said staff had been handing out bottled water.

A spokesperson added: "Our staff are on hand to support passengers and provide assistance where needed, some restaurant partners have opened to provide additional seating."

Gatwick said additional teams had been deployed across both terminals to support passengers.

The airport added there had been no flight cancellations as a result of the supply issues and that it was working closely with SES Water to minimise the impact.

"Our teams are working hard to reopen toilets and other facilities as quickly and safely as possible," a spokesperson said.

News.title: Four people including baby die after car crash
News.content:
Four people, including a baby, have died after a car crashed into trees on a busy dual carriageway in Derby.

Emergency services were called after a red Hyundai car left the A38 and crashed into trees - between the A50 Toyota Island and the A516 - at about 23:00 BST on Saturday.

Derbyshire Police said the passengers, two women, 18 and 30, and a man, 36, died at the scene. The baby girl was taken to hospital where she died shortly after. The force said all were from Leeds.

The driver, a 33-year-old man, was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving. He was subsequently taken to hospital for serious injuries.

The victim's relatives have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers, police said.

"Our thoughts are with them at this most distressing time," a spokesperson said.

In a statement, Derbyshire Fire and Rescue Service said three crews attended the scene following a 999 call to its control room.

The fire service added: "Our thoughts are with everyone impacted by this terrible incident, the deceased and all of the emergency services who responded to the scene."

The carriageway was closed for several hours while emergency services dealt with the crash, but it has since been reopened.

Anyone who witnessed the crash or has any dashcam footage has been urged to contact police.

News.title: I took a sleeper train to Hamburg and discovered the most exciting way to travel
News.content:

I love travelling by train: no depressing airports, no hidden luggage charges and much more legroom. But it’s not just the practical stuff. There’s also the sense of freedom, possibility and immersion you only get on the rails, letting the journey become part of the holiday, not a hurdle to cross before you get there. All of which means that I’m a sucker for a sleeper train.

Many of Europe’s classic sleeper routes were axed during the 2010s and the pandemic. But in the last few years, there’s been talk of a night train renaissance: new routes, new operators and a dawning sense that a way of getting from A to B previously considered passé might just be the future of travel.

Although state railway bureaucracy doesn’t make it easy, the map of sleeper trains across Europe keeps expanding. And now there’s a new link that makes it simpler to travel flight-free from the UK to one of the great cities of northern Europe: Hamburg.

open image in gallery A new, direct overnight service from Brussels to Hamburg has just been launched by European Sleeper ( European Sleeper )

Germany’s second-biggest city, with a population significantly larger than Birmingham, Hamburg has centuries of seafaring history – and some legendary nightlife in the old sailor-town of St Pauli. I’ve wanted to visit for years, but getting there without flying involved a whole day of train-hopping, with multiple changes. Until now.

A new, direct overnight service from Brussels to Hamburg has just been launched by European Sleeper, a plucky, independent Dutch-Belgian rail company. It runs three times a week, with just one easy change of trains between London and Hamburg. This means you can leave London in the afternoon and arrive in Hamburg early the next morning, doing much of your travelling while you’re asleep. I didn’t need any more persuading to hop aboard the first ever eastbound voyage of the “Good Night Train” to Germany’s northern metropolis.

Starting in London, the first step is Eurostar, ever the gateway to European adventures. I’m always amazed at how short the cross-channel journey is. One minute you’re gazing over the industrial estates of the Thames Estuary, the next you’re surrounded by the redbrick houses and bulbous water towers of Belgium’s capital.

Brussels is in the midst of overturning its drab reputation with a new wave of genuinely cool cultural openings, such as the upcoming Kanal offshoot of Paris’s Pompidou Centre. Unfortunately, there isn’t time to gallery-hop – I’ve got just a couple of hours for a veggie couscous at a North African friterie and a stroll around the multicultural Marolles neighbourhood, before it’s time to hop the overnight train to Germany.

No “arrive two hours early for your flight” here: I rock up to the platform five minutes before the train pulls in. There’s a buzz among the waiting passengers that you never get at an airport gate. We’ve all chosen the adventurous over the obvious, and there’s a real sense of community among the student backpackers, young families, hip-looking groups of friends and solo travellers of all ages.

The train pulls in; there’s a shuffle on the platform and some polite, multilingual squeezing-past in the train corridors as everyone hops aboard and finds where they’ll be sleeping for the night. Across its ten carriages, this train can carry nearly 400 passengers – roughly two planes’ worth.

I’m booked into a couchette cabin: the classic sleeper train set-up, with five fairly basic bunks accessed via a ladder. I’ve booked the very top bunk, which is harder to climb up to, but darker, more private and with better storage space. My return ticket cost around €230 (£195), plus the price of the Eurostar. Yes, it’s more expensive than a budget flight, but a bit of a bargain once you realise you’re saving on two nights’ accommodation.

open image in gallery James stayed in a couchette cabin, but there are a range of sleeper options ( James Manning )



There are also more luxurious cabin with proper beds and duvets, sleeping up to three people (and with the option to book out the whole room for just one or two travellers). At the opposite end of the scale is the budget carriage where you kip in your seat, populated mostly by the aforementioned student backpackers.

My couchette cabin is full of different nationalities: French, Belgian, German, me. There are night-train veterans like Charles, from Toulouse. He’s on his way from Paris to Berlin, as part of an Interrail adventure that’ll take him via the Baltics all the way to Narvik, Europe’s most northerly rail station outside Russia, high up in Norway’s Arctic Circle. Then there are first-timers, like Malte, a Hamburger on his way home from Paris. He thought he’d give the sleeper train a try, and is surprised to hear that a week ago, this journey wouldn’t even have been possible.

We’re moving. The sun sets and the Belgian countryside whips by outside. After a final evening stop at Liege’s soaring Guillemins station, it’s lights off.

It is worth clarifying at this point that the European Sleeper’s “Good Night Train” is not the Orient Express. Finding suitable carriages is one of the biggest challenges for any company wanting to launch night train routes, and the train I’m riding is decidedly retro. The corridors are dotted with lights and dials that look something from a Cold War submarine, and the toilets are prone to getting blocked (hence the repeated reminders to not flush paper towels). The air conditioning leaves a lot to be desired, though it’s a blast (literally) to rattle along with the carriage window open. There’s a sort of Wes Anderson charm to the old-school atmosphere, but it’s best not to expect luxury.

open image in gallery Hamburg is Europe’s third biggest port ( Getty/iStock )

Still, I get a surprisingly decent night’s rest, woken only sporadically by metallic clanks and the rattle of other trains passing. The swaying of the train is mostly soothing – so much so that I’m woken a few times by a sudden stillness as we pull into a siding.

But I soon drift off again, and when I next wake, I get an almost magical surprise. It’s 6am, the cabin is light and the train has come to rest at Platform 5 of Hamburg Harburg station. I grab my bags, trying not to wake my fellow passengers (most of whom are still dozing, bound for Berlin), and hop down into a brand new city.

After coffee at the Elbgold roastery and a morning dip and shower at the stunning, neo-gothic Kaifubad pool complex, I spend a colourful day running around Hamburg. I climb a former Nazi bunker that’s recently been converted into a panoramic roof garden. I wander the buzzy, graffiti-decked streets of Schanzenviertel and Karolinenviertel and the peaceful paths of the Planten un Blomen botanical garden. I eat superbly: Austrian dumplings at Marend, pizza alla Norma at vibey Tazzi, and a pastel de nata in the Portuguese Quarter that could have come fresh from Lisbon.

As befits a port city (Europe’s third largest, in fact), Hamburg is an open-minded place with a thriving counterculture. The skull-and-crossbones symbol of anti-fascist football heroes FC St Pauli is everywhere, and venues like the anarchist art squat Rote Flora, the art-filled micro-neighbourhood Gängeviertel and the punk record shop Fischkopp provide a support system for the kind of alternative, creative communities that are increasingly being squeezed out of British cities.

open image in gallery The transformed Second World War bunker in the heart of the city ( Getty Images / iStockPhoto )



St Pauli’s red-light district (where The Beatles famously honed their rock ’n’ roll chops) and its waterfront are undeniably pretty touristy. But perhaps the biggest surprise: I hardly overhear anyone speaking English all day.

Could that change? Hamburg is ripe for discovery by UK travellers: it’s a creative, vibrant city with a distinctive northern character that’s very different from what you’ll find in Berlin or Munich.

And for train fans, there’s one extra draw: Hamburg is a vital link to the north. From here, direct trains (including sleepers) run all the way to Copenhagen, Stockholm and Malmo. From 2028, that list will also include Oslo and Gothenburg.

So the new European Sleeper link doesn’t just make it much simpler to get from London to an underrated city-break destination – it also unlocks a whole world of flight-free Scandinavian adventures. Who needs planes, anyway?

How to do it

Take a Eurostar from London St Pancras to Brussels-Midi (from £39 one-way), then a European Sleeper to Hamburg (from £25 one-way for a seat, or £60 for a couchette). Total travel time is from 12 hours.

Where to stay

If you’re not boarding the sleeper train straight home again, check in to Side Design Hotel Hamburg. It’s halfway between the city centre and hip Schanzenviertel, with easy U-Bahn connections across the city, and has a pool, sauna and hot tub – plus a sleek roof terrace. Rooms cost from £160 a night.

James travelled as a guest of Eurostar

Federal wildlife authorities are investigating after a viral video appeared to show a man repeatedly kicking a federally protected sea lion as it tried to flee along a Southern California beach.

The footage, which authorities say was filmed at La Jolla Cove in San Diego, shows a man throwing multiple kicks at the sea lion while another person can be heard laughing in the background. The animal scrambles away as the man follows it before the video cuts off.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration confirmed its Office of Law Enforcement has opened an investigation.

open image in gallery Sea lions on the beach in the La Jolla neighborhood of San Diego, California ( Reuters )

"NOAA Fisheries’ Office of Law Enforcement is investigating reports of a video on social media that shows an interaction between an individual and sea lion, allegedly in La Jolla Cove," the agency said. "In the video, the individual appears to be kicking the sea lion. This is an ongoing investigation, and we cannot provide further details at this time."

The person shown in the video has not been publicly identified.

Sea lions are protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, which makes it illegal to harass, harm, pursue, capture or injure marine mammals. Violations can carry fines or jail time. NOAA advises people to stay at least 50 feet away from sea lions, seals and other protected species.

open image in gallery San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria condemned the incident, calling it "a disgusting act of animal cruelty” ( Copyright 2023 The Associated Press. All rights reserved )

San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria condemned the incident, calling it "a disgusting act of animal cruelty." He said he had directed local law enforcement to review the footage while acknowledging the federal investigation.

NOAA urged anyone who witnesses potential violations of the Marine Mammal Protection Act to report them immediately, saying investigations are most effective when detailed information is provided.

The video has sparked widespread outrage online and drawn condemnation from animal welfare groups, including PETA.

"Assault is ASSAULT, no matter the species," PETA said in a statement. "This abuser laughed while harassing and kicking a sea lion who was desperately trying to escape. Thanks to everyone who reported it; the case is now under investigation. Leave animals ALONE, and always speak up when you witness abuse."

Despite reports that the San Diego Police Department was involved, police said they were not notified when the incident occurred. Lt. Cesar Jimenez said the case was reported to California Fish and Game, which referred it to NOAA for investigation.

President Donald Trump posted about everything from time travel to the Iran war in his latest bizarre Truth Social posting spree.

In a series of late night posts using A.I. images, Trump shared a fake movie poster showing himself saving George Washington at Mount Rushmore, a mocked up image of a border wall with Canada and various hints he might run again in 2028.

“The past was about to change,” the imagined “Trump x Washington” film’s tagline reads. “History was about to be saved.”

Trump’s social media spree also saw him sharing an A.I. generated poster for a sci-fi movie called“Cosmic Commander”​, using a symbol similar to the insignia in Star Trek.

open image in gallery President Trump shared a slew of Truth Social posts on Sunday night, including an A.I.-generated movie poster depicting time travel and former President George Washington ( @realDonaldTrump/Truth Social )

The main theme of his posts, though, was the U.S.’s war with Iran, which has seen hostilities increasing between the two countries in recent weeks.

One post showed U.S. fighter planes unleashing their fire on Kharg Island, a key oil terminal in the Strait of Hormuz. ​

Another showed the president looming large in the sky, while military jets soared across the country. Explosions can be seen rocking an area marked as “Iran,” while a caption reads: “Guardians of the World.”

open image in gallery Trump also shared an image of explosions rocking Iran while he loomed over the country ( @realDonaldTrump/Truth Social )

Trump sported a hat reading “FAFO” in one A.I.-generated image, while at the helm of a boat manned by military personnel.

​The posts were uploaded on the same day that Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the U.N., told Fox News Sunday that strikes on Iran had been paused as Trump was “giving talks some space.”​

Another presidential bid by Trump was the focus of several other posts, with the commander-in-chief sharing an image of himself smoking a cigar and sporting a hat reading “TRUMP 2028.” A gigantic “TRUMP 2028” mug was featured in one post, surrounded by a ring of people screaming at the sky. ​

open image in gallery Trump also shared an AI-generated image of himself sporting an 'FAFO' hat ( @realDonaldTrump/Truth Social )

The wide-ranging social media blitz also saw Trump airing old grievances, as he took swipes at Canada and CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins. ​

One image showed an “air filter barrier” spanning the U.S.-Canada border, seemingly referencing his complaints about wildfire smoke from the latter country blowing over to the former. ​The upload echoed his infamous border wall that became a central pillar of his 2016 presidential pitch.

Despite his complaints about Canada’s air quality, the image shows bright, blue skies with some cloud on both sides of the barrier. ​

open image in gallery The president shared an AI-generated image of a wall dividing Canada and the US during his Truth Social blitz ( @realDonaldTrump/Truth Social )

Kaitlan Collins was the subject of a post referencing a long-running MAGA talking point - a Budweiser promotion starring transgender social media personality Dylan Mulvaney. ​

The image showed Collins’s face being placed onto Mulvaney’s body, as she appeared in the 2023 campaign. ​

Trump had complained about both Mulvaney’s partnership with the beer brand and Collins during his poorly-received speech at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner on Friday.

Limiting the time you eat to a nine-hour window and avoiding eating four hours before bed could reduce the risk of dementia, a new clinical trial has suggested.

A pilot study looking at older women who were overweight or obese found that cognitive skills were improved for those who restricted the hours in which they ate compared with those that didn’t.

The findings were part of a weight-loss programme and suggest that it’s not just weight loss that can ward off age-related cognitive decline, but restricting the times in which you eat, Sue Shapses, professor of Rutgers University and the study’s principle investigator revealed.

“Losing weight alone will ward off some of the aging-related cognitive decline, and these data suggest that there may be additional benefits if you stop eating 4 hours prior to going to sleep and reduce food intake to 8-9 hours per day, compared to the usual eating window of 12 hours per day,” she said.

Professor Shapses’ findings are set to be presented at NUTRITION 2026, the annual meeting of the American Society for Nutrition, outside Washington DC, on Monday.

The trial enrolled 47 women between the ages of 50 and 79 who were overweight or obese. All participants were counseled to reduce their calorie intake by 500 calories per day, and 26 were asked to restrict their eating to a window of less than nine hours per day, while the rest maintained a typical eating window of about 12 hours per day.

The clinical trial looked at 47 women between the ages of 50 and 79 ( Getty Images )

In the time-restricted eating group, participants generally ate only between 10am and 6pm, with an average daily eating window of 8.2 hours, compared to 12.3 hours per day on average among those asked to maintain the standard eating window.

After six months, participants lost about 15 lbs (6.8kg) on average across the groups. But those who consumed food within the eight and nine hour window, compared to those who maintained a 12-hour eating window, were better at spatial planning and problem-solving tests at the end of the weight-loss programme.

They also experienced fewer errors on memory and learning tests, but there was no significant difference in performance on multitasking or reaction time tests.

Professor Shapses explained: "There was a modest effect of time-restricted eating to improve spatial planning and problem-solving and on reducing errors related to memory and learning.

"These outcomes suggest a better ability to remember information during everyday tasks and reducing mistakes related to memory, attention and problem-solving. Reductions in the eating window predicted greater improvements."

Further studies would be needed to confirm the findings as part of a larger group of participants, researchers said. They also hope to investigate why time-restricted eating might have these benefits, such as how it interacts with circadian rhythm, nutrient-sensing pathways, inflammation and metabolic health.

There are currently an estimated 982,000 people living with dementia in the UK, according to Alzheimer’s Society, a figure that is expected to rise to 1.4 million by 2040.

Actor Ryan Reynolds made a surprise appearance as his iconic character Deadpool at San Diego Comic Con, as he asked Robert Downey Jr for a role in the new Avengers: Doomsday.

In character and sporting a darker Deadpool suit, the 49-year-old emerged from the crowd, asking for a role in the upcoming Marvel film.

He was swiftly informed by Robert Downey Jr, who stars as Doctor Doom, that it had already been filmed.

Reynolds quipped: "This seems an awfully expensive way to announce a film. When do you start filming?"

Downey Jr, surrounded by the rest of the cast on stage, retorted: "It’s in the can bro, look around you, did you bump your head?"

Reynolds pressed further: "I see, so there’s no additional photography, overages, hot costs, maybe last-minute additions? Happy Hogan, fetch the Audi we’re leaving."

open image in gallery Ryan Reynolds in Deadpool cosplay speaks from the audience during the Marvel Studios Panel at 2026 San Diego Comic-Con ( Getty )

The actor then dropped the microphone and left the San Diego venue’s Hall H.

Despite Deadpool not being listed to appear in the upcoming film, there have been a number of rumours that Reynolds’ character will have a role.

Marvel fans got a better look at the forthcoming superhero film when an extended trailer premiered at Comic-Con in San Diego on Saturday (25 July), following the release of an “underwhelming” first clip last week.

The directors and cast took over the venue, including Doctor Doom star Robert Downey Jr and Chris Evans who is reprising his role as Captain America after a seven-year absence.

All eyes, however, were on the new footage, which begins with Downey Jr’s Von Doom sitting on a throne as voiceover from Vanessa Kirby’s Sue Storm explains: “Victor was always the smartest guy in the room. He used to be different.

“He used to be kind. He used to be caring… Everything he loved was taken from him. I knew he was lost, and I did not realise that he was broken.”

open image in gallery Actor Ryan Reynolds asked for a role in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday before Robert Downey Jr, who stars as Doctor Doom, told him it had already been filmed ( Getty )

As reported by Variety, the trailer leans into the film’s massive crossover appeal with fleeting scenes of characters across the MCU: Thor (Chris Hemsworth), Captain America (Chris Evans), Black Panther (Letitia Wright), Shang-Chi (Simu Liu), Loki (Tom Hiddleston), Cyclops (James Marsden), Magneto (Ian McKellen), Gambit (Channing Tatum) and more.

Following a shot of New York City reduced to rubble, Mr Fantastic questions whether Doom is responsible. The trailer then cuts to Doom’s chilling line: “All of you have lived stolen lives. You refuse to give them back,” offering viewers a taste of Downey Jr’s Eastern European accent in the role.

Fans also got a glimpse of Doom’s army of Sentinel robots, the androids from the X-Men movies, which he unleashes upon Thor in the trailer.

The trailer for Avengers: Doomsday was released on Monday showing Downey Jr, who played Iron Man in 10 previous Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) films, as Doctor Doom.

The film is a sequel to 2019’s Avengers: Endgame and is the 39th movie in the MCU.

open image in gallery Anthony Mackie, Danny Ramirez, Robert Downey Jr. and Pedro Pascal speak onstage during the Marvel Studios Panel at 2026 San Diego ( Getty )

Marvel’s synopsis for the film reads: “Universes collide and the Multiverse Saga begins its final chapter in Marvel Studios’ Avengers: Doomsday.

“Beloved heroes from three distinct universes will be set on a deadly collision course and ultimately face an existential threat unlike anything they’ve ever encountered.

“This epic film will lay the foundation for the future of the Marvel Cinematic Universe.”

Avengers: Doomsday will be released in cinemas on 18 December.

A notorious superbug that causes hospital-acquired infections has lately been spreading from pets to humans, Chinese scientists warn in a new study.

The bacterium Acinetobacter baumannii is one of the pathogens labelled “Priority 1” by the World Health Organisation, meaning it poses the greatest threat to human health and has developed a high level of resistance to antibiotics.

It causes conditions like meningitis and pneumonia in humans, and has been shown to cause similar symptoms – such as pneumonia, respiratory and urinary tract infections – in pet dogs, cats, and horses.

Animals that are known to suffer from A. baumannii infections include horses, cats,dogs, sheep, minks, and falcons.

Now, scientists have assessed which varieties of this bacterium infecting animals pose the most danger to humans.

In the study, researchers assessed genetic data on over 500 A. baumannii samples collected from animals in 17 countries, spanning 33 species, including white storks from Poland, as well as cats, dogs, and horses in veterinary clinics across Europe.

They also analysed samples of the bacterium from humans across the same regions.

open image in gallery A picture taken on February 12, 2023 shows Bobi, a 30 year-old Portuguese dog that has been declared the world's oldest dog by Guinness World Records, next to his cat friend ( AFP via Getty Images )

Scientists found that A. baumannii from animals can be divided into two groups of varying risk to humans.

One is a low-risk group dominated by hosts such as livestock, poultry, and wildlife.

But there is also a high antimicrobial resistance (AMR) group dominated by hosts such as horses, cats, and dogs, the study warns.

The variant of the superbug from cats, dogs, and horses is genetically almost indistinguishable from those infecting people in hospitals nearby, researchers found.

Genome similarity between strains in humans and pets was almost 99 per cent, and in some cases even over 99.5 percent, they said.

"Our study suggests that A. baumannii has a higher potential of intertransmission between companion animals and humans compared to livestock, poultry, and wildlife," scientists wrote in the study published in the journal Applied and Environmental Microbiology.

"This elevated potential may be related to the close contact of companion animals with humans,” they wrote.

open image in gallery Highly magnified cluster of Acinetobacter baumannii bacteria ( Public Health Image Library )

Strains of the superbug in pets carried two genes that make it resistant to carbapenem antibiotics, which are the last-resort drugs that doctors reach for when nothing else works.

Scientists hope to conduct more species-specific sampling of pathogenic bacteria to better understand the risk posed by superbugs from pets and other companion animals.

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Arsenal prepare record-breaking Vinicius Jr offer, Liverpool learn Bradley Barcola price, Yan Diomande nears move
News.content:
Arsenal are plotting an audacious move for Real Madrid superstar Vinicius Jr and want to sign the Brazil winger this summer. The Premier League champions are preparing to offer the 26-year-old the biggest contract in their history but have yet to make contact with Real Madrid over the move, who has just one more year on his contract, while incoming boss at the Bernabeu, Jose Mourinho, would need to sanction the transfer.

It could be a busy few weeks for Mikel Arteta’s side as they also look to sign Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes and add another centre-back, with England internationals Ezri Konsa and John Stones both of interest. Newcastle manager Eddie Howe confirmed that he wants to keep Guimaraes, but added that his future at the club is out of his control.

Elsewhere, Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola has set out his targets for the transfer window and has confirmed the Reds “definitely need to sign a winger”, while France international Bradley Barcola is reportedly open to leaving Paris Saint-Germain this summer. PSG, who are set to miss out on the signing Yan Diomande to Real Madrid, would demand a record fee, however.

Manchester United are still interested in adding another midfielder and have “reached an agreement in principle” with France international Manu Kone, according to reports in Italy. Aurelien Tchouameni remains a target, too.

People searching for a property could save significant money by looking next door to pricey postcodes, according to a new study.

Lloyds Bank compared higher-value postcodes in different parts of the UK with what it found to be the least costly neighbouring postcodes sitting right next to them.

According to Lloyds’ analysis, homes in these neighbouring areas cost 28 per cent less on average, but in many places the gap is significantly wider.

In the North East of England, Lloyds found that in the postcode of NE26, encompassing the seaside town of Whitley Bay, the average price was £304,022.

Next door in NE24, which takes in the town of Blyth, the average price of a home was £162,075 – £141,947 or 47 per cent less than in neighbouring NE26.

open image in gallery The sun rises over a lobster fishing boat near Whitley Bay, Northumberland ( PA )

Amanda Bryden, head of mortgages at Lloyds, said: “It’s easy to focus on the ‘must-have’ locations when you’re searching for a home, but this research highlights just how much value can sit right next door. Of course, neighbouring areas aren’t always directly comparable and each will have its own distinctive character, housing stock and local appeal.

“But in many parts of the country, looking just beyond the most sought-after postcodes can reveal more affordable options while still keeping buyers close to jobs, transport links, amenities and the communities that matter to them.

“For first-time buyers in particular, a small shift in location could make a big difference – not just in getting on the ladder, but in what kind of property is within reach.”

Lloyds said that in London, NW3 is among the city’s most expensive postcodes, covering locations such as Hampstead and Belsize Park. The average house price there was £778,767.

But in neighbouring NW2, including areas such as Cricklewood and Dollis Hill, the average house price was £546,348, buyers here could pay £232,419 less compared to neighbouring NW3 – a saving of around 30 per cent.

In Scotland, the EH3 postcode, covering central Edinburgh, including the West End, had an average house price of £374,650.

Neighbouring EH11, covering areas such as Gorgie and Stenhouse, had an average house price of £299,315 – a potential saving of £75,335 or 20 per cent compared with the EH3 postcode.

In Wales, the average house price in CF64, which covers Penarth, Dinas Powys and Sully, had an average house price of £342,753.

Just next door, CF63, which covers Barry, including Cadoxton and Barry Docks, the average house price was £260,234 – £82,519 less.

open image in gallery An array of To Let and For Sale signs protrude from houses in the Selly Oak area of Birmingham ( Getty )

In Northern Ireland, the BT4 postcode covering East Belfast had an average house price of £278,143.

In nearby BT16, the average house price was £247,068 – £31,075 less compared with BT4.

The analysis was based on the same mortgage approval data used to calculate the long-running Lloyds house price index. House price figures relate to sales completed in 2025.

For London, prime central locations were excluded from the research due to being small, highly localised areas.

News.title: Lando Norris comes in from the cold with dominant Hungarian GP victory
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for the 2026 Hungarian Grand Prix from the Hungaroring. This is the 40th anniversary of the race at this track and the 41st edition. I think over the years this track has had a bit of an unfair reputation but we have certainly had some interesting and exciting races over the years. Even over the last few years.

The nature of the track means it is a bit of an outlier. And that means you often get results that go away from the norm of the season. Mercedes took a couple of poles here in the ground-effect era whilst Charles Leclerc did so last year. We have had a handful of first-time winners at this track, too: Damon Hill, Fernando Alonso, Esteban Ocon, Jenson Button and… errr Heikki Kovalainen.

So far that has been true this weekend. Although McLaren and Ferrari have been closing in on Mercedes, the SIlver Arrows have usually had the edge or found it when it comes to qualifying. That was not the case yesterday: Lando Norris took the first non-Mercedes grand prix pole of the season, pipping the Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton by just 0.012sec.

Hamilton, though, takes a three-place grid penalty for impeding Oscar Piastri in Q3. Kimi Antonelli, who had qualified fourth, takes the same penalty for not slowing sufficiently under yellow flags. It was Ferrari who had been expected to be the team to beat but they were the team that dropped the ball. In fairness Norris, in the upgraded McLaren had looked competitive throughout qualifying and was simply able to deliver when Ferrari could not.

The grid is slightly mixed up because of the penalties. George Russell’s season did not get any easier after qualifying seventh but he at least moves up because of those grid drops. The Mercedes’ race pace is expected to be strong but will it be enough to put them into contention with the McLarens and the Ferraris? And let’s not forget Max Verstappen in fourth, either…

We find out at 2pm BST, when the race gets under way.

News.title: Anthony Joshua knocks out Kristian Prenga after worst round of his career
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Anthony Joshua’s heavyweight clash with Kristian Prenga, taking place in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.

The kingdom plays host to yet another major boxing event, and this is the second part of a weekend that serves as a build-up to a potentially huge match-up later this year.

Prenga’s 20 wins have come against pedestrian opposition, and if he wins tonight then it would be such an upset as to probably finish Joshua’s career as a real name in the sport.

Joshua, the former unified champion, has plenty of defeats to his name. Oleksandr Usyk, twice, as well as Daniel Dubois and Andy Ruiz Jnr.

Tonight should show us where he is. After his loss to Dubois in 2024 he did not fight again until December 2025, when he rearranged Jake Paul’s ability first to stand up, and second, to chew.

A win for Joshua tonight means that all eyes turn to the end of the year, when he is expected to finally meet Tyson Fury in the ring to settle their rivalry.

Now both are deposed champions, the interest has waned a tad, but it remains the biggest all-British clash that anybody could conceive.

Fury, for his part, had little trouble against Mariusz Wach last night, the 46-year-old journeyman who he fought in Thailand. While that was not broadcast live, the clips online hardly suggested it was a classic, but it was enough to keep Fury active as he maintained his focus and avoided his own banana skin.

Joshua now needs to show that he is capable of finishing a fight. If he struggles, he invites pressure for the next four or five months in the build-up to meeting Fury.

News.title: Adam Ramsay-Peaty breaks down in tears after settling for bronze
News.content:
Afterwards, Ramsay-Peaty, whose alleged dispute with his own family became a major distraction during his marriage earlier this year, was visibly emotional as he criticised the media which he insisted had written “rubbish” about his personal life.

“I know the s--- I’ve been through, which is no fault of my own, to be honest,” said Ramsay-Peaty, who lost his 100m breaststroke crown two years ago at the Paris Olympics. “But it does take a toll. The choices I’ve made over the last few months have been hard ones. But I’m happy at the same time that I can get here. I didn’t quit in Paris, but I deserve more.”

He added: “You don’t know who I am and people who comment, people who see the story because you read a headline, they’ve got to look themselves in the mirror,” Ramsay-Peaty told a group of reporters.

“You can’t hurt me. For me, it’s about my family and that does come at a cost. Being able to ignore that and being able to focus on my job – that hasn’t played a part in a sense of what we’re experiencing today.

“I’m still happy with that result. There’s some sense, but it has to, it has to stop. You know, look how many, how many athletes, how many people have to go for this until the media learn [a] lesson?”

Referencing Nowacki, the 18-year-old sensation from Jersey who has long been regarded as Ramsay-Peaty’s breaststroke successor, he added; “You have to learn and do better. You know, and for me, you know, I don’t want a young Filip one day to go through something like that, or these younger athletes.

“For me, that’s part of what I have to go through. I’ve got no control over that. But I think enough is enough. This is away from sport – it’s just about being decent people.”

After receiving his bronze medal, Ramsay-Peaty approached his wife, with whom he is expecting a child in December, and kissed her baby bump.

News.title: Lewis Hamilton hit with penalty in blow to Hungarian GP hopes
News.content:
Lewis Hamilton’s hopes of significantly denting Kimi Antonelli’s championship lead were dealt a blow after he was given a three-place grid penalty for Sunday’s Hungarian Grand Prix.

Hamilton looked to be the man to beat heading into qualifying at the Hungaroring and was on course for a record 10th pole position here before a messy final few minutes cost him.

Ferrari were well placed to end Mercedes’s run of having taken pole position for every grand prix this season. Instead, defending champion Lando Norris snuck in and took a superb pole for McLaren with a lap of 1min 17.207sec.

A poor final lap from Hamilton was compounded by a grid penalty for impeding the McLaren of Oscar Piastri, meaning the seven-time world champion will start fifth for the race at one of his most favoured circuits. The only consolation was that Antonelli was also given a three-place grid penalty for not slowing sufficiently under yellow flags. The Italian will start seventh while Charles Leclerc, Hamilton’s team-mate, will be alongside Norris on the front row.

Heading into the final runs in Q3, Hamilton was 0.101sec ahead of Norris, but did not improve his time. Yet Norris, who was fastest in Q1 and Q2, and was the last of the top three across the line in Q3, had no problem, beating Hamilton’s time by 0.012sec.

Hamilton was critical of his Ferrari team for sending him out first, a decision he said “shocked” him.

“I don’t know why we went first, that was a bit of a shock to me and I definitely wouldn’t have chosen to go first,” Hamilton said. “I had a clean out-lap and when I started my lap and already in turn one I had a snap [of oversteer], I was already a tenth down. The last lap was the worst lap of all... we clearly had the car to be on pole.”

Worse was on the way for Hamilton. The stewards later confirmed the three-place grid penalty to add to the disappointment of missing out on pole.

Replays showed a frustrated Piastri gesturing to Hamilton for blocking him at turn one, ruining the Australian’s final flying lap. Hamilton said he was unaware that Piastri was there, which was proved by video evidence that showed how much he impeded the McLaren. It would have been an easy decision for the stewards to make.

News.title: ‘Always in bloom, a visit really makes one’s day’: Your favourite garden centres
News.content:
Bryan, 86, from the South East, has been a customer of Henry Street Garden Centre in Arborfield, Berkshire for decades: “My wife and I often used to browse and purchase plants and garden furniture.”

But his favourite memory was watching his wife’s “delight at their incredible Christmas displays of decorations. Lights, live reindeer even and the wonderful family atmosphere all around you,” he describes. “It’s still a magical place for me where I can get close to her memory.”

For Mary, 79, from the South East, “a garden centre is special if the plants are in season and healthy and there is great choice of both plants and compost”. She nominates family-run Grovewell Garden Centres at Swingfield near Folkestone, which has three other branches based in Kent.

Not only are their plants “always beautifully displayed”, she explains, they have “an amazing choice of garden supplies, cards and gifts, as well as a nice little coffee shop”. Her favourite memory, however, was at Christmas time a few years ago. “They have a couple of beautiful, nodding and interacting reindeer with a sofa in front of them. We were admiring them and an older guy on the staff asked if we wanted a photo taken, which was so sweet of him.”

“He took my husband’s phone and got a really happy little snap of us and the reindeer, which our girls thought was hilarious,” she says. “Service with a smile.”

Community spirit

News.title: Guimaraes will not force Newcastle exit like Isak, says Howe
News.content:
Newcastle will welcome Liverpool, with whom Keegan enjoyed success in the 1970s, to St James’ Park for their Premier League opener, and the two sides are in talks over a suitable pre-match tribute. Flowers, messages and mementos have been laid outside Newcastle’s ground since Keegan’s death on Monday, including a heartfelt message penned by fellow club legend Alan Shearer, which read: “I hope you realised how much you meant, to me, to this club, to everyone. Thank you does not seem enough. Rest In Peace Boss. Alan Shearer.”

With regards to the football, there is an acceptance among Newcastle supporters that, having finished 12th in the Premier League last season and lost Anthony Gordon, Kieran Trippier and Sandro Tonali, this is a summer of transition. The uncertainty surrounding the future of £100m-rated club captain Bruno Guimarães, who is on the radar of Arsenal, will be a concern; Newcastle will be keen to avoid a repeat of the furore that circled Alexander Isak’s departure last summer. Guimarães will join the team next week following his World Cup exploits with Brazil and is expected to take part in Newcastle’s La Manga training camp, which starts on July 31.

Summer signings Sean Steur and Ewen Jaouen were each handed 45 minutes in the behind-closed-doors victory over Darlington, during which Howe used different XIs for the two halves. Bazoumana Touré – the £50m winger acquired from Hoffenheim – is expected to feature today having returned from his post-World Cup holiday. Yesterday Newcastle announced the arrival of midfielder Aladji Bamba, the France youth international, from Monaco and he was immediately integrated into team training. There is every possibility that he will feature this afternoon. Gateshead this week announced two signings of their own, as Luke Supyk, the New Zealand Under-20 forward, agreed a two-year deal having scored three goals in pre-season as a trialist. Defender Jack Robinson also joined the club.

Kick-off is at 12.30pm.

News.title: How to choose a sports bra, with advice from a netball player, bra fitter and scientist
News.content:
How do you tell if a sports bra is the wrong size?

One of the biggest mistakes shoppers make is assuming that if a sports bra feels tight, that’s enough. In reality, support comes from the right fit rather than simply compressing your chest.

Cardwell advises thoroughly testing a sports bra by moving in it in the same way as you will during the sport you will be doing. “Your breasts don’t just move up and down,” she says. “They move all around – circles, up, down, left, right. We want to try and restrict that as much as possible, but not to the extreme where you’re not able to breathe.”

What is a high impact sports bra?

High-impact sports bras are designed for activities where your breasts experience the greatest movement, such as running, HIIT, tennis and netball. Their job is to minimise breast movement in every direction, helping reduce discomfort while allowing you to move more efficiently.

To measure how high-impact a sports bra is, Wakefield-Scurr asks women to run in a laboratory, both without a bra and while wearing different sports bras. “For a bra to be classed as high support, it has to reduce breast movement above certain thresholds,” she says. “If your breasts move 10 centimetres without a bra and five centimetres in a sports bra, that bra has reduced breast movement by 50 per cent.”

In the lab, Wakefield-Scurr and her team found that “if you run in low support compared with high support, you reduce your stride length by four centimetres. Four centimetres might not sound like a lot, but over the course of a marathon, those four centimetres add up to around a mile.” This proves that wearing a high-support bra doesn’t just keep you comfortable, but it can improve your athletic performance.

Cardwell, who wears a double G cup, says high-impact support has improved dramatically in recent years. “There has been a lot more research into high-impact sports bras, especially for larger-chested women.” She also warns against assuming that every sports bra offers the same level of support. “If it’s the same material as a smaller cup size, it’s probably not going to be sufficient for someone like me with double Gs.”

How often should you replace your sports bra?

There’s no set rule for replacing a sports bra, according to Wakefield-Scurr. This is because its lifespan depends more on how you care for it than how often you wear it. “The lifespan of a sports bra is affected more by how you wash and dry it than by how often you wear it,” she says. In one of her team’s studies, support dropped by around a third after 25 washes. “Always follow the washing instructions,” she advises. “You’d be surprised how many sports bras should be hand washed or washed at a lower temperature.”

Looking after your sports bra properly will help it last longer, but no bra lasts forever. Once the underband loses its elasticity or the support noticeably decreases, it’s time to replace it to ensure you have the right level of support.

Sports.title: ‘Not sorry at all’ – Spain’s Dani Olmo claims Argentina coach ‘not telling truth’ about punch after World Cup final
Sports.content:
DANI OLMO has snubbed Roberto Ayala’s apology after being struck by the Argentina coach at the World Cup.

Ayala thrusting a hand towards Olmo’s throat was just one part of the melee that followed the final in New Jersey.



The right-handed jab appeared to come from absolutely nowhere as players and staff from both sides clashed after Spain‘s 1-0 win in extra-time.

Ayala, 53, claimed it was in response to Olmo mouthing off.



He said: “Obviously, I’m sorry. Because of my position, I can’t allow a feeling, or what I might receive from the other party, to change my mood and my actions.

“It was more of a push than anything else, it wasn’t a punch like they’re saying.



“It was a reaction to something he said, but that’s it. If I see him, I’ll obviously apologise to him in person.

“My intention was to go and separate them. Sometimes things happen and emotions run high, but that’s no excuse. And given my position, my behaviour has to be different.”

Olmo, though, is having none of it – and the Spain midfielder rubbished Ayala’s excuse.

He told Diari de Terrassa: “Someone who confesses to being sorry but justifies a punch by claiming it was a response to ‘a saying’ is someone who probably isn’t sorry at all.

“He’s not telling the truth, because I didn’t say anything to him, so I don’t need him to apologise.

“What really defines us isn’t the mistake, but the courage to own up to it.”

Fifa have been investigating the post-match tussle at the MetLife Stadium, which also saw Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes strike Gavi while he was on the ground.

The South Americans drew criticism for their behaviour at the World Cup, with Fifa also looking into the team celebrating with a Falklands banner after beating England in the semi-finals.
