Key Facts —The order. TSE president Kássio Nunes Marques gave 48 hours for a response on the use of official government channels for promotion. —Who must reply. The order names President Lula, the Brasil da Esperança coalition and Social Communication Secretary Sidônio Palmeira. —The complaint. The action was filed by the Liberal Party (PL), which flagged around 1,000 allegedly irregular posts on the government’s Canal Gov accounts on Instagram and X. —The programs. Posts cited include Gás do Povo, Pé-de-Meia installments, family-agriculture investment and the delivery of federal institute campuses. —The rule. Electoral law bars institutional advertising in the three months before an election, with limited exceptions.

Brazil’s top electoral court has given President Lula’s government 48 hours to explain its use of official government channels to promote federal programs on social media, after the opposition alleged the posts breach a pre-election advertising ban.

Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court oversees the rules of the 2026 campaign. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Test of the Pre-Election Ad Ban

The order from TSE president Kássio Nunes Marques puts the government’s official communications under scrutiny. Lula, his coalition and the Social Communication Secretariat have 48 hours to justify the posts.

At issue is the line between legitimate public information and prohibited institutional advertising. Brazilian law restricts government promotion in the three months before an election, with narrow exceptions.

What the Opposition Alleges

The case was brought by the Liberal Party, which pointed to roughly 1,000 posts on the government’s Canal Gov profiles on Instagram and X. The PL argues the content amounts to campaign-style promotion during a restricted period.

The flagged posts publicize programs such as Gás do Povo, the Pé-de-Meia student stipend, family-agriculture investment and the opening of federal institute campuses. These are among the government’s signature initiatives.

The Government’s Position

The administration casts the posts as ordinary public communication about programs and public works. The court itself noted that some content resembles preliminary institutional publicity rather than overt electioneering.

The 48-hour window is for the government to make that case formally. The TSE will then weigh whether the posts crossed the legal line.

Why It Matters

The dispute is an early skirmish over the rules governing an incumbent’s advantage heading into 2026. How the TSE rules will shape what governments can publish during the campaign.

For observers, it also signals how aggressively the opposition intends to police the government’s communications. Similar challenges are likely to multiply as the election nears.

Key Facts —The concern. Lawmakers and analysts warn that constrained Central Bank budgets threaten Pix’s security and capacity to innovate. —The alarm. One senator cautioned that “Pix is on the brink,” citing 32 servers handling 245 million daily accesses. —The fix on the table. A constitutional amendment (PEC) would give the Central Bank more freedom to manage its budget and technology spending. —The need. The proposal’s rapporteur argues the bank must invest more in digital security, artificial intelligence and infrastructure. —The delay. The measure’s vote was postponed in the Senate’s constitution committee (CCJ) after a request for further review.

A budget squeeze on Brazil’s Central Bank is raising alarm that Pix, the instant-payment system used by hundreds of millions, lacks the resources to keep scaling securely, fueling a push to give the bank more financial autonomy.

Pix has become the backbone of everyday payments in Brazil. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Payments Success Under Strain

Pix has transformed how Brazilians move money, becoming the default for everyday payments in just a few years. That very success is now the source of concern, as usage races ahead of the infrastructure behind it.

Lawmakers warn that the Central Bank, which runs Pix, lacks the budget flexibility to keep pace. The worry is that security and reliability could suffer if investment does not scale with demand.

The Numbers Behind the Alarm

The scale of the challenge was captured bluntly in the Senate, where one lawmaker warned that Pix is on the brink, pointing to 32 servers handling 245 million daily accesses. Whether or not the figure is precise, it dramatizes the strain.

Rapid growth in transactions demands continuous investment in servers, cybersecurity and fraud prevention. Budget limits, critics argue, put that investment at risk.

The Autonomy Push

The proposed remedy is a constitutional amendment granting the Central Bank greater financial and administrative autonomy. Backers say it would let the bank fund the security, AI and infrastructure that Pix now requires.

The measure’s rapporteur frames it as essential modernization rather than a power grab. Its vote, however, was postponed in the Senate’s constitution and justice committee after a request for more time.

Why It Matters

Pix is now systemic infrastructure for the Brazilian economy, so any threat to its reliability carries broad stakes. Businesses, banks and consumers all depend on it working flawlessly.

For investors and the fintech sector, the debate is a reminder that public digital infrastructure needs sustained funding. How Congress resolves the Central Bank’s autonomy will shape Pix’s next phase.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Pix’s security a concern?

Lawmakers and analysts warn that budget constraints at Brazil’s Central Bank, which runs Pix, threaten the system’s security and capacity to scale, with one senator citing 32 servers for 245 million daily accesses.

What is being proposed to fix it?

A constitutional amendment (PEC) would give the Central Bank more autonomy over its budget and technology investment, so it can fund digital security, AI and infrastructure for Pix.

Has the measure passed?

Not yet. The vote was postponed in the Senate’s constitution and justice committee (CCJ) after a request for further review.

Key Facts —The rupture. Leaders of Brazil’s app delivery workers have publicly broken with the Lula government despite repeated attempts to regulate the sector. —The scale. App-based delivery involves around 1.7 million people, according to the statistics agency IBGE. —The sticking point. A regulation bill stalled in the Chamber of Deputies, with a proposed minimum of R$10 per delivery a central dispute. —The government split. Minister Guilherme Boulos favors a minimum hourly rate, while Labor Minister Luiz Marinho backs a formal-employment (CLT) model. —The grievance. Courier leaders, including activist Paulo Galo, accuse the government of focusing on per-trip pay and pension collection while ignoring broader protections.

Brazil’s app delivery workers have soured on the Lula government, with leaders openly breaking with the administration over a stalled regulation of gig work that has satisfied neither the couriers nor the platforms.

App couriers are a large and increasingly organized political force in Brazil. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Constituency the Government Has Lost

App delivery workers were once seen as a natural constituency for the left. Now their leaders are openly at odds with the Lula government, a striking political fracture.

The rupture comes despite regulation efforts and subsidized credit aimed at the sector, which the IBGE puts at around 1.7 million people. Good intentions have not translated into support.

Why the Regulation Stalled

The central bill has stalled in the Chamber of Deputies, opposed from different directions by companies and by workers themselves. A proposed minimum of R$10 per delivery became a flashpoint.

Couriers argue the debate fixated on per-trip rates and pension (INSS) contributions while sidelining bigger issues. They point to social protection, a real minimum income and working hours as the gaps.

A Divided Government

The administration is not united on how to proceed. Minister Guilherme Boulos backs a minimum hourly rate, while Labor Minister Luiz Marinho favors a formal-employment model based on the CLT labor code.

That internal split has muddied the government’s message to a wary category. Worker leaders, including the activist Paulo Galo, a former ally of Boulos, have turned sharply critical.

Why It Matters

With 1.7 million workers and a loud online presence, couriers are a meaningful political bloc heading into 2026. Their break with the government is a warning sign for a president seeking reelection.

For the platforms, the impasse prolongs regulatory uncertainty over labor costs. For the workers, it leaves core protections unresolved as the political calendar tightens.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are Brazil’s app delivery workers at odds with the Lula government?

Courier leaders say the government’s stalled gig-work regulation focused on per-trip pay and pension contributions while ignoring broader protections, and they have publicly broken with the administration.

What is the sticking point in the regulation?

A bill stalled in the Chamber of Deputies over a proposed minimum of R$10 per delivery, with resistance from both companies and workers.

Is the government united on the issue?

No. Minister Guilherme Boulos favors a minimum hourly rate, while Labor Minister Luiz Marinho backs a formal-employment (CLT) model.

A High-Profile Name in Play

Romeu Zema, the Novo party governor of Minas Gerais, is building a presidential campaign and hunting for a running mate. He has now floated Joaquim Barbosa, the former chief justice of Brazil’s Supreme Court, as a leading option.

Zema pointed to Barbosa’s reputation in the fight against corruption, a theme central to Novo’s brand. A meeting to test the partnership is set for Rio de Janeiro in early August.

Who Joaquim Barbosa Is

Barbosa is best known for presiding over the Supreme Court during the mensalão corruption trial, which made him a national figure. His anti-corruption image gives him cross-party appeal.

Earlier in 2026 he had himself been announced as a presidential pre-candidate by the DC party, only to withdraw citing a lack of conditions. Joining Zema’s ticket would return him to the national stage in a supporting role.

Novo’s Presidential Bid Takes Shape

The Novo party was due to hold its national convention on 27 July, where Zema’s presidential candidacy is expected to be formalized. Choosing a running mate is the next step in assembling a competitive ticket.

Novo positions itself on the free-market, small-government right. A recognizable, anti-corruption running mate could broaden its reach beyond that base.

Why It Matters

The pairing, if it happens, would add another defined option to a crowded field of presidential hopefuls. It also signals how candidates are courting figures with anti-corruption credibility.

For now it remains a possibility rather than a done deal, pending the August talks. The outcome will help clarify the shape of the 2026 field.

Brazil’s PT has chosen party heavyweight Gleisi Hoffmann and veteran Doutor Rosinha as its two Senate candidates in Paraná, a hand-picked ticket that underscores President Lula’s direct role in shaping the 2026 slate.

A Hand-Picked Senate Slate

The PT has settled its Senate strategy in Paraná, naming Gleisi Hoffmann and Doutor Rosinha for the state’s two seats. Party leaders formalized the “pure slate” at a convention.

President Lula’s role was explicit: he chose Gleisi Hoffmann for one of the seats. Her candidacy signals how closely the president is managing the party’s most important tickets.

Two Well-Known Names

Gleisi Hoffmann is among the PT’s most prominent national figures, framing her bid around democracy, national sovereignty and women’s participation in politics. Her profile gives the ticket immediate visibility.

Doutor Rosinha, born Florisvaldo Fier in Rolândia, is a pediatrician and one of the PT’s founders. His long record as councilman, state deputy and federal deputy anchors the slate in the party’s history.

The Wider Paraná Strategy

The PT is contesting Paraná inside the Brasil da Esperança federation, alongside the PV and PCdoB. Rather than run for governor, it has thrown its weight behind Requião Filho of the PDT.

That choice concentrates the party’s firepower on the Senate. It also reflects the reality that Paraná has leaned against the PT in recent statewide votes.

Why It Matters

Senate seats are decisive for governing, shaping whether a future president can pass legislation. Fielding two heavyweight names signals the PT is taking the chamber seriously.

For observers, Lula’s direct involvement in Paraná is a marker of how centrally the 2026 campaign is being run. The state will test whether star candidates can overcome a difficult local map.

Who are the PT’s Senate candidates in Paraná?

The PT officialized Gleisi Hoffmann and Doutor Rosinha (Florisvaldo Fier) as its two Senate candidates in Paraná on 25 July 2026.

What is President Lula’s role?

Lula personally chose Gleisi Hoffmann to run for one of Paraná’s Senate seats, underscoring his direct involvement in the party’s 2026 slate.

Is the PT running for governor in Paraná?

Key Facts —The launch. The PDT officialized Alexandre Kalil’s candidacy for governor of Minas Gerais on 26 July at the state legislature (ALMG). —The party line. National PDT president Carlos Lupi and state chief Mário Heringer led the convention; the ticket has no running mate yet. —The tension. Kalil left the PSD and joined the PDT in October 2025; this is his second run for the state, after finishing second in 2022. —The stakes. Minas Gerais is one of Brazil’s largest electoral prizes and a traditional bellwether.

The PDT has launched former Belo Horizonte mayor Alexandre Kalil as its candidate for governor of Minas Gerais, a move that exposes a rift on the Brazilian left as the party backs Lula nationally while the president favors a rival in the state.

Minas Gerais is one of Brazil’s most electorally decisive states. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Second Run at Minas

Alexandre Kalil, who governed Belo Horizonte as mayor, is trying again for the Minas Gerais statehouse. The PDT formalized his candidacy at the state assembly, though it has yet to name a running mate.

Kalil finished second in the 2022 gubernatorial race. Since then he has switched parties, leaving the PSD for the PDT in October 2025, and is now the Pdetista standard-bearer in the state.

A Rift on the Left

The candidacy lays bare a contradiction. Nationally, the PDT backs President Lula’s reelection, but in Minas, Lula supports the PT’s Patrus Ananias for governor.

That leaves two allied parties on opposite sides of a major state race. How the left resolves the split will shape its competitiveness in a state it cannot afford to cede.

Why Minas Matters

Minas Gerais is second only to São Paulo in voters and has long been a national bellwether. Winning it is often seen as essential to winning Brazil.

A divided left there hands an opening to the opposition. Alliances in Minas are therefore watched closely as a signal for the broader 2026 map.

What to Watch

The immediate questions are who joins Kalil’s ticket and whether the PT and PDT can avoid splitting the left-leaning vote. Negotiations over alliances are still open.

For observers, the Minas contest is an early test of how disciplined Brazil’s governing coalition will be at the state level. The outcome could ripple into the presidential race.

Who is the PDT’s candidate for governor of Minas Gerais?

The PDT officialized former Belo Horizonte mayor Alexandre Kalil as its candidate for governor of Minas Gerais on 26 July 2026.

Why is the candidacy controversial on the left?

The PDT backs Lula nationally, but Lula supports the PT’s Patrus Ananias for governor of Minas, putting two allied parties on opposite sides of the state race.

Has Kalil run for governor before?

Yes. Kalil finished second in the 2022 Minas Gerais gubernatorial race; he later left the PSD and joined the PDT in October 2025.

World.title: Brazil’s Ronaldo Caiado Launches 2026 Presidential Bid
World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Politics · Brazil

Key Facts —The ticket. The PSD officialized Ronaldo Caiado for president on 26 July, with party leader Gilberto Kassab as his running mate. —The convention. The national convention was held in São Paulo, formalizing a “pure slate” made up only of PSD members. —The positioning. Caiado is being pitched as a third way, distinct from President Lula (PT) and the Bolsonaro-aligned right. —The profile. Caiado is a two-term governor of Goiás and a figure of the center-right; Kassab is a veteran power broker who leads the PSD. —The context. The move formalizes one of the first major candidacies as Brazil’s 2026 presidential race takes shape.

Brazil’s PSD has formally launched former Goiás governor Ronaldo Caiado as its candidate for president in 2026, positioning him as a center-right alternative to the widely expected clash between the Lula and Bolsonaro camps.

Brazil’s 2026 presidential race is taking shape in Brasília. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Center-Right Bid Goes Official

The PSD used its national convention in São Paulo to make Ronaldo Caiado its presidential candidate. Party president Gilberto Kassab, one of Brazil’s most experienced political operators, joins the ticket as running mate.

The party opted for a “pure slate,” fielding only its own members rather than building a broad coalition at the outset. That keeps the PSD in control of its own message as the campaign begins.

The Third-Way Pitch

Caiado’s team is presenting him as an alternative to a polarized contest. On one side sits President Lula and the PT; on the other, the Bolsonaro-aligned right led by figures such as Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

Whether a center-right governor can carve out space between those blocs is the central question of his campaign. Third-way bids in Brazil have struggled historically against strong polarization.

Who the Candidates Are

Caiado governed Goiás for two terms and built a reputation on law-and-order and agribusiness-friendly policy. Kassab, a former São Paulo mayor, is known less for the ballot than for assembling alliances behind the scenes.

Together they offer a pragmatic, business-oriented profile. The PSD holds significant weight in Congress and among state governments, giving the ticket an institutional base.

Why It Matters

For investors and observers, an early, credible center-right candidacy adds a variable to a race many assumed would be a Lula-versus-Bolsonaro-camp rematch. It could reshape alliances as other parties decide where to stand.

The launch is a starting gun rather than a finish line, and coalitions will keep shifting until the campaign formally opens. Caiado’s challenge is to convert institutional strength into national voter appeal.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the PSD’s presidential candidate for 2026?

The PSD officialized former Goiás governor Ronaldo Caiado as its 2026 presidential candidate on 26 July, with party leader Gilberto Kassab as his running mate.

What is Caiado’s positioning?

Caiado is being presented as a center-right third way, an alternative to President Lula (PT) and the Bolsonaro-aligned right.

What is a “pure slate”?

It means the ticket is composed only of PSD members, rather than a broad multi-party coalition, at least at this stage of the race.
