World.title: Costa Rica’s President Praises Diablo Capture and Defends Cutting the Courts That Made It
World.content:
President Laura Fernández Delgado has spent the days since Costa Rica’s most significant arrest in a decade making two arguments at once. She has praised the Judicial Investigation Agency for capturing Alejandro Arias Monge, known as Diablo, and she has defended her government’s reduction of the Judiciary’s budget, describing the cut as small and saying it does not touch substantive work. The agency that carried out the operation says otherwise, and on the morning of the raid its director learned of a further reduction he had not expected.

The capture came before dawn on Friday, July 24 surveillance and tracking unit and its tactical response team, known as SERT, moved in alongside prosecutors and exchanged fire with the occupants for roughly 45 to 50 minutes. Five officers were wounded, four of them SERT members.

At first light Arias Monge walked out of the house, sat down against a column and surrendered. He had been a fugitive since October 28, 2016, when he was released from preventive detention as a suspect in two homicides, a period of nine years and nine months. Also detained were Jonathan Pérez Méndez, alias Tan, described by investigators as Arias Monge’s successor, Jorge David Núñez Aguilar, alias Coco Pastilla, and a man identified by the surnames Matarrita Rodríguez, alias Coco Mono. A fourth man, Ríos Oconitrillo, alias Coco Guácimo, was killed by tactical officers at the scene.

Agents seized five high-calibre rifles, including AK-47 pattern weapons, and three pistols. The United States government had offered a $500,000 reward for information leading to Arias Monge’s capture. He was taken to the courts of the First Judicial Circuit of San José and then to the maximum security module at La Reforma prison in Alajuela, where the Ministry of Justice and Peace says he is held in an isolation cell without yard access or visits. He has not been tried on any of the allegations that made him the country’s most wanted man.

Speaking to reporters during a tour of Guanacaste hours after the operation, Fernández congratulated the OIJ, the SERT team and the officers involved, saying she was grateful on behalf of Costa Rica and that credit belonged where credit was due. She described Arias Monge as a high-end criminal and said responsibility now fell to her government to ensure he remained imprisoned. She also said she hoped prosecutors and judges would not fail Costa Ricans and that Diablo would not go free.

According to the president, Arias Monge ended the lives of approximately 100 Costa Ricans during the years he spent as a fugitive. That figure is her characterization and has not been independently established; no court has attributed those deaths to him. Separately, OIJ interim director Michael Soto told reporters that the organizations run by Arias Monge, Ríos Oconitrillo and Pérez Méndez are believed to be connected to some 360 homicides in fights over drug trafficking territory, a count that covers three groups rather than one man.

In the same remarks in which she celebrated the operation, Fernández defended the budget adjustment her government has requested of the Judiciary, saying the reduction is small and does not affect substantive functions. The dispute behind that claim has been running since late June.

Rodrigo Chaves, who holds both the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of the Presidency in her cabinet, asked the Judiciary to cut 5% of its budget for both 2026 and 2027, amounts equal to ₡27,076 million and ₡26,549 million, or roughly $59.8 million and $58.6 million at the Central Bank reference rate. On June 29 the Corte Plena, the full 22-member Supreme Court, agreed to a reduction of ₡13,242 million, about $29.2 million, and rejected the rest.

Of the amount it accepted, ₡8,687 million, some $19.2 million, consisted of funds the Legislative Assembly had already approved in the previous term to create new posts in the OIJ and the Public Ministry, open OIJ sub-delegations in La Cruz and Cabo Velas and establish a police office in Puerto Jiménez. Those funds were written into the Judiciary’s budget but Finance never authorized their execution, and the ministry subsequently removed them from the 2027 draft.

The remaining ₡4,555 million, about $10.1 million, came from exchange rate remainders, procurement processes that drew no bids and rescheduled construction. The Court declined to apply a comparable cut in 2027, saying it would damage the fight against organized crime, access to justice, programs to reduce case backlogs and services for victims.

The operational effect of the current year’s squeeze has narrowed to a specific number. The Judiciary has told the Corte Plena that Finance applied a retention of roughly ₡3,053 million, about $6.7 million, for the remainder of 2026, which the institution calculates as close to 42% of the operating spending it had planned to close out the year.

That category covers per diems, fuel, maintenance, forensic examinations, technology licences, translation, transport, victim services and territorial operations. Soto has said that if the reduction holds, the agency could face serious problems operating before the year ends, with the fuel budget for police units among the first lines affected, and that raids, surveillance and other proceedings central to dismantling criminal organizations would be exposed.

He confirmed the OIJ has already stopped buying firearms for the rest of the year to protect its year-end position, while saying ammunition supplies were adequate. He put the cost of the Riverside case at close to ₡230 million, roughly $508,000, in per diems, hydration, fuel and logistics for 1,500 officers, and a 37-raid operation earlier in the week at about ₡80 million, some $177,000.

Then came Friday. Soto told a press conference that he was informed that morning, in the middle of the operation, that a further ₡5,731 million, about $12.7 million, would not be transferred. The money is provided for under norma 10 of article 7 of the 2026 national budget law, which directs that savings from public sector posts left vacant in the first half of the year be split equally between the OIJ and the Ministry of Public Security.

Soto said the agency has traditionally received those funds at year end and used them for per diems, fuel, spare parts, bulletproof vests, pistols, helmets, scientific supplies and infrastructure, and that during the Diablo operation some officers positioned to the rear did not have protective helmets. He addressed Chaves directly, asking the minister to help with the norma 10 money.

Attorney General Carlo Díaz said the Public Ministry would keep working with what little it has. Orlando Aguirre, president of the Judiciary, said the institution cannot move funds between line items on its own initiative without risking irregularities, and that legislative approval is required to shift resources between programs.

Fernández responded to Soto at her first Council of Government session in Nicoya. She said she would believe him if the Judiciary did not have money set aside at Banco de Costa Rica, that the public no longer accepts the argument and that his statements were not acceptable to her, questioning judicial salaries and budget management. She also questioned how long Arias Monge had spent as a fugitive.

The 2027 request has not been settled and may not be the government’s to settle alone. Rodrigo Campos, the Judiciary’s legal director, has argued that a modification of this kind must be submitted to the Supreme Court under article 167 of the Constitution, and that if the Court finds the measure affects the organization or functioning of the Judiciary, the Legislative Assembly needs a two-thirds majority, or 38 of 84 votes, to approve it.

Judiciary planning director Allan Pow Hing and executive director Ana Eugenia Romero have said a ₡26,549 million cut in 2027 would mean closing judicial offices and contravention courts, largely because of building rent and utilities, pausing infrastructure projects and creating obstacles for criminal investigations and police operations. Roughly 80% of the Judiciary’s budget goes to payroll, which leaves the operating remainder carrying the full weight of any percentage reduction.

What sits unresolved is not the arithmetic but the argument. The government has presented a decade-long manhunt ending in a rented house in Sarapiquí as evidence that the justice system is capable of delivering results within its means. The people who ran that operation have presented the same morning as evidence of the opposite, describing officers without helmets and a fuel line they expect to strain before December. Whichever reading prevails will shape what the OIJ can put in the field next year, and the answer will arrive in the Legislative Assembly rather than in either side’s press conference.

World.title: Costa Rica Investigated Possible Drug Money Inside Soccer Club
World.content:
Costa Rican investigators examined whether money from an alleged international cocaine-trafficking organization was invested in Puerto Golfito F.C., a former second-division soccer club based in the country’s Southern Zone. The allegations form part of the Distrito organized-crime case, which is scheduled to go to trial on August 3.

The proceedings are expected to continue through late 2027, as prosecutors present telephone recordings, surveillance reports, photographs and extensive financial records. One of the main defendants is businessman Rehan Fraile Pérez, known as “Rey.” Investigators allege that Fraile received money connected to the criminal organization and moved it into businesses and sports projects, including Puerto Golfito F.C. and a soccer training operation called Premier Academy CR.

Fraile is accused alongside Hilary Walker Fowlker, known as “Hilario,” whom investigators identified as the suspected leader of the organization. A confidential Judicial Investigation Agency report included in the case file says Fraile maintained relationships with Puerto Golfito players and officials. Some of those individuals were suspected of having links to the alleged trafficking network, although the accusations have not been proven in court.

Investigators also documented meetings in Golfito and San José between Fraile and a club official identified by the surname Barquero and the nickname “Ceviche.” Undercover officers reportedly saw Fraile repeatedly at Fortunato Atencio Stadium, where Puerto Golfito played its home matches.

The investigation also recorded several trips by Walker to Costa Rica’s Southern Zone to meet Fraile. Prosecutors contend that these contacts formed part of a broader effort to move and disguise money generated by cocaine trafficking. The criminal case also examines Premier Academy CR. Investigators allege that former judicial employee Steven Mesén Bolaños acted as an intermediary between Fraile and Walker, helping arrange meetings, transfer money and handle matters connected to the academy.

Authorities say Mesén also collected two foreign visitors from Juan Santamaría International Airport and took them to facilities associated with the soccer project. During an August 2022 search of a gym linked to Fraile, investigators seized documents involving Puerto Golfito’s debts, academy employment contracts, accounting books and administrative records. Those materials are expected to be examined during the trial.

Prosecutors allege that the wider trafficking organization obtained cocaine along Costa Rica’s Pacific and Caribbean coasts before moving it into the Central Valley. The drugs were then allegedly shipped to the United States and Europe inside contaminated cargo containers and modified machinery.

The case has been linked to the seizure of 1,263 kilograms (2,784 pounds) of cocaine in Belgium and another 1,200 kilograms (2,646 pounds) in England. Costa Rican authorities also discovered vehicles with hidden compartments containing 33 kilograms (73 pounds) and 269 kilograms (593 pounds) of cocaine.

Puerto Golfito F.C. later became involved in a separate controversy over match-fixing. In March 2024, Costa Rica’s soccer federation banned the club and three senior officials from all federated soccer activities for 10 years. The officials sanctioned were club president Roy Telles Campos, majority shareholder Deivis Antonio Barquero and sporting director Arturo Alberoni Palma Fallas. The disciplinary proceeding began after suspicious betting activity was identified and reviewed through soccer integrity monitoring systems.

That disciplinary ruling was administrative and separate from the Distrito criminal case. However, the criminal file reportedly includes communications between Barquero and individuals accused in the trafficking investigation. The upcoming trial will determine whether prosecutors can prove that Fraile and the other defendants participated in the alleged trafficking organization and whether soccer projects were used to conceal or legitimize illegal profits.

The claims against Fraile, Walker and the other defendants remain allegations. None of the accusations involving the financing of Puerto Golfito F.C. has been proven in court.

World.title: Costa Rica Officials Clash Over Detention of Alias “Diablo’s” Daughter
World.content:
Costa Rican security officials have given conflicting accounts of whether the daughter of alleged crime boss Alejandro Arias Monge, alias “Diablo,” was formally detained after police intercepted her outside La Reforma prison. The woman, identified by authorities by the surnames Arias Fonseca, was stopped Saturday near the prison’s main entrance in San Rafael de Alajuela. She was carrying a firearm and traveling in a fully armored Toyota Prado, according to officials.



An initial account described the intervention as a detention carried out by the Directorate of Intelligence and National Security, known as the DIS, in coordination with the Fuerza Pública and the Penitentiary Police. A later account from the Public Security Ministry said Arias Fonseca was identified and removed from the area but was not detained because she held a valid permit to carry a firearm. The ministry said she was subsequently allowed to leave.

The ministry has not clarified whether officers briefly held her while checking her identity and documents, formally placed her under arrest and then released her, or simply stopped and questioned her at the security perimeter. Security Minister Gerald Campos said the woman was carrying a firearm and permits and was traveling in a completely armored vehicle. He also suggested that additional weapons could exist, but authorities did not announce that any other firearms were found inside the Prado.

Campos said authorities will continue checking people and vehicles and watching for unusual movement around La Reforma. The prison has been under heightened security since Arias Monge and another suspected criminal leader, Jonathan Pérez Méndez, alias “Tan,” were transferred there.

The firearm permit appears to explain why the woman was allowed to leave despite the unusual circumstances surrounding the stop. The Costa Rica’s Arms and Explosives Law requires anyone carrying a firearm to have a permit. Regulations allow an authorized person to carry a loaded, legally permitted weapon in populated areas for personal protection.

Carrying a permitted firearm without a valid license can result in two to four years in prison. When the firearm is properly permitted and the person has a valid carry license, however, possession of the weapon by itself does not establish a crime. Authorities have not said whether the firearm was temporarily seized during the document check, whether its registration was verified or whether it was returned to Arias Fonseca. They also did not report any legal problem involving the armored vehicle.

Police could still order her to leave the immediate prison perimeter as part of the security controls without arresting her or filing criminal charges. Arias Monge was captured Friday, July 24, in Sarapiquí after nearly a decade as one of Costa Rica’s most wanted fugitives. The operation included a prolonged gunfight that left eight Judicial Investigation Agency officers injured.

He and Pérez Méndez are being held under strict security measures at La Reforma while the criminal proceedings against them move forward. For now, the status of Saturday’s intervention remains unresolved. Public Security’s most recent account indicates Arias Fonseca was legally carrying the firearm and was released after being identified, while other official descriptions characterized the same encounter as a detention.

World.title: Latin American Players to Watch at the 2026 Cincinnati Open
World.content:
Latin America will send one of its deepest groups of men’s players in recent years to the 2026 Cincinnati Open, led by established Argentine contender Francisco Cerúndolo, Brazilian star João Fonseca and Peru’s rapidly rising Ignacio Buse. The combined ATP and WTA 1000 tournament will hold qualifying rounds on August 11 and 12 at the Lindner Family Tennis Center in Mason, Ohio. The expanded 96-player main draws begin August 13, with the singles finals scheduled for August 23.

The tournament field includes players from Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Peru and Paraguay. Several will arrive with realistic hopes of advancing beyond the opening rounds rather than simply adding regional representation to a field headed by the world’s leading players.

Fonseca is likely to attract the most attention. The 19-year-old Brazilian is listed at No. 28 in the Cincinnati field and has already developed one of the loudest and most visible fan bases on the men’s tour. Tournament organizers specifically identified him as a player whose supporters bring flags, noise and energy wherever he competes.

His 2026 season has included interruptions caused by back and shoulder problems, but he reached two clay-court quarterfinals and advanced to the third round at Wimbledon. Cincinnati will offer another test of how quickly he can adjust to the faster North American hard courts ahead of the US Open.

Francisco Cerúndolo enters as Latin America’s highest-ranked man in the announced field at No. 22. The 27-year-old has produced one of the strongest seasons of his career, winning titles in Buenos Aires and at Queen’s Club in London.

His Queen’s Club victory was especially significant. Cerúndolo became the first Argentine to win the tournament and earned the first ATP 500 title of his career, showing that his success is no longer limited to clay. That versatility could make him the region’s most credible candidate for a deep Cincinnati run.

Cerúndolo also leads an unusually large Argentine contingent. Tomás Martín Etcheverry, Mariano Navone, Juan Manuel Cerúndolo, Sebastián Báez, Román Andrés Burruchaga, Thiago Agustín Tirante and Camilo Ugo Carabelli are all listed in the main draw.

Etcheverry is ranked No. 31 in the field after reaching the semifinals in Kitzbühel, while Navone, Báez and the younger Cerúndolo brother give Argentina additional depth. The size of the delegation reflects the country’s continuing ability to produce tour-level players even without a current superstar competing near the very top of the rankings.

One of the more intriguing names is Ignacio Buse. The 21-year-old Peruvian is listed at No. 35 and has climbed rapidly enough to enter the discussion around possible seeding at major tournaments.

Buse reached the Rio Open semifinals earlier this year after defeating former Wimbledon finalist Matteo Berrettini. His rise is particularly notable because Peru does not have the player-development depth or tournament infrastructure associated with Argentina or Brazil. Cincinnati will provide another opportunity to measure his progress against a field containing nearly every leading player in the world.

Chile’s Alejandro Tabilo is another dangerous opponent. The left-hander is ranked No. 30 in the Cincinnati field and reached the semifinals in Bastad in July before losing a close three-set match to Andrey Rublev. Tabilo’s serve and left-handed patterns can make him an uncomfortable early-round matchup, particularly if he can transfer his recent clay-court form to the hard courts. He has already defeated Fonseca this season, winning their three-set meeting in Buenos Aires.

Paraguay will be represented by Adolfo Daniel Vallejo, who is listed at No. 63. His presence adds another country to a men’s field that is considerably more geographically diverse than Latin American representation on the women’s side.

Colombia’s Camila Osorio is currently the region’s only confirmed direct entrant in the women’s main draw. Her speed, defensive ability and willingness to extend points have helped her compete effectively across surfaces, but she will face a difficult field containing the full women’s top 10 and numerous Grand Slam champions.

Other Latin American women will have to earn their places through qualifying. Colombia’s Emiliana Arango, Argentina’s Solana Sierra and Nadia Podoroska, and Mexico’s Renata Zarazúa are included in the 48-player qualifying field. Twelve women will advance to the main draw after two rounds.

The final draw will determine whether Latin America’s leading players receive manageable openings or immediate assignments against the tournament favorites. Even before those matchups are known, Cincinnati offers a revealing test. Cerúndolo has already demonstrated that he can win a major title away from clay.

Fonseca is trying to convert exceptional promise into consistent results. Buse is carrying Peruvian tennis into unfamiliar territory, while Tabilo and Argentina’s deep group remain capable of disrupting almost any section of the draw.For Latin American tennis, the question in Cincinnati will not be whether the region is represented. It will be how many of its players remain standing when the tournament reaches its decisive second week.

World.title: Crown seeks video-link testimony from witness in Robert Arnold murder trial
World.content:
Crown seeks video-link testimony from witness in Robert Arnold murder trial

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Crown intends to apply for its main witness to testify by video link in the upcoming murder trial of Belize City resident Robert Arnold, citing concerns for the woman’s safety and immigration status.

Arnold, 21, is charged with the June 3, 2024 murder of Cruz Magana, who was shot and killed during an armed robbery at his family’s home and shop in the Fresh Pond Community of Burrell Boom.

During Arnold’s appearance before Justice Candace Nanton on Wednesday, Crown Counsel Joseph Perez told the High Court that the witness has left Belize and is seeking asylum in the United States.

According to the Crown, the woman remains fearful for her life and does not intend to return to Belize. Prosecutors also argued that travelling back to testify could affect her asylum application.

Justice Nanton instructed the Crown to formally file its application and set September 18, 2026, to deliver her decision on whether the witness will be permitted to testify remotely.

Arnold, who is represented by attorney Dale Cayetano, is scheduled to stand trial between October 18 and 23, 2026.

Police allege that two armed men entered the Magana family’s home and business, stole cash and a cellphone, and fatally shot the 32-year-old victim. Witnesses reportedly told investigators that they were able to identify the gunman.

Arnold previously faced a separate murder charge in connection with the death of Rudolph “Bobo Youth” Lewis. However, the case against Arnold and co-accused Travis Jamaal Herbert ended in June 2026 after the Crown entered a nolle prosequi.

World.title: Pre-trial hearing set for Kentroy McKoy in Mark Francisco murder case
World.content:
Pre-trial hearing set for Kentroy McKoy in Mark Francisco murder case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A pre-trial hearing has been scheduled for October 1, 2026, for Kentroy McKoy, the sole remaining accused in the August 2024 murder of Belize City fisherman Mark Francisco.

McKoy appeared before Justice Candace Nanton in the High Court on Wednesday, accompanied by his attorney, Oscar Selgado. He remains on remand while awaiting trial.

McKoy was initially charged alongside Degron Shakeel Joseph, but the murder charge against Joseph was withdrawn earlier this year on the direction of the Director of Public Prosecutions. Joseph was reportedly granted immunity in exchange for his testimony in the case.

Francisco, 53, was fatally shot on the morning of August 4, 2024, while preparing for a fishing trip near Cemetery Lane and Yarborough Road.

Police said a gunman exited a silver Toyota 4Runner and opened fire before fleeing. Investigators reportedly tracked the vehicle through surveillance footage from Ladyville into Belize City and later to Santa Barbara Street.

The investigation allegedly linked Joseph and McKoy to the vehicle shortly before the shooting. Both men were arraigned for murder on August 13, 2024.

World.title: Trial of Three San Pedro men accused of shooting at fishermen and burning their boat deferred to 2027
World.content:
Trial of Three San Pedro men accused of shooting at fishermen and burning their boat deferred to 2027

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The trial of three San Pedro residents accused of pursuing and firing at two fishermen before allegedly setting their boat ablaze has been pushed into the High Court’s 2027 criminal calendar.

John Hernandez, 26, Shelby Jonathan Hernandez, 22, and Hector Pop, 29, appeared before Justice Nigel Pilgrim on Wednesday, July 22. The judge informed the accused men that the court’s remaining 2026 trial calendar was full and their case could not proceed until sometime in 2027.

The matter was adjourned until September 16, 2026, for mention, when the court is expected to consider a tentative trial date.

The three men are jointly charged with one count of arson and two counts of aggravated assault stemming from an incident on July 31, 2024, in the Tranquility Bay area of northern Ambergris Caye.

According to reports published shortly after the incident, then-23-year-old fisherman Eliezer Aldana and another man were fishing at around 4:30 a.m. when they were intercepted by a boat carrying four men. The men allegedly threatened the fishermen and ordered them to leave the area.

When Aldana attempted to leave, the other vessel allegedly pursued them while its occupants fired several shots in their direction. The fishermen were not injured and managed to reach a nearby resort, where they sought refuge.

The prosecution alleges that the fishermen’s 18-foot white boat, named La Gringa, was subsequently taken farther out to sea and deliberately set on fire. The burning vessel reportedly drifted onto the beach and sank before it was later recovered and taken to a mechanic shop.

The boat was valued at $21,000.

Public reports indicate that John Hernandez and Pop were the first two men taken before the court in August 2024 in connection with the incident. They were represented at the time by attorney Orson “OJ” Elrington, who indicated that he would apply for bail on their behalf.

John Hernandez and Pop are presently out on bail. Shelby Hernandez remains on remand in connection with a separate case in which he is charged with the March 2026 murders of Karim Nazim Espat, Oscar Modesto Mas and Yerlin Marisol Bueso Alvarez in San Pedro. No plea has been taken in that matter.

World.title: Burrell Boom man fined $2,000 for breaking into Fresh Pond house while 13-year-old girl was at home; He didn’t steal anything – Girl locked herself in room
World.content:
Burrell Boom man fined $2,000 for breaking into Fresh Pond house while 13-year-old girl was at home; He didn’t steal anything – Girl locked herself in room

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Burrell Boom resident has avoided imprisonment after pleading guilty to burglarizing a woman’s home while her 13-year-old daughter was inside.

Christopher Smith Jr. was fined $2,000, along with $5 in court costs, when he appeared for sentencing in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, July 20. He must pay the fine by November 15, 2026, or serve six months in prison.

Smith had pleaded guilty to burglary on July 17 and was remanded until sentencing.

The court heard that on May 5, the homeowner left her daughter doing homework inside their Fresh Pond Community residence while she briefly visited her mother. During that time, Smith allegedly damaged a lock and entered through the rear of the house.

The frightened child later called her mother and reported seeing a man standing outside her bedroom door. He reportedly said “hello” before leaving. The girl locked herself inside the room and was found crying when her mother returned.

Nothing was stolen, and no one was physically harmed.

In determining the sentence, the Senior Magistrate considered the minimal property damage, Smith’s early guilty plea and the apparent lack of planning. A starting fine of $3,300 was reduced because he had no previous burglary conviction and received a further one-third discount for pleading guilty.

Smith previously faced two murder charges in connection with a double killing in Hattieville, but the charges against him were withdrawn in November 2025. Two other accused men remain before the court.

World.title: Tatiana Alvarado dies in fiery collision near Bella Vista village
World.content:
Tatiana Alvarado dies in fiery collision near Bella Vista village

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a fatal road traffic accident that claimed the life of a 39-year-old woman near Bella Vista Village on Saturday afternoon.

The accident occurred at approximately 4:35 p.m. on July 25, 2026, along the Thomas Vincent Ramos Highway between Miles 44 and 45.

Initial investigations indicate that 26-year-old Daunte Oliver Eden Noralez, of a Belmopan address, was driving a Ford Escape toward Punta Gorda when he allegedly attempted to overtake a Lifan 150 motorcycle travelling in the same direction.

During the attempted overtaking maneuver, the vehicles collided, causing the motorcyclist, Tatiana Alvarado of Bella Vista Village, to sustain fatal injuries. Police arrived at the scene and found the motorcycle engulfed in flames.

Alvarado was transported to the Southern Regional Hospital, where she was pronounced dead on arrival.

Noralez has been detained pending further investigation.

World.title: 19-year-old injured in early-morning Cemetery Road shooting
World.content:
19-year-old injured in early-morning Cemetery Road shooting

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 19-year-old construction worker was injured in an early-morning shooting in Belize City on Sunday following the Jouvert in July event.

Police say the incident occurred at approximately 4:55 a.m. on July 26 as Arnize Young was walking along Cemetery Road.

Two men travelling on a motorcycle reportedly approached and fired several shots in Young’s direction, causing him to sustain gunshot injuries.

Young’s injuries have been classified as non-life-threatening. Police have not announced a motive or any arrests as their investigation continues.

World.title: BREAKING: Denvoy Bartley identified as tonight’s murder victim in Unitedville triple shooting
World.content:
BREAKING: Denvoy Bartley identified as tonight’s murder victim in Unitedville triple shooting

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Breaking Belize News has confirmed that Denvoy Feliciano Bartley of Banak Street, Belize City, is the man who was murdered in a triple shooting in Unitedville Village on Saturday night.

Bartley was reportedly travelling with his twin brother and another man when the group was targeted near a bus stop while carrying out an errand in the village. All three men were rushed to the Western Regional Hospital, where Bartley later succumbed to his injuries. The two other victims remain hospitalized.

Bartley had previously survived a shooting in Belize City in April 2021. He was later charged in 2023 with the murder of Lionel Budna; however, the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions discontinued the case in November 2024 by entering a nolle prosequi, and Bartley was released after spending more than a year on remand.

Police investigations into Saturday night’s murder are continuing.

World.title: BREAKING: Belize City man murdered in triple shooting in Unitedville, Cayo
World.content:
BREAKING: Belize City man murdered in triple shooting in Unitedville, Cayo

By Jose Luis Cruz: A Belize City man was murdered in a triple shooting that occurred on Saturday night in Unitedville Village in the Cayo District. The incident occurred near a bus stop in the village in the same vicinity that a policeman in uniform was also shot and killed.

A group of young men had gone to do an errand in the village when they were targeted by the gunman(men). Three (3) of the men received shooting injuries and were rushed to the Western Regional Hospital in Belmopan for treatment.

One of the shooting victims has succumbed to his injuries while the other two (2) are receiving treatment. The victim who died is a resident of Banak Street in Belize City.

This murder is the latest in a recent spike of shootings and murder that has occurred in Unitedville in the last two (2) years.

World.title: Sitting duck
World.content:
The 10 per cent General Consumption Tax that had softened the blows suffered by tourism activities is expected to move to the standard 15 per cent, effective next year April

ATTENTION will turn this Wednesday to a crucial meeting between the finance ministry and anxious tourism leaders fearing that a General Consumption Tax (GCT) increase being proposed for the sector will badly hurt its viability for the immediate future.

Nervously awaiting the outcome of the discussions also are sectors like domestic agriculture and manufacturing — broken down into produce, poultry, dairy, juices, sauces, water, electricity, packaging, furniture, uniforms, amenities, and transport and services, for which tourism is the anchor customer.

The tourism industry and its spin-off entities have been fretful in recent years over its future profitability after a series of financial shocks, mostly stemming from natural weather events, left the sector reeling.

Sector leaders interviewed by the Jamaica Observer for this story said Hurricane Melissa caused more than US$8 billion in physical damage, pointing out that rebuilding room stock, restoring attractions, and repairing the infrastructure that moves visitors around the island is not a one-season exercise. Much of that work is still under way.

Industry-wide, it was accepted that the Andrew Holness Administration was bound to ask the sector to help carry the burden of funding the expansive post-Hurricane Melissa recovery, as has always been the approach by governments after major disasters.

But when Finance Minister Fayval Williams tabled revenue measures in this year’s budget, she shook the tourism sector by announcing that the 10 per cent GCT, that had softened the blows suffered by tourism activities would move to the standard 15 per cent, effective next year April.

Williams said the one-year notice would give the tourism sector itself more time to recover from Melissa. What the finance minister’s calculations did not factor in, however, was the flow of earnings from the sector.

Notably, most rates were already negotiated and inked with overseas partners like tour operators. Jamaica’s tourist entities were, therefore, being asked to pass off a 50 per cent rate increase where other sophisticated tourism markets are fighting for the same global tourism traveller.

Passing on GCT increases would, at best, be impossible without doing further critical damage to the sector and leaving it naked and exposed to its overseas competitors, the leaders concurred.

“For the most part, hotel room sales are contracted often 18 months to two years in advance with tour operators and wholesalers in source markets,” said new Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association (JHTA) President O’Brien Heron when queried by the Observer.

“It means that a contract signed with a tour operator or wholesaler in 2026 involves a significant share of the room nights that will be sold in the 2027 season [and beyond] at the current 2026 room rates, inclusive of GCT.

“…Those contracts cannot be reopened just because Jamaica’s tax rate changed, which means that the local hotel or attraction will have to absorb the difference between the old and new GCT rate through to the end of the current contract period,” he added.

Moreover, industry leaders insist recovery is not the only pressure that has intensified since the measure was announced. Energy costs have soared, exacerbated by war in the Middle East that has pushed up global oil prices from roughly US$60 a barrel in December 2025 to near US$100 by March 2026.

Jamaica generates much of its electricity from imported fuel, so that increase passes almost directly into the cost of running a hotel.

“It lands on an industry that was already paying among the highest electricity rates in the hemisphere,” added the JHTA head. “Business electricity in Jamaica runs well above the global average — a structural disadvantage that has nothing to do with how well any individual property is managed.

“For a resort, electricity is not overhead at the margin. Air conditioning, refrigeration, laundry and water production run 24 hours a day, every day, whether the room is occupied or not,” he explained.

Heron roundly disagreed with government number crunchers’ description that it was “a five-percentage-point increase”, reiterating that it was a 50 per cent GCT increase — from 10 to 15 per cent.

“What is at stake here is the economic fabric of tourism, and tourism is the engine that drives Jamaica’s economy,” he said. “When you compress this sector you do not compress one industry. You compress the farmer who supplies it, the manufacturer who packages for it, the transport operator who moves its guests, and the worker whose household depends on it.”

Speaking for the small hotels, JHTA past President Evelyn Smith stressed the struggles facing the sector after being hit by significant disasters like the COVID-19 pandemic, hurricanes Beryl and Melissa; a northerly that threw up angry waves that badly damaged some Negril beachfront properties; and the recent water problem that “forced us to pay huge sums of money to have water trucked to the properties”.

“During these disastrous events, some properties had to shut down altogether; others remained open but retained staff at tremendous sacrifice,” said Smith.

“Negril is well known as having the largest collection of small hotels. We have kept the life of Negril going during these many shocks, especially after Melissa, the worst hurricane to hit Jamaica. We kept our doors open even as cash depleted.”

Smith said she strongly disagreed with the Government that the industry has matured.

“Tourism is an export industry, so our competition is overseas, and we can’t just pass on any increase. Our rates are already set. Our revenues are already very thin, and now we are being asked to absorb further increases. Something is going to have to give.

“This significant increase will hit what we have to do in order to simply remain alive,” she reasoned.

The JHTA’s present leadership is also worried about the dim prospects facing the allied sectors, such as ground transportation and attractions, said Nadine Spence, the 4th vice-president.

“While we fully appreciate the Government’s responsibility to generate revenue to fund national development, timing is critical. The transportation, attractions, and allied sectors are still recovering from Hurricane Melissa and a challenging tourism environment,” Spence pointed out.

“A 50 per cent increase in the GCT applied to hotel accommodation risks weakening Jamaica’s competitiveness at a time when every visitor matters. We depend directly on hotel occupancy, and any decline in arrivals or visitor spending flows immediately through our sector, affecting jobs, investment, and small businesses across the island,” she argued.

“If higher taxes reduce arrivals or visitor spending, transportation and attractions businesses immediately feel the impact. A tax on hotels inevitably becomes a tax on the wider tourism value chain.

“Furthermore, this tax proposal comes at the worst possible time,” she suggested. “An industry facing this level of compounding strain requires temporary relief, incentives, and structural support to rebuild, not an aggressive tax hike.

“Taxing local businesses into submission during a recovery period will only push more players out of the formal market and exacerbate the very revenue shortfall the Government is trying to solve.

“If Jamaica wants a sustainable, high-yielding tourism sector… we need policies that nurture Jamaican-owned ground transport and attraction businesses, enabling them to build domestic wealth that stays right here in the economy.

“An increase in GCT at this critical time is not good for a sector on the rebound, especially when arrivals are down 30 to 40 per cent… Lower pricing will increase volumes which will increase traffic and that means additional revenue,” said Spence.

Martin Zsifkovicks, co-chair of the association’s linkages and agriculture committees, cautioned about the indirect harm threatening agriculture.

“The GCT increase will not automatically damage agriculture fruits, vegetables, as most agricultural inputs remain GCT-free, which is fundamentally important. However, the mechanism runs through hotel profitability rather than the tax code directly,” he suggested.

“When hotels come under margin pressure, procurement is historically one of the first places operators look to cut, precisely because it’s a variable cost that can be scaled up or down quickly, unlike staffing contracts, utilities, or debt service. We have already seen how directly that plays out for farmers: During COVID, when hotel demand collapsed, Government had to step in with a buy-back scheme because produce already planted for the hotel trade had nowhere to go.”

Zsifkovicks agreed that the timing of the increase was bad, saying that close to 5,000 rooms remain off stream since Hurricane Melissa hit in October 2025, and hurricane recovery of this scale typically takes years, not months.

“That means the industry is already absorbing pressure on revenue and cash flow before the GCT increase even takes effect. Layering a tax increase on top of a sector that hasn’t yet returned to full inventory only adds to that strain, and procurement is likely to be one of the first places it shows up.

“A GCT-driven margin squeeze is a different kind of shock than a pandemic shutdown, but the transmission line is the same — pressure on hotel revenue shows up quickly in what and how much hotels are willing to commit to buying from local farmers. That’s the risk worth watching, even though the produce itself isn’t being taxed,” he said.

President Heron also warned that absorbing a tax increase does not simply reduce profit but reduces the cash available for everything that sits below the operating line, like debt service, refurbishment, and reinvestment.

“Most properties in this market are carrying storm-related capital expenditure and, in many cases, related borrowing. Compress operating earnings and the first casualties are not investor dividends. They are the deferred room refresh, the delayed energy-efficiency retrofit, the postponed hire.

“An industry that defers reinvestment does not announce a crisis. It simply becomes gradually less competitive, and the consequences arrive later, when they are far more expensive to reverse,” charged Heron.

He said that when hotel margins compress, procurement is one of the first places operators look to trim costs. And the path of least resistance begins with buying harder. That means suppliers will feel the squeeze through both rate and volume pressures. Not out of any lack of national commitment, but because a buyer under margin pressure buys on price.

“This is where the policy tension becomes difficult to ignore. The Government’s own Tourism 3.0 and Local First agenda commit to prioritising Jamaican farmers, artisans, manufacturers, and micro-entrepreneurs as first suppliers to hotels and attractions. That is a genuinely good policy, and the industry supports it.

“… There is also a principle worth stating plainly. Under Jamaica’s own GCT Act, exports are zero-rated. Tourism is an export industry — it earns foreign exchange and it is consumed primarily by non-residents. By that logic, the tax code, fairly applied across all exporters, tourism services should also be zero-rated.

“Successive government administrations have repeatedly accepted this fact and, while some adjustments have been made to the GCT rate differential, the principle supporting tourism having a lower rate than the national rate is well documented and, up ’til now, was assumed a settled matter,” he added.

Heron said that what the industry is asking for is to be in a position to show the Government the disastrous implications expected to tourism businesses by the proposed change.

Heron confirmed that the JHTA would be meeting with the finance minister this week and that work is under way to put independent evidence in front of Government.

“Tourism’s bottom lines to watch is not only about the hotel’s. It is also the farmer’s, the manufacturer’s, the worker’s, and the country’s. That is precisely why the timing, and the terms of this increase are worth getting right — together,” he said.

World.title: Jamaica edge Honduras with dramatic late winner in Concacaf U20 opener
World.content:
Jamaica beat Honduras 2-1 in their opening Concacaf Under-20 Championships Group C game at Estadio Universitario BUAP in Puebla, Mexico on Sunday.

A stoppage time goal from Brandon Bent broke the 1-1 tie as Jamaica won their first game in the Championships since 2022 and are tied for the group lead with Canada who beat Panama 3-0 in the other game in the zone played earlier in the day.

Jamaica had taken the lead in the first half before giving up the lead in the 75th minute as the Central Americans took over the game in the second half.

Jahmarie Nolan scored the game’s first goal in the 21st minute when his shot from the right side of the Honduras 18-yard box got by goalkeeper Alan Cury and just inside the far post.

Kimarly Scott had a chance to double the lead later in the half when he faced Cury alone but shot straight to the Honduran goalkeeper.

Honduras rallied in the second half, pushing the Jamaican team back into their own area and were rewarded in the 75th minute when Victor Salazar finished off a smart team move, scoring with their first shot on target.

Jamaica got the winner late, in time added, when Honduras failed to clear a ball from a corner and Bent was quickest to it, shifted to his left to create space before firing the ball over the diving Cury.

Starting team

Joshua Grant, Jaquan Brown, Jahmarie Nolan, Jermaine Young, Jabarie Howell, Jahmani Bell, Sean Leighton, Duwayne Burgher, Santana Headley, Kimarly Scott, Brandon Bent.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: WATCH: NaRRA voicenotes don’t represent official position of PNP, says Golding
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica – People’s National Party (PNP) President Mark Golding says leaked voicenotes of party members discussing tactics to undermine the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA) do not represent the official position of the PNP.

In the voicenotes which were leaked on social media, individuals are heard discussing strategies to undermine NaRRA and smear its CEO Major General Antony Anderson.

The recordings were allegedly made shortly after the controversial appointment of Anderson as head of the agency set up to manage Jamaica’s post-disaster reconstruction and resilience.

READ: JLP condemns ‘vile’ alleged NaRRA voicenotes featuring PNP executives

However, in a statement on the issue at the PNP’s National Executive Council meeting on Sunday, Golding said the individuals heard in the voicenotes are not officers of the party and were not speaking in any official capacity.

“This was a WhatsApp group formed by individuals within the party and the views expressed were their personal views,” Golding said. “So those recordings do not represent the official position of the PNP or any policy of the PNP.”

He added that, “The PNP takes responsible for its official position – those that are set by our constitutional organs… and those that are communicated by our authorised representatives.”

World.title: Cabinet yet to receive BOJ Governor shortlist
World.content:
Fayval Williams

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Minister of Finance and the Public Service Fayval Williams says the committee searching for the next governor of Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) has not yet submitted its shortlist to Cabinet, pushing back against a Sunday Finance report that identified Senior Deputy Governor Dr Wayne Robinson as the front-runner for the post.

In a statement issued Sunday, Williams said Cabinet had not been informed of any front-runner and warned that speculation and the naming of candidates could undermine the selection process.

She said applications were received and reviewed solely by the search committee, which has not yet tendered its shortlist.

The statement did not say whether Robinson had applied, been interviewed or was among the candidates being considered. It confined its response to the status of the formal process and the fact that no shortlist had reached Cabinet.

The Sunday Finance report, which was based on information from a senior Government source, said Robinson was regarded as the leading candidate to replace outgoing Governor Richard Byles. The report made clear that no final decision had been announced and that it was not known whether Cabinet had received a recommendation.

Efforts to obtain a comment from Williams before publication were unsuccessful, as calls to her cellular phone went unanswered. Further calls to the minister following the release of Sunday’s statement were also unsuccessful.

Williams said the committee process was similar to the one used seven years ago to select Byles, with candidates interviewed before findings were presented.

She added that the current committee’s work is expected to be completed by the end of July.

The committee, appointed in April, is responsible for identifying a shortlist of suitable candidates. Cabinet will then consider the names and decide on the individual to be recommended to the governor general for appointment under the Bank of Jamaica Act.

Byles was appointed governor effective August 19, 2019, after coming out of retirement. His tenure is scheduled to end in August.

Robinson is BOJ’s second-ranking executive and an ex-officio member of its board, Monetary Policy Committee, Financial Policy Committee, Supervisory Committee and Financial System Stability Committee. The career central banker has played a leading role in the design and implementation of Jamaica’s monetary policy and financial market reforms.

World.title: Sunshine Girls fall to New Zealand at Commonwealth Games
World.content:
Jamaica’s Romelda Aiken-George (left) tries to block a shot from a New Zealand player (right) during a Fast5 Series match at Christchurch Arena in New Zealand in 2023. Jamaica’s Kimone Shaw looks on..

Jamaica’s Sunshine Girls will hope to rebound against Uganda in the Commonwealth Games netball competition on Monday after they went down by five goals, 48-53, to New Zealand in their second Pool B Preliminary Round game at the Hyra Arena in Glasgow, Scotland.

A day after the Jamaicans beat Trinidad and Tobago 81-22 in their opening game, they were held in check by New Zealand who took a measure of revenge after losing to them in the semi-finals four years ago.

Led by Grace Nweke, who scored 47 goals from 56 attempts, New Zealand led by two goals after the first quarter, 14-12; they were up by one goal, 26-25, at halftime; and were ahead 39-35 going into the final period.

Romelda Aiken scored 34 goals from 38 attempts and Shanice Beckford scored 14 from 15 attempts for the Jamaicans.

Uganda are ahead of Jamaica in the Pool B tables after winning both of their games played so far, 59-50 over Wales and 80-36 over Trinidad and Tobago.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: PEP transfer trap
World.content:
Head of the Jamaica Association of Principals of Secondary Schools (JAPSS), Anniona Jones, is urging parents to carefully consider requests to transfer their children to other high schools following the Primary Exit Profile (PEP) placement process, warning that such decisions should be based on what is best for the child’s development rather than the perceived prestige of an institution.

Jones also cautioned school administrators against accepting an influx of transfer students primarily for financial gain, arguing that overcrowding can undermine the quality of education and place unnecessary strain on teachers and school resources.

She said she is aware that some schools have received 60 or more transfer requests and, while she understands that every parent wants the best for their child, not every school is equipped to provide the type of academic intervention some students need.

“We have to be very careful about how we think of some schools as intervention schools or schools for children with low academic aptitudes, because as the children start to do better, people are still not going to want to place their children necessarily in those schools. You have schools that have low levels of enrolment, and then you have other schools that are bursting at the seams.

“It becomes an issue, though, for school governance to be able to say to a principal and have that conversation at the board level that, ‘Listen, this school was built for X amount.’ I still don’t know why we have schools on [the] shift [system] when we have so many schools that are underpopulated.

“It’s really…a policy issue, but a board can make a decision that we are going to limit our school sizes to no more than 22 to 30 children per class,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Jones argued that limiting class sizes is particularly important for schools offering science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) subjects, which she said are best taught in smaller classes. She added that smaller class sizes would also ease the burden on teachers by reducing the volume of books to be marked and allowing more targeted feedback and individual attention for students.

She noted that, in many cases, schools are reluctant to reduce enrolment because funding is largely allocated on a per-student basis, making lower student numbers financially disadvantageous. However, she welcomed the Government’s move toward a more equitable funding model, describing it as a positive step in the right direction.

Jones also expressed concern about the growing costs parents incur while seeking transfers, noting that some schools charge application fees between $1,000 and $5,000.

“If you look at the cost for transfer requests, you could have a school, in theory, getting a request of 100 children wanting to come in. If you charge each child $1,000, that’s $100,000 even if your school can only take in 20, so you could do a lot with an additional $100,000. Some parents are going around paying five schools $1,000 a pop or more,” said Jones.

She added: “Some schools, I hear, transfers are as much as $5,000 just to request a transfer, and they are not guaranteed to get in. Parents have to also look at that as well and understand that placing your child in a school where your child may be in the bottom quarter, or smack in the middle, may not be as good for your child as placing them in a school where your child may come first, second, or third and get a confidence boost, or placing a child in a school that can cater to their needs,” she reasoned.

Jones, who is the principal at Haile Selassie High School, added that, while traditional high schools often have a wider range of programmes and extracurricular activities, they can also place a greater financial burden on families.

In contrast, she said some non-traditional

schools may offer programmes that are better suited to a child’s interests and abilities while remaining more affordable.

“Sometimes we have to be very discerning that we don’t spend all the money to buy the car but turn around and can’t buy gas and can’t change the tyre, or can’t deal with the servicing and upkeep after the free servicing is finished.

“Schools need support to grow, so allow your child to be placed in an institution that can give you the financial wiggle room as well, to do some other things for your child. Otherwise, your child may go into these spaces, can’t function, and you can’t participate fully to keep the school offering what you say you want,” said Jones.

She further urged parents to do their part in ensuring that the children they send off to these institutions can have a positive impact, especially for non-traditional high schools that have a stigma of being violent environments.

“Send us the best version of your children, then we wouldn’t have to worry about the children, and every space can be a safe, developing, nurturing space for every child to be able to do all the things that they want to do, if parents are willing to help build it, fund it, create it,” she said.

She added: “We have the buildings, we have these teachers, we have the class sizes; it makes better sense to me to place your child in a smaller school to treat with the PEP score,” said Jones.

World.title: 140% spike in deportees to Jamaica last year
World.content:
In this Jamaica Observer file photo, Deportees from the US are on the move after arriving in Jamaica and being processed by local security officials.

SIXTY of the 1,317 people deported to Jamaica in 2025 were convicted of murder, manslaughter or attempted murder in the deporting country, with 52 of them being sent from the United States.

One was deported from Canada, five from England, and two from ‘other’ countries.

The information is outlined in the 2025 edition of the Economic and Social Survey Jamaica, a publication of the Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ).

It listed 171 of the deportees having possession of drugs convictions, with a significant majority – 142 – coming from the USA. Two were deported from Canada, three from England, while 24 were sent back from other countries.

The 2025 list of deportees also included 134 people convicted for the serious offences of wounding, assault and battery.

The US again topped the list of these deportees with 115.

The sexual offences category listed 63 deportees last year, with the US sending back 50, Canada four, England five, while four came from other countries.

However for the vast majority of deportees, 610 were sent back to Jamaica for immigration violations including illegal entry, overstay of visa, and illegal re-entry.

There were 95 deportees convicted of firearm offences, with 88 running afoul of the law in the US. Other offences on the list included larceny, fraud/false document, kidnapping, and money laundering.

Of the total 1,317 deportees in 2025, 967 came from the US, which has a set policy of deporting Jamaicans to their homeland on the last Thursday of each month.

Last year saw Jamaica also receiving 70 deportees from Canada, 25 from England, and 255 from other countries.

The total represents a 140 per cent increase when compared to the 547 who were returned to Jamaica in 2024.

In May, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith said approximately 2,500 Jamaicans have been confirmed for deportation from the US this year.

Johnson Smith provided the update while speaking at a press conference at the Office of the Prime Minister as she moved to dismiss reports that some 4,000 Jamaicans are set to be deported from the US as part of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

“Allow me to be clear that 4,000 Jamaicans are not being returned now. For some time it has been in the public domain that the US authorities had close to 4,000 persons in their records with final orders for deportation against their names. It is now our understanding that approximately 2,500 have been confirmed for removal over a period of time, to be determined by logistics, their own legal processes, and other factors,” said Johnson Smith.

She pointed out that the deportation of Jamaicans is not a new phenomenon, and said the Government remains committed to honouring its international obligations to receive its citizens while safeguarding national security and public safety.

“It is not a new phenomenon. For decades, Jamaica has facilitated the repatriation of its citizens under established international arrangements. We receive our citizens when they are returned to us. Just as we expect, and we do, repatriate foreign nationals who commit serious crimes or breaches of our immigration laws,” added Johnson Smith.

The foreign affairs minister further pointed out that the Government has expanded the National Reintegration and Rehabilitation Strategy to coordinate reintegration services for the deportees.

“On May 5th, Cabinet approved the establishment of a National Technical Working Group on Voluntary and Involuntary Migrants, recognising that not only is the grouping not homogeneous in and of itself, but we now have a sub-grouping of those who are returning of their own motion — determining the circumstances in the US to not be where they wish to remain — and those who are being returned, those who have the decision made for them. This technical group is chaired by the Planning Institute of Jamaica. Oversight is provided by the ministries of national security and foreign affairs and foreign trade; and the technical group comprises several ministries, departments, and agencies, as well as civil society partners.

“Its mandate is to coordinate reintegration services and to ensure that returnees are supported in a structured, sustainable manner — and this includes their reception, verification, health checks, security, vetting, and access to social and legal support where necessary,” Johnson Smith said as she sought to allay fears about the possible security threats the deportees might bring.

“Monitoring and detention measures are in place [and] they will be applied. Again, stakeholders play key roles in helping us as partners in this reintegration and return process,” declared Johnson Smith.

Meanwhile, the PIOJ also reported that the total number of voluntary returned migrants stood at 852 in 2025, an increase of 52.1 per cent when compared with the 560 who returned home in 2024.

Voluntary returned migrants are people who choose to return to their homeland.

World.title: Sunday Jones transforms ‘pain 2 power’
World.content:
Sunday Jones addresses the media launch for her five-day Jamaica Tour, Ink Breath and Bars: Pain 2 Power, on July 20, 2026 at Sador’s Ethiopian Restaurant in Negril, Westmoreland. (Photo: Rosalee Wood Condell)

NEGRIL, Westmoreland — Poet and author Sunday Jones officially launched her five-day Jamaica tour, Ink Breath and Bars: Pain 2 Power, on Monday, July 20, bringing a message of healing, reflection, and creative empowerment to audiences across Jamaica.

Rooted in the mission of transforming personal pain into purpose through spoken word, the July tour blends live poetry performances, youth engagement, and community building.

A native of Atlanta, Georgia, Sunday Jones is a poet, author, and community leader known for founding Sunday Jones Productions and the Prison Brat Foundation. She functions as an ordained minister, certified life coach, event curator, and radio personality dedicated to giving a voice to the unheard and unseen. Her work focuses on healing from childhood trauma, faith, and personal evolution.

“Ink Breath and Bars is the ink of our soul, of our journeys, our writings, our poetry, our life.” Jones explained to the

Jamaica Observer. “The breath is the breath that we take, through word sound, through healing, through all of the things. It’s the breath that we need to take sometimes. All the time we breathe, but we sometimes need to take breaths. And the bars are the lyrical word sound that come from the ink and the breath. The tour is about community, culture, love, and liberation. It is to bring people together, to pull light from people who don’t understand that they have the light, or to elevate those that do have the light and want to go further. That is Ink Breath & Bars, to sum it up shortly.”

The tour features a line-up of community showcases, school visits, and curated intimate gatherings designed to inspire, connect, and celebrate. The journey began on July 21 at Kingston Night Market, followed by a visit to Haile Selassie High School on July 23. On July 25 the tour headed to Sador’s Ethiopian Restaurant in Negril for a special community gathering. It concludes on July 30 with an exclusive healing experience and Jones’ Solar Return Celebration.

The Ink Breath and Bars tour has gained significant backing from internationally renowned Jamaican dub poet and performance artist Yasus Afari. He highlighted the vital role poetry plays in community upliftment and personal transformation, endorsing Jones’ vision to use creative expression as a vehicle for emotional wellness and youth empowerment.

“Let us use the language and the arts to heal and to redeem our people from what I described earlier as neurolinguistic sorcery, and so bring neurolinguistic healing, so that we can heal in a wholesome and full-some way. So that even our tongue can be an instrument of life. We don’t have to have so much dissing and cussing and quarrelling as a small country who have been through such great tribulation,” he stated.

The poet seized the opportunity to issue a charge: “So we are calling on our fellow so-called entertainers, which I prefer to call edutainers, let us rise to that occasion. We are a great country, unprecedented in human recorded history. We are a talented and great set of people. Let us use this gift of art, music, poetry, film, dance, comedy, literature, photography, videography to empower our people, to uplift our people, to heal our people, and to help fulfil Jamaica’s sacred, national pledge to advance the entire welfare of the entire human race. Honour, love, and prosperity. Rastafari blessings.”

In addition to live performances, the tour serves as a promotional platform for Jones’ latest book, The Art of Rising: A Love Letter to My Becoming, allowing readers and lovers of dub and spoken word poetry to connect deeply with her published works.

With stops spanning from the vibrant creative spaces of Kingston to the west coast in Negril, Ink Breath and Bars: Pain 2 Power promises an uplifting cultural journey celebrating resilience, truth, and the transformative power of the Jamaican voice.

World.title: Cold calculation or plucked from thin air? How the EU determines those big fines against Big Tech
World.content:
On the Digital Markets Act, which is a regulatory law but works differently from traditional antitrust law — the fines are intended less to penalize a firm than to incentivize compliance. They also come with less of a sticker shock.

When the Commission started issuing multi-million euro fines under the DMA in 2025, to the opprobrium of some 'Big Tech' opponents, it pointed to the short duration of the conduct as one reason why the fines come far below the 10 percent of global turnover the regulation threatens. The most recent Google fine came in at a very modest 0.22 percent of the annual revenue of parent company Alphabet.

Though revenue is always considered a ceiling and enforcers always consider the same factors like how serious the infringement was, it's difficult to avoid the conclusion that the penalties are to some extent arbitrary — and not immune to political considerations.

The Google fine was actually the sum of two penalties (€460 million for Google’s favoring its own results in search, and €430 million for unfair practices in how the Play Store is installed on smartphones) that conveniently arrived just under the €1 billion mark in a moment of fraught transatlantic trade relations.

European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier denied that politics is part of the fining process. The EU "always follows due process," he told POLITICO. Regnier said numerous objective criteria — the seriousness and length of the breach, mitigating factors and threshold keeping the penalties under a certain percentage of revenue — help "ensure that fines remain proportional under all circumstances."

Penalties issued under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU’s landmark content moderation law, are also contested. Chinese e-commerce giant Temu has argued a Commission fine of €200 million levied against it in May is “disproportionate” — though it’s far below the DSA’s higher threshold for fines, which is 6 percent of the company’s annual global revenue.

World.title: Iceland opposition chief to Europe: Don’t meddle in our referendum
World.content:
The Nordic country will vote on Aug. 29 on whether to resume accession talks with Brussels, with early voting beginning Monday. The referendum will not decide whether Iceland joins the EU — any eventual membership agreement would require a second public vote.

Polls suggest the question of reopening discussions is finely balanced, although a clearer majority remains opposed to membership itself. “We are divided into nearly equal groups for yes and no” on the former, Hafsteinsdóttir said in a phone interview from Vatnajökull, Iceland’s largest glacier. “The referendum will be very tight.”

The vote fulfills a pledge made by Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir’s three-party coalition when it took office in late 2024. The alliance — dubbed the “Valkyrie government” because all three parties are led by women — includes a party that supports EU membership. Frostadóttir has said the referendum is intended to settle “a debate that has hung over the Icelandic nation.”

Several prominent European figures have sounded positive about the prospect of renewed talks. French MEP and Renew Europe leader Valérie Hayer traveled to Iceland in June and called for the EU to make accession easier. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos welcomed the vote and said the bloc “will be ready” if Iceland chooses to join, while French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Reykjavík had “nothing to lose” by restarting negotiations.

The warm tone comes as Brussels seeks to revive enlargement as a geopolitical project, drawing Ukraine, Moldova and the Western Balkans closer while showing the EU can still attract new members amid strained relations with Washington and growing competition with China.

Iceland’s case is different from those of most current candidates. The North Atlantic nation of around 400,000 people is already closely integrated with the bloc through the European Economic Area and the Schengen zone, and conducts most of its trade with the EU.

World.title: French politicians can’t get enough of ‘De Gaulle’
World.content:
The epic tale of a solitary, dogged patriot fighting to save his country from annihilation while standing up to an overbearing ally across the Atlantic captures the zeitgeist of French politics today.

As France again faces questions about the future of its alliance with the United States, French people find themselves forced to choose between various leaders portraying themselves as national saviors ahead of the presidential election next year.

So presidential hopefuls from across the political spectrum, including those from parties that view De Gaulle less favorably, are hailing the film’s portrayal of the wartime general’s brilliance in times of trouble — and, in thinly veiled casting attempts, trying to portray themselves as France’s next providential leader.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu last week said the movie’s success spoke to the French need of “meaning” and “perspectives” in a rare interview with glossy magazine Paris Match.

Perhaps the most surprising endorsement came from anticapitalist firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whose party France Unbowed opposes conservative movements that have claimed to carry on De Gaulle’s legacy, despite the general himself equally despising all political parties.

During his Bastille Day address in the western city of Paimpont, the left-wing leader, one of the top contenders in next year’s election, strongly encouraged his supporters to watch a “magnificent movie,” drawing parallels between De Gaulle’s uphill battle to build up the country’s free forces during the war and his own campaign.

World.title: City gears up for a fight on bank tax under Burnham
World.content:
Rigby was a popular City minister for almost a year before being promoted a couple of months ago under Keir Starmer's government. Her return to the role has been particularly welcomed by the financial services industry, with hopes she will see through reforms put forward under Reeves, including controversial changes to the financial ombudsman.

Rigby comes back with a pay bump, as her role as economic secretary to the Treasury now falls under the higher bracket as a minister of state under Burnham’s government, a roughly £10,000 difference from its previous classification as a parliamentary secretary.

That pay rise sends a strong signal to the industry: the City minister will have almost complete control over financial services policy. That will mean continuity on the nitty gritty regulation side of things — a relief for the sector — but it may also free up new chancellor Healey up to focus on the fiscal side of things.

“The chancellor has big issues to consider over this parliament which may mean he spends less time on financial services reforms and policy than his predecessor,” Conway said. “If that’s true, Lucy Rigby may have more autonomy in her role as City minister.”

The main fear for finance executives is that the government could hike the bank surcharge, a specific tax on banks’ profits. The Trades Union Congress, which has been pushing for a windfall tax and has been in close contact with Burnham’s team on the issue, estimates a 16 percent surcharge would raise £24 billion over four years, while a 35 percent surcharge would raise £60 billion. It currently stands at 3 percent.

Those colossal sums would be more than welcome for the chancellor and his team will need to find mounds of cash to fill giant holes in public finances, as the new prime minister has ambitious goals to make a dent in the U.K.'s cost-of-living crisis.

World.title: Farage’s latest gamble clouds Reform’s path to power
World.content:
Faced with a parliamentary inquiry into a financial scandal, Farage stunned Westminster by resigning as a member of parliament for his constituency in Clacton, then immediately announcing he would run in the resulting by-election.

The aim was to present the race as a chance for voters — and not parliament — to judge the allegations, but Farage’s strategy quickly unraveled. Rather than take the bait, the country’s main political parties dismissed the exercise as a political stunt and declined to contest the Reform leader’s seat, leaving him to campaign in an increasingly surreal contest against Britain’s fringe candidates.

Chief among Farage’s current opponents is Count Binface. An “intergalactic space warrior” from the planet Sigma IX, Binface campaigns in a silver cape and trash can-shaped helmet on a manifesto that includes capping the price of a 99 Flake ice cream at 99 pence, and granting television presenter Claudia Winkleman’s bangs a listed-building status. Also, Binface is not alone — eight other fringe candidates have also entered the Clacton race.

A man holds a placard reading “Clacton Vote Binface,” in reference to the snap Aug. 13 Clacton by-election that pits Farage against Count Binface, outside Downing Street in London on July 20, 2026. | Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images

Farage’s plan was to stage a defining political confrontation, a showdown with the political establishment. Yet his campaign has become one dominated by ridicule.

Of course, there is little reason to believe he will lose. Clacton is Reform’s safest parliamentary seat, and he won almost half the vote there in 2024. Binface, meanwhile, has never secured more than 1 percent in any election.

But the contest has acquired an uncomfortable symbolism for the Reform leader. According to an Ipsos poll, nationally, more people would like Binface to win — which says a lot about the extent to which this by-election has become a vehicle for mocking Farage rather than reinforcing his authority.
