World.title: Stromovka: A Green Paradise in the Heart of Prague
World.content:
Stromovka is one of the largest and most popular parks in Prague, drawing visitors with its beautiful nature, rich history, and numerous activities.

Let’s explore what Stromovka offers and how to get there.

Why Visit Stromovka?

Looking for a break from the city’s hustle and bustle or the perfect spot for a picnic with friends? Stromovka is your ideal choice. This vast park features green meadows, shady alleys, and ample opportunities for sports and cultural events.

What is Stromovka?

Stromovka, officially known as Královská obora, spans more than 95 hectares, making it one of Prague’s largest green spaces. Located in Prague 7, the park is a favorite among joggers, cyclists, families, and anyone looking to escape into nature without leaving the city.

It’s perfect for walks, picnics, sports, or simply relaxing on the grass.

A Brief History

Stromovka’s history dates back to the 13th century when it was established as a royal hunting ground. Over time, it evolved and expanded, becoming a public park in the 19th century. The park is home to the original Vltava Creek and several ponds, which host various water birds.

Throughout its history, Stromovka has undergone many changes, shaping it into the popular relaxation spot it is today.

Activities in Stromovka

Stromovka offers a wide range of activities for all ages. Here are some ideas:

Walking and Running: Enjoy the scenic trails.

Cycling: Explore the park on two wheels.

Picnics: Large meadows and shady spots are perfect for a picnic.

Sports: Play football, volleyball, and other sports.

Cultural Events: Attend various events hosted in the park.

How to Get to Stromovka

By Metro: The nearest metro station is Nádraží Holešovice (line C). From there, it’s just a few minutes’ walk to Stromovka.

By Tram: Trams also reach the park. The nearest stops are Výstaviště Holešovice (lines 6, 12, 17) and Planetarium Prague (line 6).

By Bike: Cycling enthusiasts can easily access Stromovka by bike. Bike-sharing stations like Rekola and Nextbike are available around the park, allowing you to ride directly into this natural haven.

World.title: August 12-31: Prague to Host Festival of New Circus Letní Letná
World.content:
The international festival of new circus and theatre, Letní Letná 2026, will take place in Prague on August 12-31.

The festival will feature over 200 performances, workshops, concerts, and various acts by circus artists from 14 countries, including a special program for children.

This year marks the 23rd edition of the festival. Letenské sady park will once again be the main venue, with tents set up to create a mini-town complete with a coffee shop and an evening bar.

Many performances will be free of charge. Additionally, the festival will offer a rich and varied daily program: children’s shows, circus, juggling and acrobat workshops, music concerts, exhibitions, lectures, creative workshops, and more.

One of this year’s highlights is Wolf by Australia’s renowned Circa ensemble. The international lineup also includes Switzerland’s Accademia Teatro Dimitri, presenting its graduate production La Grinta, and Seismic, a collaboration between French choreographer Marie Gourdain and German artist Felix Baumann, featuring Czech performers.

The Czech program includes the premiere of Vertige by AirGym Art Company, Enola by Eliška Brtnická, new productions from Losers Cirque Company, and Hey, Earth! by Cirque La Putyka.

Emerging talent will also take center stage, with performances by CZirkidz Dance Company, Teens Cirkabaret, and recent graduates of international circus schools.

Audiences will have the chance to experience works in progress, including K voknu by Michaela Stará and Filip Zahradnický, followed by discussions with the artists.

For adults, Světla a stíny by Silk&Steel explores the darker sides of human experience through aerial and ground acrobatics, while family-friendly performances include the popular (Not Only) Juggling Galashow and Orbiting Zero by Czech juggler Aleš Hrdlička.

Beyond the performances, visitors can enjoy free workshops, children’s activities, concerts, open-air events, food stalls, bars, and relaxation areas throughout the festival grounds. Babysitting is available during selected performances, and the venue is fully accessible, making Letní Letná a festival for all ages.

World.title: New Railway Tunnel to Cut Prague to Pilsen Journey to 45 Minutes
World.content:
The Czech government has approved the next phase of one of its largest railway infrastructure projects: a new tunnel connecting Prague and Beroun.

Construction is expected to begin in 2032, with completion scheduled for 2044.

The 24.7-kilometre double-track tunnel will significantly shorten travel times on one of the country’s busiest rail corridors.

Once completed, trains will travel between Prague-Smíchov station and Beroun in around 13 minutes, reducing the current journey time by more than 30 minutes.

The project will also improve connections towards western Czechia and neighbouring Germany. The journey from Prague to Pilsen is expected to take approximately 45 minutes, while international rail services to Munich and Nuremberg will become faster and more reliable.

New railway line designed for speeds of up to 200 km/h

The planned railway route will include a new high-speed section designed for trains travelling at up to 200 km/h. The tunnel will begin near Prague-Smíchov station, pass beneath the Barrandov area, and emerge near Beroun.

A separate connection on the Prague side is also planned, linking the new line with Braník Bridge and Prague-Krč. The additional infrastructure will improve connections within the capital while increasing capacity on the wider railway network.

Construction preparation underway

Preparatory work for the tunnel is already in progress. Geological surveys and technical documentation are currently being completed, with the application for a construction permit expected to be submitted between 2028 and 2029.

After the approval process, Správa železnic will launch a tender to select the construction company responsible for building the tunnel.

The Czech Railway Administration estimates the total cost of the project will continue to rise due to inflation and increasing construction expenses. However, its director general Tomáš Tóth said the estimated cost of around CZK 3 billion per kilometre remains comparable with similar railway tunnel projects abroad.

The project is expected to increase railway capacity towards western Czechia, improve timetable reliability, and strengthen connections between Prague, Pilsen, and major German cities.

World.title: Thailand Brings Its Culture and Flavours to Prague at Thai Market 2026
World.content:
The colours, flavours, and warm spirit of Thailand return to the capital on Friday, 4 September 2026, as the Royal Thai Embassy proudly hosts Thai Market 2026 at the historic Písecká brána.

Organised alongside Team Thailand—comprising the Thai Trade Centre and the Tourism Authority of Thailand in Prague—this year’s flagship event is held in active cooperation with the Prague 6 Municipality.

“Thai Market has become a meaningful platform to bring Thailand closer to the Czech public through friendship, creativity, and people-to-people connections,” said H.E. Mr. Pichit Boonsud, Ambassador of the Kingdom of Thailand to the Czech Republic.

“This year, we are thrilled to celebrate Prague 6 Day with our Thai Market to show our true partnership with the local municipality. This event is a heartfelt cultural exchange and our way of actively engaging with the wonderful community that hosts us.”

Open to all ages with free admission, the event will offer a full day of authentic Thai experiences, from traditional cuisine and refreshing drinks such as Thai iced tea to popular desserts including Mango Sticky Rice and Thai tea ice cream.

Visitors can also take part in interactive workshops, including a mini Loy Krathong celebration with origami lotus basket-making, traditional Thai clothing photo sessions, and postcard design with Thai stickers.

The programme will also feature live stage performances, premium Thai products from Czech importers, traditional Thai massages, and activities where guests can win vouchers to spend at the event.

A dedicated tourism section will provide inspiration and information for those planning their next trip to Thailand. Thai Market 2026 promises to be a vibrant celebration of Thai culture, flavours, and community in the heart of Prague.

Time: 11.00-17.30

World.title: Future of Prague’s Výtoň Bridge Could Be Decided by the End of This Year
World.content:
The Railway Administration (Správa železnic) is expected to decide on the future design of Prague’s Výtoň Railway Bridge by the end of this year.

If the final plan is approved, construction could begin in 2028.

The long-delayed project has become the centre of a dispute between transport authorities and heritage experts. While railway officials argue that a new three-track structure is necessary to meet future transport demands, conservationists continue to push for the preservation of the existing historic bridge.

The Railway Administration has warned that the current condition of the bridge requires a final decision soon.

Dispute over historic structure

The main proposal currently under consideration is the construction of a new three-track railway bridge. Správa železnic selected a project team last year, but the plan remains controversial due to opposition from heritage authorities and groups seeking to preserve the original structure.

The debate has also attracted international attention. UNESCO representatives are preparing a Heritage Impact Assessment (HIA), which will examine how the planned changes could affect Prague’s cultural heritage.

The Transport Association supports the construction of a new bridge, arguing that rebuilding the existing structure would be more expensive and would not provide enough additional capacity.

Construction could start in 2028

According to earlier plans from Správa železnic, work on the project was originally expected to begin sooner. A tender process was completed in 2025, with companies SUDOP Praha and TOP CON SERVIS selected for the preparation of the three-track bridge project.

The estimated cost of the entire project is around CZK 3.4 billion.

Because of the bridge’s deteriorating condition, trains currently operate on only one track and must reduce speed when crossing the structure. The construction of the additional third track alone is expected to cost approximately CZK 129 million.

World.title: Prague Compared to 11 European Cities: Housing, Jobs, Transport,
World.content:
A new report from the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR) compares life in Prague with 11 other European cities, following a typical resident’s day—from housing and commuting to work, education, and leisure.

Based on verified data collected directly from partner cities, the study highlights both Prague’s strengths and its biggest challenges.

Prague Has Some of Europe’s Least Affordable Housing

The report found that Prague has the least affordable owner-occupied housing among the cities compared.

Buying an apartment requires more than 13 years of gross salary, placing Prague alongside cities such as Barcelona, Munich, and Amsterdam. Unlike many Western European cities, Prague also lacks relatively affordable rental housing.

Renting a 60-square-meter apartment costs around 40% of the average salary in Prague. By comparison, the same apartment would consume about 28% of average income in Munich and just 14% in Vienna.

Strong Job Market, But Lower Incomes

Prague continues to have one of the lowest unemployment rates in Europe, making it relatively easy to find work.

However, real incomes remain below those of most Western European capitals. Workers in Munich earn roughly 50% more than those in Prague, while wages in cities such as Copenhagen have grown steadily over the past decade.

Although Prague residents now work fewer hours than they did ten years ago—less than 39 hours per week on average—they still work around three hours more each week than people in many Western European cities.

Public Transport Is One of Prague’s Biggest Strengths

Prague ranks among Europe’s top cities for public transport.

Around 70% of residents use public transport regularly, while 87% report being satisfied with the service. The city’s extensive tram, metro, and rail networks make commuting easy, and the system stands out for its reliability, dense coverage, and affordability.

A monthly public transport pass costs less than 1% of the average monthly income, making Prague one of the most affordable cities for public transport after Barcelona.

Car Ownership Continues to Rise

Despite having one of Europe’s best public transport systems, Prague continues to see a steady increase in car ownership.

Together with Warsaw and Bucharest, Prague is one of the few cities in the study where the number of registered cars is still growing significantly. By contrast, cities such as Stockholm, Copenhagen, and Vienna have between one-third and one-half fewer cars per capita and a much higher share of electric and hybrid vehicles.

The report warns that increasing car ownership contributes to traffic congestion, road accidents, poorer air quality, and greater pressure on public space.

World.title: Meet the Four Prague Pizzerias Recognized in 50 Top Pizza Europa 2026
World.content:
Prague’s growing pizza scene gained international attention after four local restaurants were recognized in the 50 Top Pizza Europa 2026 guide.

The biggest success went to Pizza Nuova, which secured 30th place among the best pizzerias in Europe outside Italy. While the restaurant slipped a few places compared with last year’s ranking, it remains the only Czech establishment to appear in the guide’s main European list.

Located near Prague’s Kotva department store, Pizza Nuova has built its reputation on authentic Neapolitan pizza made with premium Italian ingredients. The restaurant also holds certification from the Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana, an organization that promotes traditional Neapolitan pizza-making standards.

Prague’s recognition extended beyond a single restaurant. Three additional venues received the guide’s Excellent Pizzerias distinction, awarded to restaurants that consistently demonstrate outstanding quality.

This year’s recipients are Da Pietro, Sasy The Original, and Diskotéka in Prague’s Dejvice district.

Diskotéka is one of this year’s notable newcomers. Shortly after opening, the restaurant attracted attention for its distinctive interior, centered around a large silver pizza oven designed to resemble a disco ball.

Alongside its food, the venue hosts DJ nights and combines a traditional pizzeria with a relaxed social gathering space.

Their assessments go well beyond the pizza itself, taking into account ingredient quality, dough preparation, baking technique, service, beverage selection, atmosphere, and the overall dining experience.

World.title: Putin again suggests Hungary could regain territory from Ukraine: what he may have meant
World.content:
Following a meeting with decorated senior officers of the Russian navy, Russian President Vladimir Putin once again hinted that Hungary could regain territory from Ukraine. According to the Russian president, Ukraine will “sooner or later lose” these lands.

Could Hungary receive territory from Ukraine?

In recent years, President Putin has seized every opportunity to weaken and divide NATO and the European Union, which he regards as his principal European adversaries. In doing so, he has not limited himself to attempting to redraw Ukraine’s eastern borders. He has also voiced opinions on the country’s western frontiers, apparently in the hope of finding political parties willing to revive grievances rooted in the period between the two world wars or in the aftermath of the Second World War. In Hungary, this approach proved successful at the time.

Speaking after a meeting with several decorated officers of the Russian navy, Putin said he was convinced that Ukraine would eventually lose its western territories.

Trump and Putin in Alaska: no success in making peace, just words. Source: Kremlin Press Office/Anadolu

“These territories once belonged to Poland, Hungary and Romania. Sooner or later – not tomorrow, perhaps not the day after tomorrow, but in one, two, ten or fifteen years – history will ultimately put everything back in its proper place,” said the Russian president, who launched the invasion of Ukraine at the end of February 2022.

Putin seeks to divide and rule

There is a reason why Putin is trying to stir unrest behind Ukraine’s front lines. According to military reports, Ukraine’s drone forces have achieved such battlefield superiority that they are now capable of seriously disrupting Russia’s rear areas. A war that only a few years ago seemed distant to the residents of Moscow and St Petersburg has become a reality, with Ukrainian strikes capable of disabling ports, military bases and critical energy infrastructure for extended periods.

There is no protection yet against the vast numbers of (AI-controlled) drone swarms. Photo: depositphotos.com

It is therefore hardly surprising that thousands of Russians now find themselves queuing for petrol – if they can obtain any at all – something virtually unheard of in recent decades.

We have rejected the idea before

This is not the first time Russian leaders have spoken about partitioning Ukraine. Former president Dmitry Medvedev previously shared a map illustrating such a scenario. Unsurprisingly, the proposal allocated Transcarpathia to Hungary, as the region belonged to Hungary until 1918 and again between 1938/39 and 1944. Around Berehove, a Hungarian community of approximately 60,000 to 70,000 people still lives today.

However, that community now accounts for only around five per cent of the population of Ukraine’s westernmost region. The same map also envisaged territorial gains for Romania and Poland.

On 4 November 2022, Putin had already suggested that these territories could be returned to the states concerned. Poland and Romania quickly and firmly rejected the proposal. The Orbán government responded later, but likewise rejected the idea, stating that such declarations were not what was needed and that the priority should instead be a ceasefire and peace negotiations. The Tisza government has not yet commented on Putin’s latest remarks.

The map shared by Putin’s ally, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev. Photo: Telegram/Medvedev

In Hungary, meanwhile, a persistent myth has circulated since the democratic transition that Mikhail Gorbachev offered Transcarpathia to the Antall government in settlement of Soviet debt, but that Hungary’s political leadership rejected the proposal and instead became the first country to recognise the territorial integrity of the newly independent Ukraine. Since then, numerous studies – as well as those directly involved – have refuted this claim.

Putin’s ally urges the Russian president to ‘freeze’ Ukraine war

Kremlin: Putin and Orbán never held talks in Russian

Russian President Vladimir Putin and former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán always conducted their talks through interpreters and never conversed in Russian, Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, told the government newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta.

President Putin and former PM Orbán last December in Moscow. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

Peskov was asked about the matter after Viktor Orbán quoted the Russian title of Nikolai Chernyshevsky’s novel What Is to Be Done? (Chto delat?) during his speech at the Tusványos Summer University on Saturday, attracting the attention of the Russian media.

“To be honest, I believe he was simply quoting the title of the work. He is an educated man,” Peskov said.

“The negotiations were never conducted in Russian; they always took place with the assistance of interpreters,” the spokesman added in the interview, as quoted by Russian news agencies.

Who is “Magyar”? The Ukrainian drone commander Russia has learned to fear

World.title: Magyar government reveals historic modernisation programme of Budapest’s suburban railway system
World.content:
The Hungarian government is repaying a decades-old debt and will upgrade the Csepel suburban railway (HÉV) line thanks to the availability of EU funds to finance the project, Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy announced on Facebook on Sunday evening.

42 brand-new suburban trains in Budapest

The minister said new low-floor, air-conditioned trains would be introduced on the Csepel, Ráckeve, and Szentendre lines, with the government to launch tenders for 42 new trains this year alone. In addition to replacing the rolling stock, platforms, power supply, and tracks will also be modernised so that “the HÉV finally provides a 21st-century service”, Vitézy said as per the Hungarian news agency.

The old, MXA-type DDR-made HÉV (suburban railway) train commuting in Budapest. They are at least 60 years old. Photo: Facebook/Dr. Kátai-Németh Vilmos

In his post, the minister said he had visited Szent Imre Square with Vilmos Kátai-Nemeth, the minister for social and family affairs (who is also the MP for Csepel, Budapest’s 21st district), to mark the adoption of the Baross Gábor Railway Development Plan.

In an attached video, Vitézy said the current trains on the line are too hot in summer, too cold in winter and not low-floor. He added that accessibility improvements are also part of the project, so platforms will be raised, and the entire road and the Csepel terminus on II. Rákóczi Ferenc street will need to be rebuilt.

Transport Minister Vitézy vows to end bus shortages across Hungary

Kátai-Németh, who lost his sight at the age of 16, remarked in the video that the trains on the Csepel HÉV line are so old that he had still been able to “see” them.

World.title: Magyar government unveils 12-point plan to save Lake Velence after water levels hit historic lows
World.content:
The Hungarian government has outlined its strategy to rescue Lake Velence, combining immediate dredging works with long-term water retention measures and new legislation aimed at protecting one of the country’s most vulnerable lakes from climate change and overdevelopment.

With the lake’s water level having fallen to around 40 centimetres, one of the lowest levels ever recorded, officials say this year will focus on damage limitation, while a broader recovery strategy is being prepared.

Emergency measures for 2026

Viktória Bögi, State Secretary for Environmental Protection, told Index that the priority is to preserve what remains of the lake by dredging parts of the lakebed. The measure is intended to keep the remaining water connected, preventing the lake from breaking into isolated pools while also helping to protect fish stocks and other wildlife.

Despite the exceptionally low water level, Bögi stressed that the water quality remains suitable for bathing, with continuous monitoring showing that the lake is currently safe for swimmers (except for 5 beaches where bathing has been prohibited until further notice: details here.)

Government rejects karst water replenishment

The government has ruled out replenishing the lake with karst water, arguing that the measure would have increased the water level by only about one centimetre while placing unnecessary pressure on valuable drinking water reserves.

Officials also said transferring water from the Danube is not currently a realistic solution. Such a project would require new pipeline infrastructure, while open canals would suffer excessive evaporation. In addition, maintaining sufficient water levels in the Danube remains essential for cooling the Paks Nuclear Power Plant during periods of low river flow.

Instead, the government believes the long-term solution lies in retaining more winter and spring precipitation within the lake’s catchment area.

A new 12-point action plan

Experts at the Ministry for a Living Environment are preparing a 12-point action plan that will address several aspects of water management. Among the proposals under consideration are:

improving existing reservoirs;

investigating water abstraction throughout the lake’s catchment area;

expanding the reuse of highly treated wastewater;

introducing measures to improve long-term water retention.

The government is also preparing a dedicated Lake Velence Act, which would introduce stricter planning rules to limit further overdevelopment along the shoreline.

Major lakeside project halted

As part of the new approach, the government has already halted a major development planned for Sukoró on the lake’s shore.

The project, previously designated as a priority investment, reportedly included plans for a 400-apartment residential complex alongside youth facilities. Officials argue that the already heavily developed lakeside could not sustain such a water-intensive project without placing additional strain on the shrinking lake.

Missing water management plans

Bögi also criticised previous administrations for failing to address the lake’s deteriorating condition. She said that while a HUF 51 billion canoe and kayaking academy had been built on the lakeshore, officials have been unable to locate documentation relating to a previously announced HUF 40 billion water replenishment plan, which had reportedly been classified for ten years.

According to the ministry, no trace of the documents has been found in official records following the handover of government departments. The state secretary also said local municipalities, businesses and civil organisations are now being included in discussions about the lake’s future after years of limited consultation.

Have you read this? Hungary gripped by alarming drought as iconic lakes and rivers face unprecedented peril

Climate adaptation becoming essential

Bögi argued that Lake Velence illustrates the broader challenges posed by climate change and increasingly frequent droughts across Hungary.

She said protecting the lake will require not only new legislation but also changes in public attitudes towards water management, including greater use of rainwater harvesting and more sustainable water consumption.

Although boating and many water sports are currently limited due to the low water level, the government continues to encourage visitors to explore the Lake Velence region, highlighting its cycling routes, hiking trails, restaurants and wellness facilities.

World.title: 14-year-old girl falls from roof of children’s home in Hungary after climbing through skylight
World.content:
A 14-year-old girl was taken to hospital after falling from the roof of a children’s home in Pécs, southern Hungary, in an incident that occurred two weeks ago. Police have confirmed that a criminal investigation is underway, while the institution has also launched an internal inquiry into the circumstances of the accident.

According to the Baranya County Police Headquarters, the investigation is being conducted as criminal proceedings, but no further details have been released.

Girl had recently been returned to the home by police

Speaking to Telex, Szilárd Sinkó, director of the Baranya Child Protection Centre, said the girl had been returned to the children’s home by police after spending more than ten days away without permission.

After arriving back at the institution, she was taken to the room designated for overnight accommodation. According to the director, she then removed the screws securing the safety chains on a kitchen skylight connected to the room and climbed out onto the roof.

The staff member on duty noticed that the girl had disappeared and was about to call the emergency services when police officers arrived at the home with another child who had also been missing.

One of the home’s residents reported seeing someone on the roof. Police immediately alerted firefighters and paramedics before searching the area around the building, where they found the girl lying on the ground below.

She received treatment at the scene before being transported to the hospital. The institution said it could not provide any information about her current condition.

Safety measures reviewed after the accident

Sinkó said an internal investigation is examining exactly how the incident occurred. He noted that standard upstairs windows had already been fitted with additional safety restraints before the accident, but the girl had managed to bypass the security chain on the roof window.

The temporary safety chain has since been replaced with a tamper-resistant fixing, while a permanent technical solution will be installed by a specialist.

Director highlights wider problems in child protection system

The director also described broader challenges facing Hungary’s child protection system. He said that during night shifts, only one child supervisor is typically responsible for an entire group of children, with additional staff available only during daytime hours.

According to Sinkó, children entering institutional care are arriving with increasingly serious mental health issues, while staff shortages, low pay, aggressive behaviour towards employees, a lack of specialist placements and growing administrative burdens continue to put pressure on the system.

He added that children who leave the institution without permission often do so because they seek greater freedom, relationships outside the home or substance use, rather than because they wish to escape the institution itself.

The Baranya branch of Hungary’s Directorate-General for Social Affairs and Child Protection described the accident as deeply distressing for the injured girl, staff members and other children living at the home. Officials said the investigation aims not only to establish the circumstances and any potential responsibility, but also to prevent similar incidents from happening again.

World.title: Putin’s ally urges the Russian president to ‘freeze’ Ukraine war
World.content:
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Saturday met with Russian President Vladimir Putin, urging him to “freeze” the Ukraine conflict and return to what he described as the “Istanbul Formula 2.0,” where “significant results were achieved.”

During a meeting with Putin in the Russian city of Omsk, Tokayev said Kazakhstan was not an outsider to the ongoing conflict but would not seek to play a mediator role, expressing confidence that “a great country,” Russia, would resolve issues on its own.

“Perhaps this conflict should be frozen, and we should return to the ‘Istanbul Formula 2.0,’ since significant results were achieved there,” Tokayev said. “Then, naturally, under guarantees from the major powers, including Russia, we can move toward the long-awaited peace.”

Tokayev said he had received numerous signals from Europe and the United States regarding the conflict, which he described as an interstate war.

He also praised what he called Putin’s “maximum diplomatic flexibility” during the summit in Anchorage, Alaska, between the Russian president and US President Donald Trump in August last year.

“And all of this must be stopped, because what is happening, in my convinced opinion, is to the advantage and delight of the opponents of both Russia and the Ukrainian state,” he added.

Tokayev did not clarify his remarks concerning the “Istanbul formula,” but the Turkish metropolis has hosted peace talks between Russia and Ukraine, first in the initial weeks of the ongoing war, which produced a framework for a possible deal.

In mid-2025, three rounds of renewed peace talks were also held in Istanbul — on 16 May, 2 June, and 23 July — which produced major prisoner swaps and draft memorandums outlining positions of both sides for a potential peace deal.

Astana International Forum 2025, Kazakhstan. Photo: Kazakhstan Presidential Press Office

Developing ties

Tokayev further commented on Kazakh-Russian ties, saying Russia is effectively becoming the leading investor in his country’s economy, with volumes reaching nearly $30 billion.

“Interestingly, through joint efforts, we have identified a pool of 177 promising industrial projects, 122 of which have already been implemented, with a total project value of $53 billion,” Tokayev said.

Defining this to be a significant number “given the challenging geopolitical conditions of the current era,” Tokayev went on to speak about Kazakhstan’s project of building its first nuclear power plant. Tokayev stated he has been informed that field work on the site near Lake Balkhash is nearing completion.

“This project isn’t just about producing a new form of energy in Kazakhstan. It’s a project that will bring our countries and, most importantly, our peoples, particularly the younger generation, closer together,” Tokayev said.

“After all, we’re talking about training technical personnel with Russia’s help, local Kazakh personnel who would then be capable of working in this very complex field, the nuclear industry. Therefore, I believe all other issues are progressing quite well,” he added.

For his part, Putin praised the development of Russian-Kazakh ties, describing them as “truly strategic in nature—not just in words, but in deeds.”

“This is evidenced by the growing level of trade turnover. Last year, we had almost $28 billion, $27.8 billion, to be precise—a decent figure,” he said.

Describing this as a “positive trend” indicating they have good prospects, Putin said these prospects are determined, among other things, by investment.

“Here, too, we have something to brag about: we have 70 projects involving Russian companies and Russian businesses, totalling approximately $30 billion,” Putin said, noting Russia is the largest investor in the Kazakh economy in this sense, and in a wide range of sectors.

He also said that they actively cooperate internationally and are actively involved in all regional organisations, including the Collective Security Treaty Organisation and the Eurasian Economic Union.

Concerning the topic of Ukraine, Putin later told his Kazakh counterpart that he would inform him about it in detail during their conversation.

Russia: Kazakh proposal impossible due to Kyiv’s position

The Kremlin said on Saturday that Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s proposal to “freeze” the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war is “impossible” given Kyiv’s position. “Freezing (the war) as such is not possible,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted as saying by Russian media outlets, including state news agency Tass.

Peskov was quoted as saying that Russia’s conditions for a halt to hostilities are clear and the war could end “by the end of the day” if Ukraine makes the “appropriate decisions,” referring to Moscow’s demand for a Ukrainian withdrawal from the Donbas region, as well as Kyiv’s abandonment of plans to join NATO.

“For us there is one main condition –- we must achieve our goals,” Peskov went on to say, adding Russian President Vladimir Putin provided Tokayev with a detailed update on the progress of what Moscow calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin on 17 June 2026. Photo: Anadolu Agency

Kyiv welcomes Kazakh president’s call to freeze the war

Ukraine on Sunday welcomed Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s call to “freeze” the war Russia launched in 2022, with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha describing the suggestion as “realistic, timely, and wise.”

“We appreciate President @TokayevKZ telling Putin it is time to stop the war. A realistic, timely, and wise message,” Sybiha wrote on US social media platform X.

We appreciate President @TokayevKZ telling Putin it is time to stop the war. A realistic, timely, and wise message. Ukraine has proposed stopping the war along current frontlines and turning to diplomacy, but the Kremlin continues to reject this clear path to peace. He said Ukraine proposed halting the fighting along the current front lines and turning to diplomacy, claiming that the Kremlin “continues to reject this clear path to peace.”

“Putin’s spokesman has already dismissed the Kazakh President’s proposal as well,” Sybiha added. “The bottom line: Moscow must feel more pressure before it accepts realistic peace proposals.”

World.title: Budapest Mayor calls for renewal of Népliget as opportunity comes with government change
World.content:
Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony has welcomed the government’s willingness to consider renovating the long-abandoned Budapest Planetarium and the Népliget, while sharply criticising the previous Orbán administration for allowing the landmark educational attraction to fall into disrepair.

In a Facebook post published over the weekend, Karácsony said the Planetarium, located in the Népliget (People’s Park in English), had been an important place of learning for generations before closing in 2017. Since then, he said, the building’s condition has steadily deteriorated.

“Among the Orbán government’s many failures was allowing the Planetarium in Népliget to decay,” the mayor wrote.

Minister signals support for renovation

Karácsony revealed that he had recently raised the Planetarium’s future with Zoltán Tanács, Hungary’s Minister for Science and Technology, who announced on Friday that he intends to recommend to the government that the building be renovated and given a new purpose.

The mayor described the announcement as encouraging, arguing that the future of the Planetarium cannot be separated from the wider regeneration of Népliget. “The renewal of the Planetarium and Népliget is inconceivable without one another,” he said.

Hungary’s largest historic public park

Karácsony described Népliget as Hungary’s largest historic public park, stressing that its restoration is not merely a Budapest issue but a project of national importance encompassing urban development, environmental protection and cultural heritage.

The park, jointly owned by the capital, the state and the district authority, has suffered decades of decline despite its valuable tree stock and protected status as a historic garden since 2005. According to the mayor, the deteriorating condition of the Planetarium has contributed to the park’s broader decline.

Masterplan already prepared

The Budapest Municipality says it has spent several years preparing a comprehensive redevelopment strategy for Népliget as part of its Radó Dezső Plan.

The project has included public consultations, cooperation with government bodies and district authorities, the preparation of a strategic development plan and a landscape architecture design competition held in 2022. Based on the winning proposals, the city is now finalising an implementation plan that would guide the park’s gradual transformation.

The plans include renovating green spaces throughout the park, improving pedestrian, cycling and public transport access, expanding recreational and leisure facilities, calming traffic on roads that currently divide the park, demolishing abandoned pavilions, and resolving long-standing land ownership issues. Here are the original plans from 2022:

Transport improvements could transform the park

Karácsony also highlighted several major transport projects that could significantly improve access to Népliget. The Hungarian Museum of Transport will remain adjacent to the park, while the planned development of Budapest’s Orbital Railway (Körvasút) is expected to include a new railway station serving the area.

Combined with existing metro, tram, bus and cycling links, these investments could make Népliget one of the capital’s most accessible public parks, opening up new opportunities for recreation and tourism.

Funding dispute with previous government

The mayor argued that the first phase of the regeneration could have been financed through European Union funding, but claimed the previous government blocked the project for political reasons. He expressed hope that Hungary’s new government would instead become a partner in delivering both the Planetarium’s restoration and the wider renewal of Népliget.

Karácsony said he has already sent the detailed redevelopment plans to Science and Technology Minister Zoltán Tanács, seeking cooperation on what he described as a historic opportunity to restore one of Budapest’s most significant public spaces.

More on Budapest: Easier after dark: Budapest expands night transport to a lot more suburbs

A park with more than 120 years of history

Népliget’s origins date back to the late 19th century, when landscaping began on the site of a former sand quarry and landfill. Its development accelerated ahead of Hungary’s Millennium celebrations in 1896, providing new green space while nearby City Park was occupied by exhibition grounds.

The park enjoyed its heyday between the two world wars, featuring amusement attractions and entertainment venues, while prestigious motor races were held there until the 1970s. From 1977 until its closure in 2017, the Budapest Planetarium became one of the city’s best-known educational attractions, introducing generations of visitors to astronomy and space science.

World.title: PM Magyar presents Hungarian Grand Prix trophy to Lando Norris after record-breaking race
World.content:
Lando Norris received the prestigious Herend porcelain winner’s trophy from Prime Minister Péter Magyar after claiming victory at the 41st Hungarian Grand Prix at the Hungaroring on Sunday.

The McLaren driver finished ahead of Max Verstappen and Kimi Antonelli in front of a record crowd at the Hungarian circuit. As part of the traditional podium ceremony, Magyar also presented Norris with the winner’s medal.

PM congratulates drivers and event organisers

Following the race, the prime minister shared photographs with all three podium finishers on Facebook.

“Incredible excitement, a fantastic race and a record number of spectators,” Magyar wrote. “Congratulations to all the drivers and to the thousands of our fellow Hungarians who helped organise the event.”

Awarding trophies at Formula 1 races by local political leaders is a long-established tradition. Previous Hungarian Grands Prix have featured senior government officials presenting the trophies, and this year Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai also took part in the podium ceremony alongside the prime minister.

Norris avoids repeat of 2023 trophy mishap

Norris handled the famous Herend porcelain trophy with extra care this year, avoiding a repeat of the memorable 2023 podium incident when Max Verstappen accidentally smashed his Herend trophy during the celebrations.

Hungary aims to secure Formula 1 beyond 2032

Before the race, Magyar held talks at the Hungaroring with Formula 1 President and CEO Stefano Domenicali. Following the meeting, the prime minister said negotiations would continue over extending Hungary’s place on the Formula 1 calendar after the current agreement expires in 2032.

“Our goal is to ensure that the Hungaroring continues to host Formula 1 under the best possible conditions,” Magyar said, adding that the government remains committed to maintaining the race in Hungary for years to come.

The Hungarian Grand Prix, first held in 1986, was the first Formula 1 race staged behind the Iron Curtain and remains one of the championship’s most historic venues.

World.title: PM Magyar holds talks with F1 CEO: Here’s what he said about keeping Formula 1 beyond 2032
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has confirmed that Hungary wants to remain on the Formula 1 calendar well beyond the current contract, following talks with Formula 1 President and CEO Stefano Domenicali at the Hungaroring during the 41st Hungarian Grand Prix.

Speaking after the meeting in Mogyoród on Sunday, Magyar said the government’s objective is to ensure that Formula 1 continues to be held in Hungary under the best possible conditions after the current agreement expires.

Hungary and Formula 1 discussing the future

Hungary’s contract with Liberty Media currently runs until 2032, but Magyar revealed that discussions have already begun about a possible five-year extension included as an option in the agreement.

“We agreed with Formula 1’s leadership to continue negotiations. The goal is to secure the best possible conditions so that the Hungaroring and Formula 1 remain in Hungary,” the prime minister said.

He described the Hungarian Grand Prix as a major success, noting that a record number of spectators attended the event, Sunday’s race was sold out, and tickets had been unavailable for some time.

Photo: MTI

More than just a race weekend

Magyar said discussions with Domenicali also focused on extending Formula 1 weekends into longer events that generate greater economic and tourism benefits for host countries.

He pointed out that the temporary facilities in the paddock also serve as venues for business leaders holding investment talks during the race weekend, creating additional economic opportunities beyond motorsport.

According to the prime minister, Hungary should make the most of both the tourism and investment potential generated by Formula 1.

Péter Magyar (l), Czech President Petr Pavel (c) and International Automobile Federation President Mohammed Ben Sulayem (r). Photo: MTI

Hungaroring support remains unchanged

Magyar stressed that the change of government will not affect support for the Hungaroring. However, he said the new administration intends to review the previous government’s spending on the circuit’s redevelopment. Under the existing contract, approximately HUF 90 billion was spent on renovating and constructing facilities at the venue.

“At first glance the investment appears successful, but the devil is in the details,” Magyar said, adding that the government wants to examine how public funds were used and whether costs could have been managed more efficiently.

He also announced that Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai, who is responsible for sport within the government, will conduct a detailed review of the financial figures in the coming days.

Have you read this? Two centuries of history: Why the Hungarian Grand Prix trophy is so iconic

Hungarian fans and a historic circuit

Reflecting on Formula 1’s place in Hungary, Magyar said he had been a supporter of Nigel Mansell, later cheering for Ayrton Senna and Michael Schumacher.

He added that he would like to see more Hungarian fans attending the race, even though 70–80% of spectators currently come from abroad, making the event an important tourism and country-branding asset.

Magyar also highlighted Hungary’s historic place in Formula 1, recalling that the 1986 Hungarian Grand Prix was the first Formula 1 race held behind the Iron Curtain.

According to the prime minister, Domenicali praised the enthusiasm of Hungarian fans and acknowledged the long-standing popularity of Formula 1 in the country. Magyar concluded by saying the championship benefits from a highly professional team and that Hungarians should be proud of the significant contribution made by local professionals to the success of the event.

World.title: Six symphonic concerts to headline 2026 Enescu International Competition in Bucharest
World.content:
Six symphonic concerts featuring internationally renowned conductors, Romanian orchestras, and young musicians from around the world will form the centerpiece of the 2026 George Enescu International Competition. The 20th edition will take place in Bucharest from August 23 to September 19.

The concerts, all scheduled to take place at the Romanian Athenaeum, will include the opening concert, the Composition Section final, the conducting masterclass closing concert, and the finals of the cello, violin, and piano competitions.

The competition will open on August 23 with the Romanian Radio National Orchestra conducted by artistic director Cristian Măcelaru. The program will feature the three winners of the 2024 edition - violinist Mayumi Kanagawa, cellist Yo Kitamura, and pianist Roman Lopatynskyi - and include works by Diego Santamaria, Dan Dediu, and George Enescu.

On August 27, the Composition Section final will feature the Romanian National Radio Orchestra under conductor Marin Alsop. Composer and pianist Zygmunt Krauze, who chairs the composition jury, will perform his own Piano Concerto No. 3 - Fragments of Memory. The program will also include works by Sarah Kirkland Snider, Steven Mackey, and Doina Rotaru.

The conducting masterclass will conclude on August 28 with a concert by the Romanian Youth Orchestra led by Cristian Măcelaru and three young conductors selected from the masterclass participants. The program includes works by George Enescu, Livia Teodorescu-Ciocănea, Giuseppe Verdi, and Béla Bartók.

The instrumental finals begin with the cello competition on September 7, accompanied by the Romanian Radio National Orchestra under American conductor Case Scaglione.

The violin final will take place on September 13, featuring the George Enescu Philharmonic Orchestra conducted by Harry Ogg, while the competition will conclude on September 19 with the piano final, performed with the George Enescu Philharmonic Orchestra under conductor Daniela Candillari.

Tickets and season passes are available through Eventim, as well as at Cărturești and Humanitas bookstores across Romania. Students, pupils, and teachers from music schools and universities, as well as people with disabilities and their companions, are eligible for free admission, subject to availability.

World.title: Drone briefly enters Romanian airspace on fourth consecutive day of incursions
World.content:
Another drone briefly entered Romanian airspace on Monday morning, July 27, before flying to Ukraine, prompting the Romanian Air Force to scramble two F-16 fighter jets and authorities to issue a RO-Alert warning to residents in Tulcea County. Unlike the previous three incidents, the drone was not shot down.

The Ministry of National Defense said its radar surveillance system detected the aerial target east of Sulina. Two F-16 fighter jets from the 86th Air Base in Borcea took off at 8:53 a.m. to monitor the situation, while the National Military Command Centre instructed the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations to send a RO-Alert message to residents in Tulcea County at 8:47 a.m.

“The target briefly entered Romanian airspace before crossing the border and heading toward Ukraine. Shortly afterwards, explosions were reported on Ukrainian territory,” the ministry said.

Monday’s incident marks the fourth consecutive day in which a drone has entered Romanian airspace. The previous three drones, which crossed into the country on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, were intercepted and shot down by Romanian Air Force F-16 fighter jets.

Following Friday's incident, president Nicușor Dan said the drone destroyed that day was a Russian Shahed model and announced that Romania would lodge a diplomatic protest with Russia.

Separately, interim foreign minister Oana Țoiu told Digi24 that Romania has the option of invoking Article 4 of the North Atlantic Treaty, under which any NATO member can request consultations whenever it considers its security or territorial integrity to be under threat.

Țoiu also said Romania's decision to summon the Russian ambassador to Bucharest was a diplomatic protest, noting that similar steps had been taken in the past, including after a Russian drone crashed into an apartment building in Galați a few weeks ago.

World.title: Works of Romanian sculptor Constantin Brâncuși drawing large crowds to Berlin museum
World.content:
The works of Romanian sculptor Constantin Brâncuși (1876-1957) are drawing large crowds to the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin, according to an announcement by the museum cited by BZ Berlin.

The museum is currently hosting the first comprehensive Brâncuși exhibition organized in Germany for more than 50 years. The exhibition, scheduled until August 9, is already the most visited since the one dedicated to German painter Gerhard Richter, held in 2012.

The organization of the event was made possible due to the temporary closure for renovation of the Centre Pompidou in Paris, one of the institutions holding the most important collection of the artist’s works. This context made it possible to borrow rare works and bring them together in a landmark exhibition in Berlin.

According to the museum, the exhibition will likely draw 300,000 visitors in total, confirming the international impact of the work of the artist born in Romania.

Brâncuși is considered the founder of modern sculpture. “His organic forms, reduced to their essence, established him as a pioneer of sculptural abstraction in the early 20th century. Brâncuși’s continuous search for an artistic ideal is reflected in the formal variations of a few central motifs and his playful use of different materials and surfaces. He masterfully employed pedestals, light, movement, as well as photography and film to stage his sculptures,” the institution said on its website.

“'Brâncuși' is one of the most important exhibitions in the history of the Neue Nationalgalerie,” said museum director Klaus Biesenbach. “We are grateful to be able to present this grand master of early modernism, who is surprisingly less well-known in Germany, to a truly large audience,” he added.

Given the high public interest, the museum decided to extend visiting hours during the final two days of the exhibition, on August 7 and 8. One ticket to the Brâncuși show costs EUR 16.

Constantin Brâncuși, born in Romania and later settled in France, is considered by historians and the world’s major museums as one of the founders of modern sculpture, having decisively influenced the evolution of contemporary art.

World.title: Rețele Electrice Romania modernizes transformer substation in Timișoara after EUR 5 million investment
World.content:
Rețele Electrice Romania, part of the PPC group in Romania, has completed the modernization works for the 110/20 kV Freidorf transformer substation in Timișoara after a RON 26 million (approximately EUR 5.13 million) investment.

The station serves around 9,000 customers in the Freidorf area of the city.

The 110/20 kV Freidorf transformer substation was built in 1979. In the event of unplanned interruptions, it can take over the power supply of adjacent stations, thus supplying up to 60,000 customers.

The substation's modernization works began in April 2024. The works involved replacing both the primary equipment that ensures the proper functioning of the transformer station, as well as the secondary protections and circuits. The Freidorf substation is equipped with two transformers of 110/20 kV with a power of 25MVA each, two overhead line bays of 110 kV, 17 medium-voltage bays of 20 kV each, one coupling bay of 20 kV, two neutral treatment group bays, and internal services of 20/0.4kV.

The equipment replaced during the modernization works includes a 110/20 kV power transformer; all 20 kV medium-voltage bays, the internal services, the medium-voltage network's neutral treatment groups and the associated arc suppression coils. In addition, the secondary circuits and electromechanical protections were replaced with digital protections, both for the 110 kV line bays and the 110/20 kV transformers, as well as those for the medium-voltage bays.

Rețele Electrice Romania operates networks with a total length of about 136.000 kilometers in three major areas of the country: Muntenia Sud (including Bucharest), Banat and Dobrogea, covering one third of the local distribution market. The electricity infrastructure operated by Rețele Electrice Romania includes 293 power stations and over 26.000 secondary substations.

World.title: Verita's Strongest IB Results Yet and What the Diploma Is Really Teaching Students: 'The Goal Is Not Only to Acquire Knowledge, but to Think with Flexibility, Judgement, and Intellectual Curiosity'
World.content:
Business Views

As more Romanian families weigh international education options, the IB Diploma Programme stands out for combining academic breadth with independent research and critical thinking.

Romania Insider spoke with Doria Draghiciu, Deputy Head of Secondary High School at Verita International School in Bucharest, about how the IB's inquiry-based approach differs from traditional education, how universities view the diploma, and the school's recent highlights, including its strongest IB results in recent years, with a cohort average of 32.2 points and one student scoring 44 out of 45.

How does the IB's inquiry-based approach differ from more traditional models of education?

Doria Draghiciu: The IB inquiry-based approach differs from more traditional models of education mainly in the way knowledge is constructed and used. In a traditional model, knowledge is transferred from the teacher to the student directly. The student uses it to solve some kind of exercise and is then assessed on whether they can reproduce that knowledge on a test.



The IB does not reject knowledge taken in this way or direct instruction. In fact, strong inquiry cannot happen without subject knowledge. Where the IB differs is that it asks students to go beyond the acquisition of knowledge. Students are challenged to question, make connections, investigate and build models in unfamiliar situations, as well as reflect on the process of learning itself. In order to do this, the process starts from the practical experience and builds the abstract concepts afterwards. Students start with an applied example and find the general rules after identifying the patterns.



In this sense, the role of the teacher is central and shifts from the traditional model. The teacher is still an expert and provides knowledge, explanation, feedback, and assessment, but the lessons are transformed into learning experiences that require students to be conceptual learners and independent thinkers. The goal is not only for students to acquire knowledge, but that they look at what they know with more flexibility, judgement, and intellectual curiosity.

How do universities weigh the IB Diploma against A-Levels, AP, or national curricula in admissions decisions?

Doria Draghiciu: Universities recognise the IB Diploma as a strong and challenging qualification, alongside A Levels, AP, and national curricula. Each system has its own strengths. A Levels allow students to specialise earlier, and AP offers flexibility, especially for students applying within the American system.



At Verita, one of the reasons we value the IB Diploma is that it gives students both breadth and depth. Students study six subjects, so they continue to develop across languages, humanities, sciences, mathematics, and the arts or electives, while also going deeper in their Higher Level subjects. This means they do not close doors too early, but they still have the academic depth needed for competitive university courses.



Through its Diploma Core, the IB also gives universities a fuller picture of the student. Through the Extended Essay (EE), students complete independent research. Through the Theory of Knowledge (TOK), they learn to question how knowledge is built and evaluated. Through Creativity, Activity, Service (CAS), they engage with creativity, activity, and service beyond the classroom. So universities are not only seeing subject grades, but also evidence of research skills, critical thinking, time management, reflection, and balance.



I would not frame the IB as better than every other system for every student. But I do think its advantage is that it prepares students very well for university life, not only because of what they study, but because of how they learn to think, manage work, and take responsibility for their own learning.

How does Verita support students in their IBDP?

Doria Draghiciu: At Verita, we support students in the IB DP through both academic and pastoral structures. Students have strong subject teaching, but they are also supported through Core time, TOK, CAS, Extended Essay guidance, mock exams, reflection meetings, academic tracking, university counselling, and individual follow-up.



The DP is not only challenging because of the content. It is challenging because students have to manage deadlines, independent research, internal assessments, exams, CAS, and university planning at the same time. So our role is to help students understand the programme, plan ahead, and build the habits they need to manage it well.



We also work closely as a team. Teachers, the DP Coordinator, the counsellor, learning support, parents, and students themselves are all part of the support system. Our aim is to help students become independent, but not isolated. They are expected to take ownership, but we give them the structures and guidance to learn how to do that.

How do you involve parents in their child's DP journey?

Doria Draghiciu: We involve parents by trying to make the Diploma Programme less mysterious. From the outside, the DP can look like just another school programme with final exams at the end, but it is much more layered than that. There are internal assessments, the Extended Essay, TOK, CAS, predicted grades, university applications, and deadlines that come at different moments across the two-year programme.



So our role is to communicate clearly and early on, not only when something has gone wrong. We use parent information sessions, individual meetings, reports, emails, and follow-up conversations to help parents understand both the programme and their child's progress.



I think parents are an important part of the DP journey, but their role is not to manage things for the student. Their role is to understand the pressure points, support routines at home, encourage balance, and help students become more independent over time.

What were the school's highlights in the past academic year?

Doria Draghiciu: The Class of 2026 delivered Verita's strongest IB Diploma results in recent years, marking the highest cohort average of 32.2 points. One student's near-perfect score of 44 out of a possible 45 points stands out as an exceptional achievement, placing them among the very top IB performers worldwide.



One of the main highlights of the past academic year was our IB evaluation visit. It was an important moment for Verita because it allowed us to pause, reflect on the Diploma Programme, and look honestly at both our strengths and our next steps. The process confirmed many things we are proud of, especially our culture of care, our student support, and the way teachers work together around students.



We also continued to strengthen the Core of the programme, especially TOK, CAS, and the Extended Essay. The TOK Exhibition was a real highlight this year. It was a hit with students, teachers, and the wider school community, and it gave students a meaningful opportunity to show how they are thinking about knowledge, perspective, evidence, and real-world objects.



Another important highlight was the development of our university counselling programme, supported by the Dukes network, which has significantly improved the way we support students in thinking about pathways, careers, and university choices. This has made the process more intentional and has helped students and families have these conversations earlier and with more clarity.



For me, the highlight is not a single event. It is seeing the programme become more intentional, more coherent, and more connected to who we are as a school.



*This business view wast edited by Romania Insider for Verita.

World.title: Trade union federation Sanitas prepares for general strike in Romanian hospitals
World.content:
The Sanitas Federation of trade unions in the Romanian medical system is preparing to launch a general strike, scheduled for Tuesday, July 28, according to Informat.ro. The interim Labour Ministry assured, however, that most of the employees in the public health system will earn more and none will earn less under the new Wage Law.

The day before, on July 27 at 1:00 PM, the National Council of the Federation will meet to decide the details of the protest, with the main dissatisfaction being the draft Wage Law for the budgetary sector.

According to union leaders, the strike will affect 400 hospitals, meaning the majority of public hospitals in Romania. The law requires a plan, which must ensure the continuity of emergency services, with at least a third of employees at work.

The federation has obtained a provisional suspension of the consultations for the Wage Law, but it is not a final decision.

The unionists are challenging persistent wage inequities and a bonus system that does not accurately reflect working conditions. They have also requested mediation from the Romanian president.

Responding to unionists' concerns, the interim minister of labour, Dragoș Pîslaru, claimed that over two-thirds of employees in the healthcare sector will benefit from salary increases under the Wage Law, emphasising that no decrease in income will occur.

"The truth is that no income [total income, including bonuses] will decrease under the proposed Wage Law. This is a principle that was agreed upon with the political parties, and it serves as a very clear protection, and I can tell you without any hesitation that there is no question of anyone in the health sector earning less under the new Wage Law," the minister said.

He dismissed the information about salary cuts as false and explained that the unions' protests are caused by their desire to obtain higher increases.

Pîslaru mentioned that RON 2.5 billion is supplementary allocated for the healthcare sector next year, and the number of employees who will not benefit from income raises could drop below 15% through adjustments to the regulations.

iulian@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Inquam Photos/George Călin)

World.title: New poll shows Social Democrats ahead of Liberals, competing for second place in Romania
World.content:
The Alliance for the Unity of Romanians (AUR) continues to lead in Romanians' voting intentions, according to a CURS poll published on July 26, while the fight for second place is tight – with the difference between Social Democrats (PSD, second place) and Liberals (PNL, third place) being smaller than the margin of error. The poll also indicated that most Romanians do not wish for early elections (58% versus 33%) or the dismissal of president Nicusor Dan (57% versus 31%).

While early elections may result in a similar distribution of seats in Parliament, small changes such as PSD losing ground and falling to third place may have major implications at the top of the parties, possibly giving a chance to the formation of a ruling coalition that seems impossible at this moment.

According to the CURS survey, AUR is credited with 34% of voting intentions. In second place is PSD, with 23%, closely followed by PNL, with 21%, Adevarul reported. The ranking is completed by USR, with 9%, and UDMR, with 4%.

SOS Romania would be below the electoral threshold, with 3% of voting options. PNRR, founded by Cristian Popescu Piedone, and the Conservative Action (ACT), led by former AUR leader Claudiu Târziu, are each credited with 2% of voting intentions, as is the "Other Party" option.

POT, a party that crossed the electoral threshold in 2024, does not appear in the opinion poll.

An IRES poll published last week also placed AUR in first place, but credited the party with a higher score, 40%. In the same survey, commissioned by PSD, the Social Democrats were in second place, with 21%, and the PNL in third place, with 17%.

In contrast, the survey by the Political Rating Agency, conducted between June 30 and July 3, placed PNL in second place, ahead of PSD. AUR was credited with 36.4% of voting intentions, followed by PNL, with 22.4%, and PSD, with 17.9%. USR was credited with 10.5%, and UDMR with 4.9%.
