Instead, they rely on candidates’ experience, references from previous employers and personal interviews.

“Over the past few years, salaries at our company have increased by around 30% on average. Higher levels of professionalism among staff have largely driven that increase. Every employee takes professional development courses or retrains in a new field. As people gain knowledge and experience, they expect higher pay. If they don’t receive the salary they believe they deserve, they start looking for another job. That staff turnover has become a major challenge for large companies,” the HR specialist explains.

She says employers have also started investing more in their employees’ skills. Many companies now pay for foreign language courses, mainly English, as well as training abroad in manufacturing, technology and other fields.

She believes this growing coordination has improved the quality of Armenia’s labour market. When someone from another company applies for a job with her employer, she can now openly discuss the candidate’s abilities and professional qualities with HR managers at their previous workplace.

“In the past, asking someone for an opinion about a job applicant felt awkward. Now I simply send an email and receive a reply within a few days. The only real difficulty today is finding highly specialised professionals and technical staff. Problems usually arise when we urgently need to hire someone like a driver, security guard or cleaner. Candidates for these jobs tend to be very conservative. For example, if they need to stay just 10 minutes beyond the end of their shift, they often show little flexibility. Some may even leave work during the day without informing anyone.”

According to her, wages for these positions have risen by a larger percentage than salaries for many higher-skilled professions, including finance specialists and translators.

Working conditions are more attractive at foreign companies

Ilona Khachatryan is a logistics specialist. She now works for an American company and earns four times more than she did two years ago in the same role at a local firm. But salary is only part of the reason she left. She says unhealthy relations with management at her former company also played a major role. More broadly, she is critical of hiring practices and personnel management at many local organisations.

“At the company where I worked, it was extremely difficult to receive the bonuses that management itself had promised. To avoid paying them, they would even falsify hourly timesheets.

I applied for jobs at other local companies as well. I attended interviews and then waited for months without hearing back. Even if they decide not to hire you, shouldn’t they at least tell you? After all, you invest your time and effort preparing for those interviews. Foreign companies treat candidates much more fairly. They make transparent hiring decisions. If they decide not to hire someone, they explain in detail why they cannot move forward with the candidate.”

Ilona says her current employer hired her after the first interview. The company immediately explained the salary, holiday entitlement, employment rights and job responsibilities.

“Hearing the words ‘thank you for your work’ genuinely motivates me. It gives me energy and makes me work with greater enthusiasm and commitment. And when your employer also recognises your achievements, you realise just how undervalued professionals are in the local labour market.”

Analysis of labour market trends in Armenia

World.title: Azerbaijan changes status of internally displaced people: What do new rules provide?
World.content:
The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

On 23 July, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed into law amendments to the Law on the Status of Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons and the Law on the Social Protection of Internally Displaced Persons and Persons Equated with Them.

The amendments to the Housing Code provide for the creation of a Permanent Resettlement Fund in the territories liberated from occupation. Housing from the fund will be used to resettle internally displaced persons (IDPs) to the reclaimed territories and will later be transferred to them as private property.

The legislation also clarifies the grounds on which a person may lose IDP status. This applies to those who refuse housing offered by the state, as well as to those who are provided with alternative housing that meets the officially established housing standard for the relevant region instead of accommodation in their previous place of residence. At the same time, social protection measures will remain in place for three years after a person loses or voluntarily relinquishes their IDP status.

The changes are intended to strengthen the legal framework for the Great Return programme. In practice, however, they could significantly affect the lives of hundreds of thousands of people who have spent decades building their lives in Baku and other parts of Azerbaijan.

The purpose of the law and the benefits linked to IDP status

Under the previous legislation, internally displaced person (IDP) status entitled holders to a range of social benefits, including a monthly allowance of 60 manats (about $35) for each family member, state-funded tuition at fee-paying departments of public universities, and exemptions from certain government fees and utility payments.

For people forced to flee their homes in the early 1990s and who had spent decades living in dormitories, temporary housing units or other makeshift accommodation, these benefits represented a basic form of social support. The status also carried legal significance, as it formally recognised that they had been displaced against their will.

Under the new rules, the state is deemed to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers an internally displaced person permanent housing. If the person accepts the apartment, ownership is transferred to them, but they simultaneously lose their IDP status. Those who refuse the offer also lose their status and may forfeit the temporary accommodation provided to them in Baku or another city.

During a three-year transition period, only social support measures, including financial assistance and education benefits, will remain in place. The legal status itself, along with the other rights and guarantees associated with it, will cease to apply.

Freedom of choice and the problem of “any available housing”

The law refers to “alternative housing that complies with the standards established for the region of residence”. In practice, this means that internally displaced people are not necessarily offered housing in their native village or on their ancestral land.

For example, a person who owned several hectares of farmland before being displaced may now be offered a house in a newly built settlement with a plot of only 100–200 square metres. Ownership of their original land is not restored, as the state provides housing only. As a result, the concept of “returning home” is significantly narrowed.

According to dozens of families whose accounts have been shared on social media and in public appeals, many of the homes offered to them suffer from poor construction. They report leaking roofs during rainfall, flooded yards, and repeated disruptions to gas, water and electricity supplies. In some cases, applicants say they have been told verbally: “You’ve been given a house — be grateful, or you’ll lose that too.”

Similar complaints have also been submitted through official grievance mechanisms, although the issue has yet to generate wider public debate.

Life in Baku after three decades of integration

A large proportion of Azerbaijan’s internally displaced people have spent more than 30 years living in Baku and other major economic centres. Over that time, they have found employment, received an education, gained access to healthcare and established stable social networks. After losing their homes in the early 1990s, they were provided with temporary accommodation by the state, including places in dormitories, unfinished buildings and container settlements, as well as apartments in purpose-built residential complexes.

Under the new rules, however, this housing may be reclaimed once a person loses IDP status. As a result, many people face a difficult choice: accept an apartment in Karabakh and leave behind the life they have built in Baku, or lose both their IDP status and the accommodation provided to them by the state.

International human rights standards, including the UN Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement, require that return be voluntary, safe and carried out in dignity. These principles are based on freedom of choice, the provision of adequate housing and, wherever possible, the restoration of rights to former property. Under Azerbaijan’s new legislation, however, the state is considered to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers housing, while refusing that offer results in the loss of IDP status. This weakens the principle that return should be voluntary.

Official position and expert assessments

Pro-government media outlets, including Milli.az, Report.az and APA, have presented the amendments in a positive light, using phrases such as “restoring property rights”, “sustainable social support” and “providing a legal framework for the Great Return programme”.

MP Vugar Bayramov has also argued that the three-year transition period demonstrates the state’s continued commitment to social support. Official statements emphasise that the new housing is transferred into private ownership rather than provided on a rental basis, which the authorities say will encourage people to settle permanently in the region.

At the same time, independent observers and some human rights advocates argue that the changes restrict freedom of choice, fail to fully restore land rights and raise other concerns. They also point to the contrast between the urban lifestyles that many IDPs have built over the past three decades and the newly established rural settlements, as well as the risks of unemployment and inadequate infrastructure.

The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

World.title: EU’s 21st sanctions package targets Kulevi oil terminal and cryptocurrency platforms in Georgia
World.content:
Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

The European Union’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia includes an oil refinery in the Georgian town of Kulevi and several cryptocurrency platforms.

The sanctions against the Kulevi refinery, which processes and sells Russian oil, include a six-month grace period. The ban on transactions will take effect after six months unless the refinery changes its business practices.

The Kulevi refinery had previously been considered for inclusion in the EU’s 20th package of sanctions against Russia, but was ultimately removed from the sanctions list.

At the time, the EU said that “the Georgian authorities and the port operator had made positive commitments.” This was stated in a letter from the EU’s Special Envoy, David O’Sullivan, to Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili.

What does the new sanctions package include?

The EU’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia, which is expected to take effect shortly, was formally approved by the permanent representatives of the EU member states on 23 July 2026.

The sanctions are expected to enter into force on 23 July following approval by EU leaders and their publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.

The measures target sectors of the Russian economy that generate significant revenue for Moscow’s war in Ukraine, including energy, financial services and the cryptocurrency sector.

The package also imposes sanctions on more than 50 companies and organisations involved in supplying military goods and weapons to Russia.

It includes the EU’s largest-ever round of individual sanctions, targeting a total of 218 entities — 48 individuals and 170 legal entities.

It is one of the most significant expansions of the EU’s sanctions regime in the past four years.

Sanctions against the Kulevi refinery

“The package introduces the possibility of banning transactions with oil refineries listed in Russia and third countries that process Russian crude oil and petroleum products. Under these measures, the EU is imposing a ban on transactions with the Georgian oil refinery in Kulevi, which processes and trades Russian oil. The ban will take effect in six months,” the EU said in a statement.

According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, citing a source familiar with the matter, the introduction of a six-month deadline is unprecedented in EU sanctions policy.

The same source said the decision reflected Tbilisi’s willingness to meet the EU’s requirements, which became apparent during discussions over sanctions related to the port.

This means that if the Kulevi refinery continues processing Russian oil over the next six months, it will become subject to EU sanctions. The refinery’s owner, Black Sea Petroleum, announced on 1 July 2026 that it would begin full-scale processing of non-Russian crude from August or September.

According to Georgia’s National Statistics Office, domestic exports rose sharply in January 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, driven largely by exports of petroleum products.

Petroleum and petroleum products ranked as Georgia’s second-largest export category in January 2026, with exports worth $58.7 million, accounting for 12.2% of the country’s total exports.

Cryptocurrency platforms added to the sanctions list

The EU has imposed transaction bans on 14 cryptocurrency platforms based in Georgia, Panama, the United Arab Emirates, Kyrgyzstan, Belarus and the Marshall Islands.

For the first time, the EU has introduced a mechanism allowing it to impose a complete ban on transactions between EU companies and cryptocurrency platforms that help Russia circumvent sanctions.

The measure also applies to crypto service providers operating in third countries if they facilitate activities that serve Russian interests.

What does the inclusion of Georgian companies in the sanctions package mean for Georgia?

The inclusion of the Kulevi refinery in the EU’s 21st sanctions package has already sparked debate in Georgia.

“The EU’s 21st sanctions package is a national disgrace: Georgian assets are being used as cannon fodder for Russia’s war machine. By allowing the Kremlin to circumvent sanctions, those in power are betraying our sovereignty. Georgia’s place is in Europe — we will never become a loophole for Russian aggression,” Georgia’s fifth president, Salome Zourabichvili, wrote on X.

Analyst Lela Djedjelava said sanctions against such an important economic asset would have an impact on the Georgian economy.

“The consequences will become increasingly visible over time. The reality is that the Kulevi refinery is probably not the only facility that could be exposed for cooperating with Russia. If other businesses in Georgia are also hit by sanctions, it will naturally have a very negative impact on the country.”

Gedevan Popkhadze, one of the leaders of the opposition Coalition for Change, said the EU sanctions against the Kulevi refinery were the result of the Georgian government’s inaction.

“If you are not helping Ukraine, why are you helping Russia? If you do not want war, why are you acting in favour of one of the parties to the conflict? We must clearly understand that these sanctions are not a message to the Kulevi refinery itself — they are a message to Georgia’s de facto government. It should realise that claiming to be neutral is hypocrisy.”

Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

World.title: Man fined $31k after botched smuggling attempt kills 55 reptiles
World.content:
A New South Wales man has been fined more than $30,000 for a bid to smuggle reptiles out of Western Australia that killed almost all of the animals.

Northam Magistrates Court heard Nicholas Thomas Havet, 28, travelled to Western Australia twice in 2023, where he captured reptiles and attempted to mail them home to NSW.

Two parcels intercepted by Australia Post at Perth Airport contained 65 animals, including bobtail lizards, ornate crevice dragons, thorny devils, western blue tongue lizards, geckos and variegated dtella.

Four of the reptiles were deceased, and a further 51 were euthanised due to their poor condition.

The haul of lizards Havet was trying to smuggle included blue tongues, like the one pictured here. (ABC Wimmera: Andrew Kelso/ File)

The remaining 10 reptiles were rehomed.

Prosecutors said Havet's motive was financial gain, with the lizards' value on the black market estimated to be between $65,000 and $1.3 million.

The 28-year-old did not appear in court for either his sentencing or a hearing in July where he was found guilty in absentia of six charges of exporting fauna without lawful authority.

Havet had travelled to WA on two occasions, collecting reptiles to smuggle to NSW. (Supplied: DBCA)

Smuggler travelled around WA

Prosecutors told that hearing Havet had travelled to WA on two occasions between March and April in 2023, renting a vehicle in Perth before travelling to the state's north west.

He was captured on CCTV purchasing two parcels from a post office in Narembeen, 290 kilometres east of Perth, before lodging the parcels containing the lizards in Merredin, 70km away.

Prosecutors say Havet's motive was profit, with the lizards worth significant amounts on the black market. (Supplied: Parks and Wildlife/ File)

The court heard Mr Havet was in WA for four days before he was apprehended at the Port Hedland Post Office, an additional 1,500km north, while waiting for a delivery.

A search of his vehicle located plastic containers with holes drilled in them, an endoscope camera and two mobile phones.

The court heard Havet had previously lodged five parcels suspected to contain lizards that were successfully delivered.

Havet was found guilty of sending fauna without legal authority. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

During sentencing, Magistrate Sarah Wisbey told the court Havet exposed the reptiles to "cruel and inhumane treatment" and was running an "illegal operation for profit".

Havet was fined a total of $31,000, with each of the six charges carrying a maximum penalty of $50,000.

World.title: Judge finds woman drove for 25 seconds with impaired vision before fatal crash
World.content:
A Canberra woman who fatally struck a motorcyclist after driving into oncoming traffic has avoided jail, with a judge finding imprisonment would "pile trauma upon trauma" for her family.

Earlier this year, an ACT Supreme Court jury found Julie Elizabeth Fallon guilty of culpable driving causing the death of 55-year-old Simon Smith in May 2024.

The 54-year-old sobbed as Chief Justice Lucy McCallum sentenced her to three years' imprisonment, to be served in the community under an Intensive Corrections Order.

Fallon was driving a red Mitsubishi Outlander when she veered across double white lines into oncoming traffic, hitting Mr Smith as he was riding to work on Athllon Drive.

Dash-cam footage played to the court captured her swerving in front of another car before hitting Mr Smith's motorbike.

He died in hospital two days later.

Canberra motorcyclist Simon Smith, 55, died in hospital two days after being hit by Julie Fallon as he was riding to work on Athllon Drive. (Supplied)

Visibility impaired for 25 seconds

A key issue during the trial was whether fog and morning sunlight impaired Fallon's vision, and whether she had looked away from the road moments before the crash.

In delivering her sentence, Chief Justice McCallum found a combination of fog on the inside of the windscreen and early morning sun shining directly into Fallon's eyes meant she was unable to properly see the road.

Justice McCallum found Fallon's vision was impaired for about 25 seconds, while she travelled about 240 metres before failing to negotiate a bend.

She also found Fallon had then turned her head to the left "for a reason unknown", saying she had "compounded the danger of continuing to drive".

"The importance of a driver always keeping their eyes on the road ahead while moving forward is obvious," Chief Justice McCallum said.

While she accepted Fallon had not knowingly or deliberately taken the risk, she found her manner of driving "involved a substantial risk of catastrophic outcome".

Chief Justice McCallum said Fallon had become "unduly preoccupied" while driving, and had "wholly failed to heed or comprehend the risk" by continuing to drive with limited visibility.

"Every time we get behind the wheel of a car we're in charge of a lethal weapon," she said.

Sentence to be served in the community

Chief Justice Lucy McCallum found imprisoning Julie Fallon would pile trauma on her family, but would not improve community safety. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

During the sentencing hearing, Fallon was removed from the courtroom after becoming distressed during victim impact statements.

She watched the remainder of the proceedings via audio-visual link, where she was seen rocking back and forth and turning away.

Chief Justice McCallum said it was regrettable Fallon had not heard the "gracious sentiments" expressed by some of Mr Smith's loved ones, but found her presentation was consistent with symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder rather than a lack of remorse.

The chief justice said the victim impact statements had raised broader issues she wanted to acknowledge, including the distress experienced by members of Mr Smith's chosen family.

She noted the distress they experienced while navigating the health system after the crash, and the pain caused by Fallon's decision to plead not guilty.

'A truly kind, decent and honourable man'

In handing down the sentence, Chief Justice McCallum said she hoped it would not be perceived as "a failure to recognise the value of the life taken from Mr Simon Smith".

She described him as "by all accounts a truly kind, decent and honourable man who meant everything to his close friends".

Chief Justice McCallum found imprisoning Fallon would "pile trauma upon trauma" for her family, without better protecting the community.

As part of the Intensive Corrections Order, Fallon was also ordered to complete 300 hours of community service, abstain from consuming alcohol, and has been disqualified from driving for at least 12 months.

World.title: 'Hear the boys crying': Men abused by Christian Brothers reveal fresh horrors
World.content:
James Peat and Chris Thorpe carried their pain for decades. Pain borne from alleged sexual abuse when they were children at schools run by Christian Brothers.

Warning: This story contains details of abuse that readers may find disturbing.

The pair, who are both seeking compensation, said they felt like they had been abused all over again, when their cases were put on hold earlier this month after the Catholic order announced it was going broke.

Victims of historic abuse are estimated to be owed around $774 million.

"I can't sleep at night and I've done nothing wrong," Mr Peat said.

"Shame on you."

James Peat says he was sexually assaulted between 1989 and 1991 at St Michael's Regional High School. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

The Christian Brothers's financial collapse follows the transfer of more than 30 schools, now worth an estimated $2 billion, to another entity associated with the Catholic Church called Edmund Rice Education Australia (EREA).

Most of those schools were gifted or transferred for $1, including St Kevin's College in Melbourne, which has a current site value of $46 million, and Christian Brothers College in Adelaide, valued at $20 million.

"Doesn't sound Christian to me," Mr Thorpe told 7.30

Chris Thorpe had reached a settlement with Christian Brothers but is yet to receive the money. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

Christian Brothers said it requested funding from the broader Catholic Church, but initially none had been provided.

The order proposed selling assets to help fund outstanding payments to abuse victims.

After mounting pressure, on Friday, Edmund Rice Education Australia announced it would pick up the abuse liabilities on behalf of Christian Brothers.

"We are committed to supporting those who have suffered abuse", EREA said in a statement.

"We are seeking to provide reassurance that we will step in to address future funding shortfalls."

However, Mr Peat said the damage had already been done.

"It's a good outcome but they were strong-armed into it. Why not do the right thing in the first place?" Mr Peat said.

Mr Thorpe is still sceptical.

"What do they say? The cheque's in the mail. So we'll wait and see," he said.

" Forgiveness, I thought about that, but I'm a long way from it at the moment. "

Convicted abuser watched the boys shower

Before the statement from EREA, 7.30 went to Wagga Wagga, in regional NSW, to meet with Mr Peat.

St Michael's Cathedral, in Wagga Wagga, NSW. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

Mr Peat alleges he was sexually abused as a student at Wagga's St Michael's Regional High School.

"What I'm feeling now has been 30 years inside bottled up," he told 7.30.

Mr Peat says the incidents occurred in 1989 when gymnastics teacher Chris Frost allegedly touched him while he stretched and watched as he showered.

"You knew it was seductively touching … and yeah, getting watched having showers was inappropriate," Mr Peat said.

"He just stood at the end. First couple of times … I feel uncomfortable, like I'm a child, and then it was just all the time, and it was just the norm.

When 7.30 visited St Michael's Cathedral the lights were on inside. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

"I would've been 15 or something."

In March this year, Frost was sentenced to three years' jail for the historic sexual abuse of students.

Mr Peat said he had been in denial for much of his adult life about what happened at St Michael's and that destructive behaviour saw him land in trouble with the law and the end of his marriage.

"I got very addicted to painkillers, alcohol and speed, and I used to use phenergans and marijuana to come down off of them and maintain a normal life," he said.

"I ended up in the Wagga police station punching on with a handful of coppers, getting maced and tasered and admitted to the acute ward."

Only now is he coming to grips with his past after a phone call from a friend.

James Peat says he has struggled with what he alleges happened to him at St Michael's Regional High School for much of his adult life. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

"He said, 'I know you were groomed like I was'," Mr Peat said.

" When he told me, I could f***ing breathe. "

Following the conviction of Frost, Mr Peat decided to seek compensation from the Church and Christian Brothers, which ran St Michael's.

He is relieved survivors will be compensated by Edmund Rice Education Australia, but said the Church had breached his trust again.

"It's not about the money. It's just my moving on and getting help," he said.

'Hear the boys crying'

Mr Thorpe had reached a settlement agreement with Christian Brothers in April but told 7.30 the past month had taken a heavy toll and even the EREA announcement hadn't helped much.

Convicted paedophile Edward Dowlan was a dorm master at St Patrick's College in Ballarat. (ABC Ballarat: Rochelle Kirkham )

"It shouldn't have come to this," he told 7.30.

"It caused a lot of anxiety, like not sleeping well now, reliving all that again."

In 1974 Mr Thorpe was 13 and a boarder at St Patrick's College in Ballarat. His dorm master was Edward Dowlan, who has subsequently been convicted and jailed for six years for sexually abusing boys at various Christian Brothers schools across Victoria.

"He [Dowlan] took a shining to me," Mr Thorpe recalls of his time at St Patrick's.

"He would walk around the dormitories at night and you could hear the boys crying sometimes.

"He came to my bed one night, and I don't want to go into all the nitty-gritty, but I knew what was going on."

Mr Thorpe fled St Patrick's soon after with a friend.

The transfer of assets from Christian Brothers to EREA came under scrutiny. (ABC News: Angelique Donnellan)

"We put the pillows in the bed while Brother Dowlan was asleep and my friend and I ran off to the train station," he recalled.

Mr Thorpe said he was speaking out against Christian Brothers to honour his friend, who has since died.

"I don't really want to be sitting here talking about this," he said.

"My friend who I ran away with, he would have loved to have done this, but he's not around anymore. So I do it for him and all the other boys that Dowlan had his little way with."

Survivors 'seeking closure'

EREA said its proposed scheme to compensate victims would have to be put to creditors for Christian Brothers and it would be at least six to eight weeks before a vote, and then court approval on the "complex arrangements".

The headquarters of Edmund Rice Education in Melbourne. (ABC News: Angelique Donnellan)

"The Trustees of EREA are committed to ensuring this occurs as expeditiously as possible," the statement said.

Christian Brothers said it had paid out more than $480 million in compensation and legal costs since 1980.

Mr Peat's lawyer, Lisa Flynn, said claims accelerated after the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, which began in 2013, with about 337 currently on foot against Christian Brothers nationwide.

"So nearly a quarter of the brothers over a period of time had credible findings of child sexual abuse against them. This abuse was horrific. It affected so many children," she told 7.30.

Ms Flynn said the asset transfer to EREA started in 2013, at around the same time as the landmark inquiry began.

"They were transferred for very nominal amounts in terms of either zero or a dollar or some other very small amount," she said.

Lawyer Lisa Flynn has questioned the timing of the transfer of assets from Christian Brothers to EREA. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

An EREA spokesperson told 7.30 in a statement that: "Christian Brothers asset transfers to EREA were done solely for the advancement of the educational mission of the schools.

"In 2007, EREA was established as a separate entity and it was entrusted with responsibility for governing, operating and stewarding the schools.

"As part of the process, the school assets were transferred from the Christian Brothers Oceania Province to EREA, together with the associated school property.

"The transfer has occurred progressively over the years since 2007 due to the complexity of transferring individual titles across multiple jurisdictions."

EREA's acceptance of abuse liabilities heads off an unprecedented courtroom clash with lawyers for victims.

A test case had been set to play out in Victoria's Supreme Court to have the Trustees of EREA named as a proper defendant, meaning the entity could be pursued over survivors claims. EREA has now accepted being a defendant.

For the victims, though, the uncertainty has been difficult to deal with and they still want accountability.

Mr Peat now lives alone and has been feeling isolated.

"It would [be] good for them to be accountable for what they've done. Who knows what people have gone through in the interim," he said.

Under the EREA agreement, Mr Thorpe should now receive his settlement, but he is still seeking closure.

"I would like to speak to one of the brothers. I would still personally like a brother to come and apologise and look at them eye-to-eye," he said.

World.title: Ousted committee to be reinstated under National Trust of SA deal
World.content:
The National Trust of South Australia (NTSA) says a deal has been struck to end an ongoing dispute with one of its regional branches, allowing popular historical sites to fully reopen to the public.

Tensions between the NTSA and its Moonta branch boiled over in February when the charity stood down its local volunteer governing committee from managing the Moonta Mines Heritage Precinct.



At the time, NTSA alleged the volunteers had breached work health and safety protocols and took over management directly.

The committee members, who said the accusations were exaggerated and they were not given procedural fairness, launched a Supreme Court action to be reinstated in May.

In a statement, NTSA's chief executive Nicolette Di Lernia said both parties had come to an agreement to start mediation but the local branch committee would be required to "discontinue legal action".

She said the NTSA was looking forward to the mediation.

Nicolette Di Lernia says the NTSA is pleased to have reached a deal with the Moonta branch. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

"We are pleased to have reached an agreement with the Moonta branch committee that will see committee members reinstated," Ms Di Lernia said.

"Mediation enables both parties to work to ensure the NTSA is meeting the responsibilities we hold for the entire organisation."

Ms Di Lernia said the museum, the sweet shop, institute building and railway would be progressively reopened after the February closures.

The NTSA says Moonta heritage attractions including the sweet shop will progressively open. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

James Levinson of HWLE Lawyers, which took on the case pro bono for the committee, said the reinstatement of the committee could not have come soon enough.

"Keeping these sites open means so much to the eight committee members, the hundreds of volunteers, and the Moonta community," he said.

"The committee members are so relieved that this saga is nearly over. They can't wait to get things up and running again."

The NTSA is a not-for-profit organisation, which conserves, manages and promotes more than 100 heritage sites across the state, including at Moonta which is home to the 19th-century Cornish Mines.

World.title: Men jailed for life after filming murder victim's 'suffering' and 'humiliation'
World.content:
Two men have been jailed for life for the murder of Alice Springs teenager Yiel Deng Gatluak after a court found their actions in a video recording "his suffering and other acts of humiliation" magnified the gravity of the crime.

Warning: This article contains content that some readers may find distressing.

Mr Gatluak, 19, was found dead on Undoolya Road, about 10 kilometres east of Alice Springs, on New Year's Day in 2024.

In May this year, after more than five weeks of evidence, a Northern Territory Supreme Court jury found 25-year-old Koang Wuordol and Guandong Guandong, 24, guilty of his murder.

Koang Wuordol will spend at least 20 years in prison under the NT's mandatory sentencing laws after being convicted of the murder of Yiel Deng Gatluak. (ABC News: Charmayne Allison)

Their co-accused, who was 17 at the time and cannot be named for legal reasons, was found not guilty of murder and manslaughter, but guilty of the lesser alternative offence of committing a violent act causing death.

Today, Justice Jenny Blokland sentenced Wuordol and Guandong to the mandatory minimum sentence of life imprisonment, with 20-year non-parole periods.

The teenage offender was sentenced to four years' imprisonment, but had the balance suspended after already serving more than two-and-a-half years in custody.

Despite the jury's verdict, Justice Blokland said there were still several unanswered questions in the case, including why the offenders attacked Mr Gatluak.

Yiel Deng Gatluak was found dead on Undoolya Road, about 10 kilometres east of Alice Springs, on New Year's Day in 2024. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"Very little has been put forward, either in the trial or in sentencing proceedings, that explains why each of the offenders offended in this way," she said.

" There was never an intention to kill, but there was an intention on the part of Koang Wuordol and Guandong Guandong to inflict serious harm. "

Footage 'brutal', 'ugly' and 'distressing'

The court heard Mr Gatluak was assaulted after being driven to Undoolya Road in a Ford Ranger in the early hours of New Year's Day.

During the trial, jurors were shown video capturing parts of what happened there, which Justice Blokland described as "brutal", "ugly" and "distressing" to watch.

She said Wuordol inflicted most of the violence as Guandong filmed the attack while making "disturbing commentary", and that one or more of the offenders urinated on or near Mr Gatluak's body as he lay on the road.

Jenny Blokland found Guandong's moral culpability was lower than Wuordol's because Guandong inflicted less physical harm, but only "marginally so". (ABC News: Michael Donnelly)

"The conduct depicted is callous and cruel," she said.

"Taking the deceased to a remote place in the darkness, being left vulnerable and unconscious, putting his phone out of reach, videoing the assaults, his suffering and other acts of humiliation magnify the gravity of the offending beyond just consideration of the assaults themselves," she said.

Justice Blokland said Mr Gatluak likely survived for several hours after the beating, but his brain function would have deteriorated and he was unlikely to have been capable of meaningful movement.

Family's grief 'never ending'

The court received victim impact statements from Mr Gatluak's family, who detailed the profound impact of his death.

Justice Blokland said Mr Gatluak's father, Deng Gatluak, described his son as a young man with "great potential, dreams and ambitions" and the court heard he was hard-working, involved in his church and focused on building a successful future.

"The impacts of grief and loss on his family are never-ending," she said.

" The family and broader community have lost the presence, the energy and talents of a young man who had all of his life ahead of him. "

In their victim impact statements, Mr Gatluak's siblings and other relatives said the pain remained "as fresh as the day it happened".

Yiel Gatluak's body was found on an access road to Undoolya Station, east of Alice Springs on New Year's Day 2024. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"This is not a loss that has lessened with time," they said.

"It is ongoing and deeply felt in our everyday lives."

Teenage offender 'remorseful'

Justice Blokland found Guandong's moral culpability was lower than Wuordol's because Guandong inflicted less physical harm, but only "marginally so".

She said Guandong also had no serious criminal history and appeared to have good prospects for rehabilitation, but the NT's mandatory sentencing laws required both men to be sentenced to life in prison.

She described that outcome as sad in Guandong's case, citing his young age and that he had rarely faced court before being tried for murder.

Justice Blokland said the teenage co-offender was in a different position to the two men convicted of murder.

Two men guilty of Alice Springs teenager's murder Two men have been found guilty of murdering 19-year-old Yiel Deng Gatluak in Alice Springs, while their teenage co-accused has been found guilty of the lesser offence of violent act causing death.

The jury found him not guilty of murder and manslaughter, but guilty of committing a violent act causing death, meaning the mandatory life minimum did not apply to him.

She said his direct involvement was at the lower end compared with the other two offenders, but he had still assaulted Mr Gatluak in circumstances where he knew he was injured and would be left without help in an isolated area.

Justice Blokland said significant weight had to be given to rehabilitation because he was 17 at the time, had offered to plead guilty to manslaughter, wrote a letter of apology and had shown remorse.

"It is often difficult to assess remorse, but having regard to his earlier offers to plead, his letter of apology and the assessment of the author of the pre-sentence report, I do find he is remorseful," she said.

The 17-year-old's suspended sentence includes an 18-month operational period, with conditions including supervision, weekly reporting, drug testing if directed, and possible electronic monitoring and curfew requirements.

World.title: Video shows croc appearing to follow group at infamous Cahills Crossing
World.content:
A close encounter between a large saltwater crocodile and a group of people at an infamous Top End river crossing has prompted renewed warnings for visitors to the area to be vigilant.

A video filmed on Friday at Cahills Crossing in Kakadu National Park shows the crocodile swimming directly towards a family, including three young children, standing near the water's edge.

The crocodile then swims parallel to them as they move away, before stopping just metres from the causeway.

Cahills Crossing is a popular spot for viewing crocodiles in the Top End. (Supplied: @tristans_gone_filming)

Crocodile expert Grahame Webb, who has worked with crocodiles in the NT for decades, said the saltie was likely following a nearby fisherman's lure, not the people on the water's edge.

"If the croc was coming right at the kids, trying to grab them off the bank … it would probably dive and swim right up next to them underwater," he said.

"This croc looked like it was ready to run something down, which is what they do if they're hunting something that's swimming."

Grahame Webb says visitors to Cahills Crossing should be conscious of safety and stay away from the water's edge. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

Professor Webb said despite the popularity of Cahills Crossing as a fishing and tourist location, standing on the edge of the water there was never completely safe.

"I think most parents in the Northern Territory would be herding their kids back as soon as the croc turned to head in that direction," he said.

Cahills Crossing visitors urged to be careful

Cahills Crossing is a low-level vehicle bridge across the East Alligator River in Kakadu which is well-known for its high population of crocodiles.

There have long been concerns about risky behaviour at the site, which have continued despite the construction of a $3 million viewing platform in 2022.

There are signs at Cahills Crossing warning visitors about dangerous crocodile activity in the area. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Tour guide David McMahon, whose business operates in Kakadu, told ABC Radio Darwin locals and visitors at Cahills Crossing were complacent about crocodiles "year after year".

"There's this big, beautiful viewing platform, you get a really good view of the crossing, but people insist on breaking the rules, heading down right to the edge of the water," he said.

"It's only a matter of time [until there's an attack]."

Fines could increase for Kakadu visitors who ignore crocodile risk Rangers in Kakadu could crack down on visitors who are too relaxed around crocodiles inside the national park, with recent footage showing people close to the water's edge at the notorious Cahills Crossing.

Mitch Owens, the owner of a fishing tour business in Kakadu, agreed.

" People think it's not going to happen to them, but at some stage, someone's going to be wrong about that. "

He told ABC Radio Darwin the issue was not with the management of crocodiles, but people's attitudes towards them.

"I don't think you can do a hell of a lot more. At some point, people have just got to take some responsibility for their own actions," he said.

Professor Webb said the way the Northern Territory managed crocodiles was "treated globally as exemplary", and despite the risks the reptiles posed, there was no need for more regulation.

"We manage crocs up here in a way that's tailored to the people up here. You can't manage it how people in Canberra think about it," he said.

"The Territory is just so different than the other states, and it's something that we want to maintain. A little bit of the frontier spirit still exists up here."

Loading...

He said most tourists were aware of the risks posed by crocodiles, and the most dangerous behaviour often came from locals.

"With local people, a little bit of misadventure takes place. Tourists are far more conscious to the dangers, so that's why, given the number of crocs and the number of people, we have a very, very low rate of attacks," he said.

"We're proactive about making sure it stays like that."

World.title: Australia's most disaster-hit state to opt out of AusAlert as government hails national test a success
World.content:
Queensland Fire and Disaster Recovery Minister Ann Leahy has said the state will not be using the AusAlert system just hours after its nationwide test.

At 2pm AEST on Monday, mobile phones and devices across the country lit up and chimed as the AusAlert system test took place.

The federal government hailed the test a success despite reports of many people not receiving the alert.

Ms Leahy said the state's fire department would continue to use its existing text message alert system this bushfire season rather than AusAlert.

"We are not opposed to having the AusAlert system and a change, but it needs to be comparable to the existing system that we have," she said.

"We won't be using the AusAlert because what we saw today was a test."

Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain said during the test 94 per cent of "targeted cell towers" successfully broadcast the AusAlert test messages across the country.

This was above the National Emergency Management Agency's target, she said, and added the 6 per cent of phone towers which missed the alert were either offline for maintenance, being upgraded or were otherwise unusable.

Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain said the test was a success. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Ms Leahy said of particular concern was ensuring the system was compatible with landlines.

Ms McBain has previously said the government was looking at AusAlert's landline compatibility, but confirmed phones connected to satellite technology instead of cell towers would not receive the alert.

"We need to make sure that we keep Queenslanders safe and that's why we will be using the emergency alert system that we currently have in place because we know that does get to landlines," Ms Leahy said.

"We need the federal government to work through the testing … we need feedback from people who didn't get the AusAlert, and we know that there is an issue with landlines."

Ms Leahy said when the system would be implemented in Queensland would be a matter for negotiation between the federal and state government.

It is unclear how many phones received the alert in total, but Ms McBain declared the test "very successful".

"So the benchmark that the National Emergency Management Agency set was for 90 per cent of towers; we've reached nearly 94 per cent of towers across the country," she said.

" We've now had a successful trial and we'll continue to refine the technology in Australia and work with states and territories to make sure it is available for use for them from October onwards. "

In the aftermath of the test the ABC received more than 1,000 comments reporting its successes and issues.

Groups reported mixed results, with some describing one out of three people at a university getting the message as well as delays leading to the alarm going off 10 to 15 minutes after the test took place.

In schools teachers described the test as revealing which students had their phones in class and students huddling around their lockers to hear the sound.

Commenter Robert Everett said he connected his hearing aid to his phone through bluetooth at the time of the test.

"The nationwide test nearly blew my ear drums out," Mr Everett said.

"Far too loud."

Kim Magee and Chelsea Stillwell were visiting Sydney from America when they received the alert. (ABC News: Digby Werthmuller)

Even tourists Kim Magee and Chelsea Stillwell, visiting Australia from the US, got the alert.

"It's like an amber alert in the states … when a child goes missing, they do it," Ms Magee said.

"We've had it [alerts] for a long time," Ms Stillwell added.

Some residents in remote areas reported issues however, some getting the alert late, others not at all.

In the outback Queensland town of Longreach, 700 kilometres from the coastline, tourists Vanessa and Tom Ranken said their phones went off minutes after the test took place.

Kyle and his family live in Ethabuka, in the Simpson Desert. (ABC Western Qld: Grace Nakamura)

In the Simpson Desert, Kyle Barton said he got no alert, suggesting his reliance of satellite internet as the reason.

"I tested [my phone] to see if I could receive and send texts before the 2 o'clock send down," Mr Barton said.

"But [at 2pm], nothing happened."

Loading...

Ms McBain told Australians who did not receive an alert not to worry.

"This could be because you are not in a coverage area," she said.

"Your software was not up to date or your device was incompatible."

Residents in bushfire prone areas welcomed the alert system with NSW resident and Black Summer bushfire survivor Jenny Robb, saying the system could be "really valuable".

Brett Hitchens from Machans Beach in Cairns was impressed by the AusAlert test which he said was "clear, audible and easy to recognise".

His house was extensively flooded during the deluge brought by ex-Tropical Cyclone Jasper in December 2023 and believed a similar warning system would have helped his family make important decisions at the time.

Brett Hitchens says the AusAlert system would have been useful during the floods which damaged his house in December 2023. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

"The first warning we had was wet feet, by the time we realised what was going on, we were wading through water everywhere," he said.

"To have some sort of early warning would've been so much more useful, especially if it had some scale of severity like prepare or run for the hills."

One commenter in the bushfire prone area of Repton, NSW said many residents did not receive an AusAlert message.

"The last time we had to evacuate the RFS was forced to doorknock 300 residences due to poor mobile coverage," they said.

"This seems to be a great example of services being designed by city-based organisations who are unaware of the configuration of telecoms in regional areas where many of the most significant natural disaster risks reside."

Commenters described being startled by the alert and said it could be dangerous for people driving cars.

The National Emergency Management Agency will be conducting a "deep dive" into aspects of today's test, according to Ms McBain.

Ms McBain said AusAlert was a "far more effective and more resilient capability than we currently have in the system".

"We'll continue to work with the technology. We'll continue to work with the telco partners and our phone manufacturers to make sure that we can hit as many people as possible," she said.

Hear that siren? That was the first test of a national emergency alert Australia gets its first taste of a new nationwide emergency warning system as millions of devices across the country sound off simultaneously.

"But again, I reiterate, there is no silver bullet in emergency management communication.

"This is another tool in the tool belt for emergency service agencies to have during a natural disaster, but as always, people need to understand their local context."

An AusAlert feedback page has since gone live for the public to access.

World.title: My suburb has a strict eight-year rule but is slowly becoming more than Range Rovers and retirees
World.content:
NationalVictoriaLife in the ’burbs My suburb has a strict eight-year rule but is slowly becoming more than Range Rovers and retirees Edwina Pearse July 27, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

We moved down to the ’Ninch in early 2021, right in the middle of when the whole country was saying “unprecedented” every second sentence. In between homeschooling, panic-bought canned goods and an alarming amount of banana bread, we somehow packed up our city life and headed south. Soon after we arrived, someone casually mentioned that it takes eight years to count as a local here in Mount Martha. Five-and-a-half years on and we are still firmly on our L-plates. The first real sign that things were different came on school drop-off at the beginning of the school year. The kids did a slow sweep of the playground, then turned to me, completely baffled. “Why does everyone look the same?” We realised pretty quickly that our new local primary school was nothing like the messy, multicultural jumble we had loved and left behind in Melbourne’s inner city. According to the last census, about three‑quarters of Mount Martha’s roughly 20,000 residents were born in Australia and most speak only English at home.



The age profile tilts well into the 40s and beyond. It has long been blue-ribbon central, or to put it plainly, full of retirees, Range Rovers and golden retrievers. I often say that if reincarnation is real, I want to come back as a golden retriever on the peninsula. That is clearly the top of the evolutionary chain and the grooming budget on those fluffy blonde locks definitely exceeds my own. We did not end up in Mount Martha by accident. We spent our weekends zigzagging down the peninsula, trying out suburbs. My husband, being the loveable nerd he is, built detailed spreadsheets to compare postcodes. Anything up to Mornington felt too much like an outer suburb of Melbourne, definitely convenient, often lovely but still in the city’s orbit. Closer to the pointy end of the peninsula, places like Dromana and Rosebud have their charms but felt busier, with more of a holiday than home vibe. Mount Martha still feels like a place with edges, even if there is not a lot of edginess. Some streets are still half-dirt, the shops are more practical than pretty and the Nepean Highway acts like a moat, stopping the sprawl from turning us into something bigger and blander. You are close enough to be back in Melbourne in “about an hour”, depending entirely on whether Peninsula Link is behaving or auditioning as a car park, but far enough that the city feels like somewhere you visit. I have even heard myself calling it “the big smoke”.



You can feel the place changing. Young families are moving in and bringing new energy and different worldviews with them. The once firmly blue political dial has started to twitch, a small sign that “stale, pale and male” thinking belongs to yesterday’s peninsula. The shift is slow (some would say glacial) but you can feel it in the school gate chatter, in community groups and in the odd rainbow flag appearing in shop windows at the local village. Yes, we still call it a village. Most nights, my husband and I end up indulging in the suburb’s favourite spectator sport, reading the Mount Martha Grapevine. It is the local Facebook page that leaves us despairing and laughing in equal measure. Forget Netflix, nothing beats the drama of a 200-comment argument about potholes, parking or an unleashed oodle on South Beach. We call it “pillow talk for peninsula people”. If you scratch the surface of a pothole thread, you often find something else underneath: anxiety about growth, outsiders and what this place is turning into. Before it became a full-time suburb, Mount Martha was mostly a summer bolthole for wealthy city-folk and a scattering of fishermen and farmers. Grand old guesthouses took pride of place on the hill, and the more modest shacks appeared nearer to the sand. Walk through the streets now, and you can see the town’s evolution in real time. Hamptons-style new builds sit beside weathered ’70s beach houses, like influencers brunching with their parents. Freshly painted weatherboards share fences with old fibro cottages and somehow it all still works.



Summer brings its own buzzy soundtrack. Every weekend, the steady mosquito-like whine of jet skis competes with the cicadas. By February, once the holiday hordes have retreated up the highway, Mount Martha exhales again. The sleepy rhythm comes back and it is all slower mornings, shorter queues and a bit of actual stillness. Related Article Opinion

Life in the ’burbs Can you guess Melbourne’s smallest, poshest or smelliest suburbs? Explore our interactive map Damien Nowicki Deputy Opinion Editor, The Age The beach feels like it belongs to locals again. On any given day you might share the water with dolphins, seals or stingrays. The water turns glassy, the sand is a mix of pretty and gritty (be careful not to step on a pufferfish) and the whole scene feels pretty darn dreamy. The kids roam free in a way that feels almost retro, like the 1980s but with more expensive mullets and an electric scooter. On a Saturday night, you see them hanging out at, behind and on top of the beach boxes that line the sand, a modern-day version of Puberty Blues. You might also find them gathering at the Pillars, although the much-loved spot is now so Insta-famous that it can be hard to find a place on the rocks to laze away a warm day. Now and then the suburb’s bubble of calm gets pricked. There was a time recently that Liam Gallagher rented a place for a short stint and the entire suburb behaved like a neighbourhood watch group for Britpop. Middle-aged men started appearing in adidas jackets and bucket hats while buying vanilla ice cream at the IGA, all hoping to chance a run-in with their hero.



The move has not been entirely idyllic. The drive home from the MCG on a Thursday night can feel very long, especially if Carlton lose. On the upside, our local footy oval has a Jacob Weitering wing, which puts a smile on the face of this Blues tragic. There are moments I miss the city, but every time I wake to the sun hitting the bay and I grab a coffee at Cibo (which is better than any city laneway cafe and, in my completely biased opinion, good enough to rival Rome) I remember why we came. Among the salt air and the suburban squabbles we have found a community that feels like ours, in the way we know our neighbours’ names, we cannot get fish ‘n’ chips without happily running into three people we know (including the teens behind the counter), and help is always on hand if we ever find ourselves in a pickle like a flat tyre or locking ourselves out. Eight years might make you a local, but even after five we feel at home and on winter mornings, when the sea wolves (the women who swim year-round) charge out of the bay laughing, it feels like the truest version of the place, slightly ridiculous, a little privileged and tougher and warmer than it first appears. Edwina Pearse is a communications consultant.

World.title: I lied about my kids’ screen time. But I don’t feel guilty about it
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessParenting Opinion I lied about my kids’ screen time. But I don’t feel guilty about it Sarah Berry Lifestyle Health Editor July 27, 2026 — 7:00pm

July 27, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Screens are the devil, or so says a teacher I know who attributes rising behavioural problems in her classroom to the increased time kids are spending on screens at home. The issue, she hypothesises, is that they are being babysat – from the time they are babies – by screens. It means they never learn to regulate their own emotions because any time they are bored, frustrated or distressed the parent distracts them with a device. By the time they arrive in kindergarten, they have no self-regulation skills to cope IRL. She’s not wrong. Only one in four Australian children meet the screen guidelines. Getty Images





If we’re being honest, the number of kids exceeding the guidelines is probably way more. That’s because there are parents, like me, who fudge their response, suspecting they’ll be judged for telling the truth. The technical term for it is social desirability bias – the tendency to alter the “truth” on self-report forms to avoid negative judgment – and it’s very common. So when the “getting to know your child” form came through to me from my children’s school, with a question about total screen time each day, I lied. I answered, one hour when the truth at the time was more like 2½. But here’s the thing: I used to feel guilty about it, and now I don’t.



This is why: guidelines can be blunt instruments, recommending the same thing across a population, regardless of individual behaviours or circumstances. As parents, we’re often judged harshly by what we do (or don’t) do. Sometimes we just have to make our own judgment calls and “let it go”, as the saying went on the movie my daughters watched on repeat possibly before the age of two. That is because context matters. Content and context both matter as much as time spent on screens. iStock A key issue with screen use is that it tends to displace physical activity, regular and good-quality sleep, as well as face-to-face social interactions with parents and peers, where children learn how to interact and how to self-regulate.



Thirty per cent of two- to five-year-olds and 60 per cent of five- to 17-year-olds use screen-based devices in the hour before they go to bed, often leading to sleep issues and then drowsiness the next day. My kids are highly active – they spend a lot of time with friends and with us, together as a family. We turn off screens 1½ hours before bedtime on school nights and don’t use screens to calm them down when they are distressed. Sometimes they watch too much because they are cooked at the end of a long day. Sometimes it’s because they have two working parents who need to prepare meals, clean and eat food themselves. They eat dinner in front of the telly more often than I’d like to admit. But, just as often, they watch movies or play Nintendo with us. Longitudinal studies have found total screen time is associated with a lower quality of life, but watching TV and gaming with your parents led to a better quality of life.



Related Article Opinion

Meta Parents like me are cheering these Facebook verdicts. But it’s not all good news David French Columnist That said, there have been recalibrations in our household as we try to find a balance that works. When we notice screens creeping into our lives too much, we dial it back. And we largely banned the crack on YouTube, putting a parental pin lock on the platform and restricting time to a 15-minute burst while I do their hair in the morning or to shows where they learn something, such as ArtsHub. Because the content matters as much as the time spent on screens. Violent content, brain-numbing content and heavy use of electronic games have a far more deleterious impact on socioemotional health than other types. Online games do not stop when they log out, compelling kids to keep playing. Also, if they see their gaming avatar as an extension of themselves and use it to compensate for their perceived deficiencies (a lack of physical strength, beauty or social status, for example), it can become a significant risk to their socioemotional wellbeing.



So, yes, screens can be highly problematic. And yes, my kids sometimes have too much screen time. But context and content matters. So I’ve stopped bothering with guilt. “Screen time is only one measure, and we seem to have become fixated on it,” says Associate Professor Joanne Orlando, a digital wellbeing expert. A better measure to consider is what kids are doing when they’re using a screen, she says. That means choosing content that focuses on problem-solving, being creative or learning something new. “These are fun but put a kid’s brain to work. I call it hard fun,” says Orlando, who recommends Sago Mini World for younger children and Procreate for older kids. “The bottom line is if your child has lots of time not on a screen, plays with toys and sport, has a good imagination and good social skills, then that’s probably OK.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: My suburb has a strict eight-year rule but is slowly becoming more than Range Rovers and retirees
World.content:
NationalVictoriaLife in the ’burbs My suburb has a strict eight-year rule but is slowly becoming more than Range Rovers and retirees Edwina Pearse July 27, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

We moved down to the ’Ninch in early 2021, right in the middle of when the whole country was saying “unprecedented” every second sentence. In between homeschooling, panic-bought canned goods and an alarming amount of banana bread, we somehow packed up our city life and headed south. Soon after we arrived, someone casually mentioned that it takes eight years to count as a local here in Mount Martha. Five-and-a-half years on and we are still firmly on our L-plates. The first real sign that things were different came on school drop-off at the beginning of the school year. The kids did a slow sweep of the playground, then turned to me, completely baffled. “Why does everyone look the same?” We realised pretty quickly that our new local primary school was nothing like the messy, multicultural jumble we had loved and left behind in Melbourne’s inner city. According to the last census, about three‑quarters of Mount Martha’s roughly 20,000 residents were born in Australia and most speak only English at home.



The age profile tilts well into the 40s and beyond. It has long been blue-ribbon central, or to put it plainly, full of retirees, Range Rovers and golden retrievers. I often say that if reincarnation is real, I want to come back as a golden retriever on the peninsula. That is clearly the top of the evolutionary chain and the grooming budget on those fluffy blonde locks definitely exceeds my own. We did not end up in Mount Martha by accident. We spent our weekends zigzagging down the peninsula, trying out suburbs. My husband, being the loveable nerd he is, built detailed spreadsheets to compare postcodes. Anything up to Mornington felt too much like an outer suburb of Melbourne, definitely convenient, often lovely but still in the city’s orbit. Closer to the pointy end of the peninsula, places like Dromana and Rosebud have their charms but felt busier, with more of a holiday than home vibe. Mount Martha still feels like a place with edges, even if there is not a lot of edginess. Some streets are still half-dirt, the shops are more practical than pretty and the Nepean Highway acts like a moat, stopping the sprawl from turning us into something bigger and blander. You are close enough to be back in Melbourne in “about an hour”, depending entirely on whether Peninsula Link is behaving or auditioning as a car park, but far enough that the city feels like somewhere you visit. I have even heard myself calling it “the big smoke”.



You can feel the place changing. Young families are moving in and bringing new energy and different worldviews with them. The once firmly blue political dial has started to twitch, a small sign that “stale, pale and male” thinking belongs to yesterday’s peninsula. The shift is slow (some would say glacial) but you can feel it in the school gate chatter, in community groups and in the odd rainbow flag appearing in shop windows at the local village. Yes, we still call it a village. Most nights, my husband and I end up indulging in the suburb’s favourite spectator sport, reading the Mount Martha Grapevine. It is the local Facebook page that leaves us despairing and laughing in equal measure. Forget Netflix, nothing beats the drama of a 200-comment argument about potholes, parking or an unleashed oodle on South Beach. We call it “pillow talk for peninsula people”. If you scratch the surface of a pothole thread, you often find something else underneath: anxiety about growth, outsiders and what this place is turning into. Before it became a full-time suburb, Mount Martha was mostly a summer bolthole for wealthy city-folk and a scattering of fishermen and farmers. Grand old guesthouses took pride of place on the hill, and the more modest shacks appeared nearer to the sand. Walk through the streets now, and you can see the town’s evolution in real time. Hamptons-style new builds sit beside weathered ’70s beach houses, like influencers brunching with their parents. Freshly painted weatherboards share fences with old fibro cottages and somehow it all still works.



Summer brings its own buzzy soundtrack. Every weekend, the steady mosquito-like whine of jet skis competes with the cicadas. By February, once the holiday hordes have retreated up the highway, Mount Martha exhales again. The sleepy rhythm comes back and it is all slower mornings, shorter queues and a bit of actual stillness. Related Article Opinion

Life in the ’burbs Can you guess Melbourne’s smallest, poshest or smelliest suburbs? Explore our interactive map Damien Nowicki Deputy Opinion Editor, The Age The beach feels like it belongs to locals again. On any given day you might share the water with dolphins, seals or stingrays. The water turns glassy, the sand is a mix of pretty and gritty (be careful not to step on a pufferfish) and the whole scene feels pretty darn dreamy. The kids roam free in a way that feels almost retro, like the 1980s but with more expensive mullets and an electric scooter. On a Saturday night, you see them hanging out at, behind and on top of the beach boxes that line the sand, a modern-day version of Puberty Blues. You might also find them gathering at the Pillars, although the much-loved spot is now so Insta-famous that it can be hard to find a place on the rocks to laze away a warm day. Now and then the suburb’s bubble of calm gets pricked. There was a time recently that Liam Gallagher rented a place for a short stint and the entire suburb behaved like a neighbourhood watch group for Britpop. Middle-aged men started appearing in adidas jackets and bucket hats while buying vanilla ice cream at the IGA, all hoping to chance a run-in with their hero.



The move has not been entirely idyllic. The drive home from the MCG on a Thursday night can feel very long, especially if Carlton lose. On the upside, our local footy oval has a Jacob Weitering wing, which puts a smile on the face of this Blues tragic. There are moments I miss the city, but every time I wake to the sun hitting the bay and I grab a coffee at Cibo (which is better than any city laneway cafe and, in my completely biased opinion, good enough to rival Rome) I remember why we came. Among the salt air and the suburban squabbles we have found a community that feels like ours, in the way we know our neighbours’ names, we cannot get fish ‘n’ chips without happily running into three people we know (including the teens behind the counter), and help is always on hand if we ever find ourselves in a pickle like a flat tyre or locking ourselves out. Eight years might make you a local, but even after five we feel at home and on winter mornings, when the sea wolves (the women who swim year-round) charge out of the bay laughing, it feels like the truest version of the place, slightly ridiculous, a little privileged and tougher and warmer than it first appears. Edwina Pearse is a communications consultant.

World.title: I lied about my kids’ screen time. But I don’t feel guilty about it
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessParenting Opinion I lied about my kids’ screen time. But I don’t feel guilty about it Sarah Berry Lifestyle Health Editor July 27, 2026 — 7:00pm

July 27, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Screens are the devil, or so says a teacher I know who attributes rising behavioural problems in her classroom to the increased time kids are spending on screens at home. The issue, she hypothesises, is that they are being babysat – from the time they are babies – by screens. It means they never learn to regulate their own emotions because any time they are bored, frustrated or distressed the parent distracts them with a device. By the time they arrive in kindergarten, they have no self-regulation skills to cope IRL. She’s not wrong. Only one in four Australian children meet the screen guidelines. Getty Images





If we’re being honest, the number of kids exceeding the guidelines is probably way more. That’s because there are parents, like me, who fudge their response, suspecting they’ll be judged for telling the truth. The technical term for it is social desirability bias – the tendency to alter the “truth” on self-report forms to avoid negative judgment – and it’s very common. So when the “getting to know your child” form came through to me from my children’s school, with a question about total screen time each day, I lied. I answered, one hour when the truth at the time was more like 2½. But here’s the thing: I used to feel guilty about it, and now I don’t.



This is why: guidelines can be blunt instruments, recommending the same thing across a population, regardless of individual behaviours or circumstances. As parents, we’re often judged harshly by what we do (or don’t) do. Sometimes we just have to make our own judgment calls and “let it go”, as the saying went on the movie my daughters watched on repeat possibly before the age of two. That is because context matters. Content and context both matter as much as time spent on screens. iStock A key issue with screen use is that it tends to displace physical activity, regular and good-quality sleep, as well as face-to-face social interactions with parents and peers, where children learn how to interact and how to self-regulate.



Thirty per cent of two- to five-year-olds and 60 per cent of five- to 17-year-olds use screen-based devices in the hour before they go to bed, often leading to sleep issues and then drowsiness the next day. My kids are highly active – they spend a lot of time with friends and with us, together as a family. We turn off screens 1½ hours before bedtime on school nights and don’t use screens to calm them down when they are distressed. Sometimes they watch too much because they are cooked at the end of a long day. Sometimes it’s because they have two working parents who need to prepare meals, clean and eat food themselves. They eat dinner in front of the telly more often than I’d like to admit. But, just as often, they watch movies or play Nintendo with us. Longitudinal studies have found total screen time is associated with a lower quality of life, but watching TV and gaming with your parents led to a better quality of life.



Related Article Opinion

Meta Parents like me are cheering these Facebook verdicts. But it’s not all good news David French Columnist That said, there have been recalibrations in our household as we try to find a balance that works. When we notice screens creeping into our lives too much, we dial it back. And we largely banned the crack on YouTube, putting a parental pin lock on the platform and restricting time to a 15-minute burst while I do their hair in the morning or to shows where they learn something, such as ArtsHub. Because the content matters as much as the time spent on screens. Violent content, brain-numbing content and heavy use of electronic games have a far more deleterious impact on socioemotional health than other types. Online games do not stop when they log out, compelling kids to keep playing. Also, if they see their gaming avatar as an extension of themselves and use it to compensate for their perceived deficiencies (a lack of physical strength, beauty or social status, for example), it can become a significant risk to their socioemotional wellbeing.



So, yes, screens can be highly problematic. And yes, my kids sometimes have too much screen time. But context and content matters. So I’ve stopped bothering with guilt. “Screen time is only one measure, and we seem to have become fixated on it,” says Associate Professor Joanne Orlando, a digital wellbeing expert. A better measure to consider is what kids are doing when they’re using a screen, she says. That means choosing content that focuses on problem-solving, being creative or learning something new. “These are fun but put a kid’s brain to work. I call it hard fun,” says Orlando, who recommends Sago Mini World for younger children and Procreate for older kids. “The bottom line is if your child has lots of time not on a screen, plays with toys and sport, has a good imagination and good social skills, then that’s probably OK.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.
